en: Source: ManuSm.txt (from Arlo Griffiths’ collection)
Manusmṛti: Typed, analyzed, and proofread by M. Yano and Y. Ikari (May–June 1991; January–April 1992; March–April 1996).

K: *Manusmṛti* with the Sanskrit commentary *Manvartha-muktāvalī* by Kullūka Bhaṭṭa, edited by J.L. Shastri, 1983 (compared with the edition of the Kashi Sanskrit Series 114 edited by Haragovinda Śāstrī).
M: *Manusmṛti* with the commentary of Medhātithi, 2 vols., Calcutta 1967;
M: *Manu-smṛti* with the “*Manubhāṣya*” of Medhātithi, edited by Nārāyaṇa Rāma Ācārya, Government of India Press, 1932, 1939, repr. 1992.

The text is based upon K, with the variants of M provided at the end of each *pāda*. There are verses found exclusively in either K or M. The discrepancy in the numbering of the *śloka*s between chapters in K and M has been noted.
Certain *saṃdhi*s have been resolved, and word-division markers such as “-” and “-” have been introduced into the text in order to facilitate the easy identification of individual word forms.
"—" indicates the resolution of an external *sandhi*; "—" indicates the word division within a compound; [M:
variants of Medhātithi’s commentary.
The difference in verse numbering between M and K is noted:
<B 1> Having approached Manu as he sat with a concentrated mind, the great seers [spoke].
Having honored him according to the prescribed rule, they spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, you ought to tell us the duties of all the social classes (varṇas) in their proper order,
as well as those born of intermediate castes."
"For you alone, O Lord, are the knower of the true purpose and the nature of the effects of this entire self-existent ordinance, which is inconceivable and immeasurable. Thus was he,
of immeasurable vigor, duly questioned by those high-souled beings.
Having honored all those great seers, he replied to them: "Listen.
In the beginning, this [universe] was enveloped in darkness—unknowable, without defining marks, beyond the reach of logic, incomprehensible, as if entirely asleep.

Then the Lord Svayambhū, the unmanifest, making this [world] manifest— his vigor consisting of the primary elements and so forth— appeared as the dispeller of darkness. He who is beyond the grasp of the senses, subtle, unmanifest, and eternal.

He alone, consisting of all beings and inconceivable, manifested himself of his own accord. Desiring to bring forth various creatures from his own body, he first meditated and emitted water; into that water, he cast his seed.
That became a golden egg, radiant like the thousand-rayed sun.
Within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds. Water is called *nara*; indeed, water is the offspring of *nara*.
Because his original abode was *nara* (the waters), he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
That which is the unmanifest cause, eternal, consisting of both being and non-being—
emanated from that, that Puruṣa is celebrated in the world as Brahmā.
Having dwelt within that egg for a full year, the Blessed One, by his own meditation, divided that egg into two parts. From those two halves,
he fashioned heaven and earth.
In the midst of the ether and the eight directions, he established the eternal abode of the waters.
From his own self, he drew forth the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
and from the mind, he drew forth the ego (ahaṃkāra), the sovereign who perceives "I am."
And [he created] the Great Self (mahān ātmā), as well as all things consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa),
and the five sense organs which gradually become the perceivers of objects; furthermore,
he created the subtle components of those six [entities] of immeasurable power.
Having placed them within their respective measures, he fashioned all beings.
Those subtle components that constitute the parts of his form—these six [elements] take up residence therein. Therefore, the wise call his form "the body" (śarīra).

The great elements, together with their functions, enter that [unmanifest], as does the mind with its subtle components— the imperishable creator of all beings. This, however, is the [result] of those seven persons of great power.
From the imperishable [Prakṛti], through subtle material constituents, the perishable [evolutes] come into being. Among these, each subsequent element acquires the quality of each preceding one;
whichever is the *n*th in this series is traditionally held to possess *n* qualities.

But he, the Lord, created in the beginning the individual names and actions of all beings, as well as their distinct social orders, from the words of the Veda alone. And that Lord created the gods, who consist of action, among living beings.
He [created] the subtle host of the Sādhyas and the eternal sacrifice.
From Agni, Vāyu, and Ravi, he milked forth the threefold eternal Brahman,
characterized by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice.
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets; the rivers, the oceans, and the mountains; the level and the uneven terrains;
austerity, speech, pleasure, desire, and anger.
Desiring to bring these creatures into existence, he emitted this entire creation;
and for the sake of distinguishing between actions, he separated right and wrong. He then joined these creatures with pairs of opposites, such as pleasure and pain.
The minute particles known as the five *mātrās*, which are subject to destruction—
along with these, all this [universe] comes into being in due succession.
And whatever action the Lord first assigned each [element] to, [that it performs].
He himself experienced that very same state as he was being created again and again.

Whatever— whether violent or non-violent, mild or cruel, dharma or adharma, truth or falsehood— he ordained for each being at the time of creation, that very quality entered into him of its own accord.
Just as the seasons, at the change of the season, themselves assume their own respective characteristics according to their seasonal signs,
so too do embodied beings perform their respective actions.
For the sake of the increase of the worlds, [the Lord] created [the four castes] from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.
He brought forth the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Having divided his own body into two, he became a male with one half;
with the other half he became a female, and in her the Lord created Virāj.

O best of the twice-born, know me to be that Virāj, the Supreme Person, whom he himself created after performing austerities; I am the creator of all this. Desiring to produce offspring, I performed most difficult austerities.
In the beginning, I created ten great seers as the lords of progeny:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas,
Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada.
Those of immense splendor created these seven Manus,
as well as the gods and their hosts, the great seers of immeasurable power,
the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, gandharvas, apsarases, and asuras.
The Nāgas, the Sarpas, the Suparṇas, and the various classes of Pitṛs;
the lightning-flashes, the thunderbolts, the clouds, and the red-hued rainbows and Indra-bows;
the meteors, the atmospheric crashes, the comets, and the various celestial luminaries.
Kinnaras, monkeys, fish, and various birds;
domestic animals, wild beasts, and humans; and those with two rows of teeth (reptiles);
as well as worms, insects, moths, lice, flies, and bugs.
And all biting and stinging insects, mosquitoes, and various kinds of stationary beings—
thus, by my command, all this world of moving and unmoving things was created by those great-souled ones according to their karma through the power of their austerity.
I shall describe to you, in due order, the specific nature of the actions of beings as proclaimed here, as well as their sequence of birth:
cattle, wild animals, and predatory beasts with two rows of teeth.
Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and humans born from the womb;
egg-born birds, serpents, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises;
and whatever other such beings there are, whether terrestrial or aquatic.
Biting insects, mosquitoes, lice, flies, and bugs are born from sweat, as are whatever other such creatures exist that arise from heat.
All stationary beings are born from sprouts; they grow from seeds or from slips.
Herbs (oṣadhī) are those that end with the ripening of their fruit and bear many flowers and fruits. Those that bear fruit without flowers are known as forest trees (vanaspati).
Trees (vṛkṣa), however, are known to possess both [flowers and fruit].

Various kinds of shrubs and thickets, as well as species of grasses, those that grow from seeds or from stems, as well as spreading creepers and climbing vines— these are all enveloped by manifold darkness, which has karma as its cause.
These [beings] possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain.
These states of existence, beginning with Brahmā, are declared to end here. In this terrible cycle of beings, which is constantly and perpetually moving, [they wander].
Having thus created all this and me as well, he of inconceivable prowess withdrew again into himself, subduing time with time. When that God is awake, then the world thus moves.

When he, whose self is tranquil, sleeps, then everything closes its eyes. But while he sleeps in his own state of well-being, the embodied beings whose nature is action cease from their respective duties, and the mind falls into exhaustion.

But when they dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self, then this Soul of all beings sleeps happily and at peace. Yet, having resorted to darkness (*tamas*), he remains for a long time together with his senses.
And when he no longer performs his own action, then he departs from the body. When, having become minute as an atom, he enters— whether it be a seed, a stationary thing, or a moving one—
he then abandons the body, being united with it.

Thus, through waking and dreaming, that Imperishable One incessantly brings to life and causes the destruction of all this world of moving and non-moving beings. Having composed this scripture himself from the very beginning, he [entrusted it] to me alone.
I caused Marīci and the other sages to receive this according to the prescribed rule: "This sage Bhṛgu shall recite this scripture to you in its entirety;
for this sage has learned all of this from me in its fullness."
Then, having been thus addressed by the great seer Manu, Bhṛgu, with a joyful soul, spoke to all those seers: "Listen! He continued:
"There are six other Manus belonging to the lineage of this Svāyambhuva Manu."
The high-souled ones of great power created their respective progeny:
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly resplendent Cākṣuṣa, and the son of Vivasvat as well.
These seven Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, possess immense splendor;
each, within his own interval (antara), produced all this world of moving and non-moving beings. Eighteen nimeṣas make one kāṣṭhā, and thirty such kāṣṭhās make one kalā.
Thirty *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*, and a day and night consist of as many [muhūrtas].
The sun divides the human and divine days and nights:
the night is for the sleep of living beings, and the day is for the performance of actions.

A month is a day and a night of the ancestors; its division consists of two fortnights. Among ritual activities, the dark fortnight is their day, and the bright fortnight is for sleep. A year is a day and a night of the gods; their division is as follows:
There, the northern course of the sun is day, and the southern course is night.
Now, learn in due order the duration of each of the Yugas, which constitutes the measure of a single day and night of Brahmā in brief.

They say that the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years; its morning twilight (saṃdhyā) lasts for as many hundreds of years, and its evening twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration. Regarding the other three ages, along with their respective twilights and the portions following the twilights:
The thousands and hundreds proceed by a decrease of one [in each age].
This cycle of four ages, which has been enumerated at the very beginning, consists of twelve thousand years; this is called a *yuga* of the gods.
A thousand cycles of the divine ages, by calculation,
should be known as one day of Brahmā, and his night is of the same duration. They know that holy day of Brahmā to end with a thousand such ages.

And those people who know day and night [reckon] his night to be of exactly the same duration. At the end of that day and night, having been asleep, he awakens; and once awakened, he creates the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.

Impelled by the desire to create, the mind undergoes transformation; from it, space is born, and they know sound to be its quality. From space, however, as it undergoes transformation, arises the pure bearer of all fragrances.
From it is born the powerful wind; that indeed is considered to have touch as its quality.
From the transforming wind, moreover, there arises the radiant light that dispels darkness;
that is said to have form as its quality.
From light, undergoing transformation, water is said to arise with the quality of taste;
from water, earth arises with the quality of smell—such is the creation from the beginning.
That which was previously described as the divine age (*yuga*) consisting of twelve thousand [years]...
That multiplied by seventy-one is here called a *manvantara*.
There are innumerable *manvantaras*, as well as creations and dissolutions;
the Supreme Lord performs these again and again, as if in play.

In the Kṛta age, Dharma was complete in all four quarters, as was Truth. No acquisition whatsoever occurred for men through unrighteousness. In the other ages, however, Dharma has been diminished by one quarter each according to the traditional accounts.
Through theft, falsehood, and deceit, righteousness (dharma) departs quarter by quarter.
In the Kṛta age, people are free from disease, have all their goals accomplished, and live for four hundred years;
however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases quarter by quarter. [In these ages, their vitality also diminishes.]

The lifespan prescribed for mortals in the Vedas, as well as the fruits of ritual actions and the powers of embodied beings, bear fruit in the world according to the respective age (yuga). The duties in the Kṛta age are of one kind, while those in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages are different.
Others [arise] for men in the Kali age in accordance with the decline of the ages: austerity is said to be supreme in the Kṛta age, knowledge in the Tretā;
they say sacrifice alone is [supreme] in the Dvāpara, and charity alone in the Kali age.
But for the protection of this entire creation, that one of great splendor ordained distinct duties for those born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet:
teaching, studying, sacrificing, and officiating at sacrifices; ||| Manu 1.87a–88a.
He ordained giving and receiving for the Brāhmaṇas.
For the Kṣatriya, he briefly prescribed the protection of subjects, giving, sacrifice, study, and non-attachment to sensual objects.
The protection of cattle, giving gifts, performing sacrifice, study, trade, money-lending, and agriculture— these are the duties of the Vaiśya. But the Lord ordained only one duty for the Śūdra.
By serving these very castes with freedom from malice,
a man is declared to be increasingly pure above the navel;
therefore, his mouth has been called the most sacred part by the Self-existent One himself.
Because he was born from the highest limb, because of his seniority, and because he maintains the Veda,
the Brāhmaṇa is by law the lord of this entire creation.
For the Self-existent One, having performed austerities, created him in the beginning from his own mouth.

For the conveyance of the *havya* (oblations to the gods) and *kavya* (oblations to the ancestors), and for the protection of all this [world]— what being could be greater than he, by whose mouth the inhabitants of heaven always eat the *havya*, and the ancestors likewise eat the *kavya*?

Among beings, those with breath are superior; among those with breath, those who live by intelligence are superior. Among the intelligent, men are superior; among men, Brāhmaṇas are traditionally held to be superior.
Among Brāhmaṇas, the learned are superior; among the learned, those whose intellects are perfected are superior.
Those who perform actions for those who have already resolved to act, and those who know Brahman for those who are performers of action—
[for them] the very birth of a Brāhmaṇa is the eternal embodiment of Dharma.
For he is born for the sake of Dharma and is destined for becoming one with Brahman.
For a Brāhmaṇa, upon being born,
is born as a sovereign on earth for the protection of the treasury of Dharma over all living beings.
Whatever exists within this world is the property of the Brāhmaṇa.
By virtue of his preeminence and noble lineage, the Brāhmaṇa indeed deserves all this.
A Brāhmaṇa eats only what is his own, he wears only what is his own, and he gives only what is his own;
for it is through the Brāhmaṇa’s compassion that other people enjoy [their possessions].
For the sake of discerning the duties of that [king], as well as those of the remaining [classes] in their proper order,
the wise Manu, son of the Self-existent, composed this treatise.
This should be studied with diligent effort by a learned Brāhmaṇa.

And this must be taught correctly to disciples by no one else. A Brāhmaṇa who studies this scripture and is firm in his vows is never tainted by the defects of actions arising from mind, speech, or body.
He purifies the row [of diners] and his lineage—seven ancestors and seven descendants—and even this entire earth; indeed, such a person alone is worthy of it.
This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect.

This [work] bestows fame and long life; this is the supreme means for attaining the highest good. In this [treatise], dharma has been declared in its entirety, as well as the merits and defects of actions, and the eternal conduct of all four social classes.
Conduct is the supreme dharma, as declared by the Śruti and the Smṛti.
Therefore, a twice-born man who possesses self-control should always be constantly devoted to it. A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda.

But one who is endowed with right conduct (ācāra) shall partake of the full fruit; he is declared to be a partaker of the complete reward. Having thus observed the course of Dharma through right conduct, the sages took right conduct to be the supreme root of all austerity.
The origin of the world and the rules for purificatory rites; the practice of vows and the procedure for the ritual bath;
the taking of a wife and the characteristics of the various forms of marriage.
The procedure for the great sacrifices, the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha),
the characteristics of the various modes of livelihood, the vows of the accomplished student (snātaka),
as well as what may and may not be eaten, purification, and the cleansing of material substances.
The duties of women, the practice of asceticism, liberation, and renunciation; the entire duty of kings and the adjudication of legal cases;
the rules for the examination of witnesses, and the law concerning men and women.
The law of partition, gambling, and the clearing away of thorns;
the conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, and the origin of mixed castes; the duties of the social orders in times of distress, as well as the rules for expiation.
The journey through the cycle of existence arising from the threefold karma,
the supreme good resulting from action, and the examination of the merits and defects of actions; as well as the eternal laws of countries, the laws of castes, and the laws of families.
In this treatise, Manu has also declared the duties of heretics and of various sects. Just as Manu formerly expounded this treatise when questioned by me, so now you too should learn it from me.
Learn that dharma which is practiced by the wise, the virtuous, and those who are always free from hatred and passion,
and which is approved by the heart.
To have desire as one's sole motive is not praised, yet here there is no such thing as being entirely free from desire;
for the acquisition of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic rituals are indeed motivated by desire.
Desire has volition as its root, and sacrifices originate from volition.
All vows and duties of self-restraint are recorded as being born of intention (*saṃkalpa*).
No action whatsoever is ever seen here in this world that is performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire.

Behaving correctly toward them, one goes to the world of the immortals and enjoys here all desires exactly as they were intended. The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛti and the conduct of those who know it.
The conduct of the virtuous and the satisfaction of one's own self [are also sources of dharma].
Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone,
all of that is declared in the Veda, for it consists of all-encompassing knowledge.
Having examined all this entirely with the eye of knowledge,

a wise man, relying on the authority of the *Śruti*, should indeed remain steadfast in his own duty (*svadharma*). For a human being who practices the dharma declared in the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti* [attains the highest goal].
In this world he attains fame, and after death, unsurpassed happiness. The Veda is to be known as Śruti, while the Dharmaśāstra is indeed Smṛti.
These two are not to be questioned in any matter, for from them Dharma has shone forth.

That twice-born man who, relying on the science of logic (*hetuśāstra*), would show contempt for its very root— the Veda— should be excluded by the virtuous as an atheist (*nāstika*) and a reviler of the Vedas. The Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the righteous, and what is pleasing to one's own self [are the sources of dharma].
They declare this fourfold [set] to be the direct definition of Dharma.
For those who are unattached to wealth and pleasure, the knowledge of Dharma is ordained;
for those desiring to know Dharma, the supreme authority is the Śruti (Revealed Scripture).
But where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are remembered as Dharma;
for both of those have been correctly declared as Dharma by the wise.
[This applies] whether the sun has risen, or has not yet risen, or when it is the time of twilight.
"In every way the sacrifice proceeds"— this is the Vedic revelation (śruti).
He for whom the rites beginning with conception and ending at the cremation ground are prescribed by means of mantras,
it should be known that he alone has the right to this scripture, and no one else whatsoever.

The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, which was created by the gods, they call Brahmāvarta. Whatever custom prevails in that land, handed down through traditional succession, [is called the conduct of the virtuous].
This is declared to be the conduct of those belonging to the intermediate castes.
Kurukṣetra, the Matsyas, the Pañcālas, and the Śūrasenakas—
this indeed is the land of the Brahman-sages, immediately adjacent to Brahmāvarta.
All men on earth should learn their respective duties from the presence of a twice-born man born in this region:
that which lies between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, and also to the east of Vinaśana.

The region between Prayāga and the western ocean is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa (the Middle Country). The wise know Āryāvarta to be the territory between those same two mountains, extending from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.

Where the black antelope roams by its very nature, that land should be known as fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas. The twice-born should diligently seek to inhabit these lands.
But a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell anywhere at all.
This origin of Dharma has been proclaimed to you in brief;
now learn its manifestation and the duties of the social classes (varṇas) for all of this.

For the twice-born, the purifying refinement of the body—beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception rite) and performed through meritorious Vedic rites—must be carried out; it is sanctifying both after death and in this world.
[This is accomplished] by oblations during pregnancy, and by the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), the tonsure (*caula*), and the tying of the girdle (*mauñjī*).
The sin pertaining to the seed and the womb of the twice-born is wiped away by the private recitation of the Veda,
by vows, by burnt offerings, by the threefold knowledge, by sacrifices, by sons,
by the great sacrifices, and by other rites; thus this body is made fit for union with Brahman.
Before the cutting of the umbilical cord, the birth-rite (jātakarma) is ordained for the male child;
it consists of the ritual feeding of him with gold, honey, and clarified butter, accompanied by sacred mantras.
On the tenth or the twelfth day, one should cause his naming ceremony (nāmadheya) to be performed.

On an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with good qualities, the name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious, that of a Kṣatriya should be connected with power,
that of a Vaiśya should be associated with wealth, while that of a Śūdra should be contemptible.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in a word denoting "shelter" (śarman); that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with a word signifying "protection" (rakṣā).
That of a Vaiśya should be connected with a word for "prosperity" (puṣṭi), and that of a Śūdra should be connected with a word for "service" (preṣya).
For women, it should be easy to pronounce, not harsh, clear in meaning, and captivating.
A name that is auspicious, ending in a long vowel, and consisting of a word of benediction [should be given].
In the fourth month, the child's first exit from the house (niṣkramaṇa) should be performed;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), or whatever auspicious rite is customary in the family.
The rite of tonsure (cūḍākarma) for all twice-born classes must, according to dharma,
be performed in the first or the third year, as enjoined by the Veda. One should perform the initiation (upanayana) of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception.
In the eleventh year from conception for a king, and in the twelfth from conception for a Vaiśya;
for a Brāhmaṇa desiring spiritual luster, it should be performed in the fifth year;
for a king seeking power, in the sixth; and for a Vaiśya seeking wealth, in the eighth.

The Sāvitrī does not pass beyond the sixteenth year for a Brāhmaṇa, nor beyond the twenty-second for a Kṣatriya, nor beyond the twenty-fourth for a Vaiśya. Beyond these times, all three of these, if not initiated at the proper time, [become fallen].

Having fallen from the Sāvitrī, they become Vratyas, despised by the Aryas. A Brāhmaṇa must never, even in times of distress, perform rites of spiritual or matrimonial alliance with those who have not been purified according to the rule.
A student of the Veda should wear, in their respective order, the skins of a black antelope, a Ruru deer, or a goat; likewise, garments made of hemp, flax, or wool.
The girdle of a Brahmin should be made of Muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth.

The bowstring of a Kṣatriya, however, should be made of muñja grass; that of a Vaiśya, of hempen threads. In the absence of muñja grass, they should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja grass, with three strands and a single knot, or with three or five knots.

The sacred thread (*upavīta*) of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward and triple-stranded; that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya of woolen threads. A Brāhmaṇa's staff should be made of Bilva or Palāśa wood, and a Kṣatriya's of Vaṭa or Khadira wood.
According to the law, a Vaiśya deserves staffs made of Pīlu or Udumbara wood. A Brāhmaṇa’s staff should be made to reach the hairline in length;
that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead, while that of a Vaiśya should reach the tip of the nose.
All those [staffs] should be straight, without blemishes, and pleasing to the sight;
they should not cause distress to men, and must have their bark intact and be undamaged by fire.
Having taken up the desired staff and having stood facing the sun, [he should perform his duties].

Having circumambulated the fire from left to right, he should go about for alms according to the prescribed rule. An initiated man of the highest twice-born class (the Brāhmaṇa) should beg for alms with the word "bhavat" at the beginning; a Kṣatriya, however, should place "bhavat" in the middle; and a Vaiśya, "bhavat" at the end.

He should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt— whichever will not treat him with contempt. Having collected that alms-food as much as is required, without guile, [he should eat it].
Having offered [the food] to his teacher, he should eat while facing the east, pure and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Facing the east, one eats for longevity; facing the south, one eats for fame;
facing the west, one eats for prosperity; and facing the north, one eats for truth.
Having sipped water, a twice-born man should always eat his food with a concentrated mind;
having eaten, he should properly sip water again and touch the cavities of the head with water. He should always honor his food and eat it without disparaging it.
Upon seeing it, he should rejoice, be gracious, and welcome it in every way. For food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor, but that which is eaten unhonored destroys both of these.

One should not give the remains of one's meal to anyone, nor should one eat between [meals]. One should never overeat, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from eating. Overeating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to the attainment of heaven.
That which is meritless and loathed by the world—one should therefore avoid it entirely.
A Brāhmaṇa should always perform his ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha;
he may also use the Kāya or Traidaśika tīrthas, but never the Pitrya.
They declare that the *brāhma* tīrtha is at the base of the thumb;
the *kāya* tīrtha is at the roots of the fingers, the *daiva* at their tips, and the *pitrya* below those two.
One should first sip water three times, and then wipe the mouth twice.

One who knows the Dharma, desiring purity, should always sip water in a secluded place while facing either the east or the north, using the proper part of the hand (tīrtha), with water that is neither hot nor frothy. He should touch the apertures of the body, as well as himself and his head, with water. (Manu 2.60c–61)
A Brahmin is purified by water that reaches the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat;
a Vaiśya, by water that has been sipped; and a Śūdra, by water merely touched at the extremity.
When the right hand is raised, the twice-born is said to be "wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder" (upavītī).
Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he should wear it around the neck (nivītī).
Having cast into the water the girdle, the skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread,
and the water-pot when they are worn out, he should take others with the appropriate mantras.
The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya, it is in the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya, it is considered to be two years later than that.
This entire sequence of rites for women, however, should be performed without the recitation of mantras.
For the sake of purifying the body, according to the proper time and sequence,
the marriage rite is recorded as the Vedic sacrament for women;
serving the husband is their residence with the guru, and the maintenance of the sacred fires is their domestic duty.

This rule for the initiation of the twice-born has been declared, which is meritorious and manifests their true birth; now learn the application of their duties. Having initiated the pupil, the teacher shall first instruct him in the rules of purification.

[He should teach] proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and the worship of the twilights. But one who is about to study— having sipped water according to the scriptures, facing north, with palms joined in the *brahmāñjali*, wearing light clothing, and having conquered his senses— should be taught.
At the beginning and at the conclusion of Vedic study, one should always grasp the feet of the teacher. Having joined the hands together, one should study; for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*.
The clasping of the teacher’s feet should be performed with crossed hands.

The left [hand] should be touched with the left [hand], and the right [hand] with the right. When about to begin his lesson, the teacher, always alert, should say to the student, "Recite, sir! and he should conclude when the teacher says, "Let there be a pause."
A Brāhmaṇa should always utter the syllable *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end [of his recitation]. What is not preceded by *oṃ* flows away, and what is not followed by it falls apart.
Sitting on grass-blades pointing eastward and purified by means of purificatory blades (*pavitra*), he should perform his recitation.

Purified by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), he then becomes worthy of the syllable Oṃ. Prajāpati milked from the three Vedas the letter A, the letter U, and the letter M, as well as the words "bhūr," "bhuvaḥ," and "svar."

From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out each quarter-verse of this Sāvitrī beginning with the word "tat. Reciting this syllable and this [Sāvitrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis, [one attains success].
A Brahmin who knows the Veda, by performing the two twilight devotions, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda. By practicing this triad outside [the village] a thousand times,
a twice-born man is released from even great sin after a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
Deprived of this Ṛg verse, and failing to perform his own duties at the proper time,
one born of the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya incurs reproach among the virtuous.
The three imperishable Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis), preceded by the syllable Oṃ— [Oṃkāra].
The Sāvitrī, consisting of three feet, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing a form of space.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity.
There is nothing superior to the Sāvitrī, and truth excels silence. All Vedic rites of oblation and sacrifice perish, but [the merit of] truth does not.

The Imperishable (akṣara) should be known as difficult to perform, as well as Brahman and Prajāpati. The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the ritual sacrifice (vidhiyajña). The whispered (upāṃśu) recitation is said to be a hundred times more effective, and the mental (mānasa) a thousand times.

The four types of *pākayajña* sacrifices, together with those prescribed by ritual injunctions (*vidhiyajña*), are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of silent recitation (*japayajña*). A Brāhmaṇa may attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he performs other [rites] or does not perform them, a Brāhmaṇa who is friendly toward all is so called.
A wise man should exert effort in restraining his senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses.
The wise men of old have spoken of eleven organs;
I shall explain them correctly and in their proper order.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth.
The anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth.
Of these, the five beginning with the ear are the sense organs (buddhīndriya) in their respective order;
the five beginning with the anus are declared to be the organs of action (karmendriya).
The mind should be understood as the eleventh; by its own nature, it partakes of the character of both.
When it is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered.
Through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault.
But by restraining those very senses, one attains perfection.
Desire is never appeased by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter.

He who attains all these [objects] and he who renounces them entirely— the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment. These [senses] cannot be so effectively restrained by mere abstinence as they can be through [the practice of yoga].
Just as [the senses] are constantly addicted to their objects through ignorance,
so too the Vedas, renunciation, sacrifices, observances,
and austerities never attain perfection for one whose disposition is corrupted.
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled,
neither rejoices nor becomes dejected, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.
For if even one among all the senses leaks away, [all the others follow suit].
By that [negligence], his wisdom flows away like water from the foot of a leather bag.
Having brought the collection of the senses under control and likewise restraining the mind,
he should accomplish all his goals through yoga without wasting his body.

Standing during the morning twilight, one should recite the Sāvitrī until the sun appears; but during the evening twilight, one should remain seated until the stars are clearly visible. By standing and reciting during the morning twilight, one destroys the sin committed during the night.

But sitting facing the west, he destroys the impurity committed during the day. He who does not stand for the morning prayer and does not sit for the evening prayer is to be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra.
Restrained and established in the daily rule, he should go to the forest with a concentrated mind and recite the Sāvitrī near water. Likewise,
he should apply himself to the study of the Vedas and to his daily private recitation.
There is no restriction regarding days forbidden for study (*anadhyāya*) with respect to the *homamantra*s;
indeed, there is no such prohibition for the daily rites (*naityaka*), for that is remembered as the "Brahma-sacrifice" (*brahmasattra*).
Meritorious is the oblation of the Veda-offering (*brahmāhuti*), even when performed on a day forbidden for study, as it is consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ* call.
He who, being self-restrained and pure, studies his own Veda for a year according to the prescribed rule—
for him this [Veda] constantly yields milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey. Tending the sacred fires, living on alms, sleeping on the ground, and doing what is beneficial for the teacher—
A twice-born man who has undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana) should perform [his studies] until his formal return home (samāvartana).

According to the law, ten types of persons are worthy of being taught: the son of a teacher, one who is obedient, one who imparts knowledge, one who is righteous, one who is pure, one who is trustworthy, one who is capable, one who provides wealth, one who is virtuous, and one's own relative.
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks in an improper manner;
for even though he knows the truth, a wise man should behave among people like one who is dull-witted. He who speaks unrighteously, and he who asks unrighteously—[both are at fault].

One of the two [teacher or pupil] perishes, or they fall into mutual enmity. Where neither Dharma nor Artha exists, nor even a corresponding service, there knowledge should not be sown, just as good seed is not sown in barren soil.
A teacher of the Veda should, if he so desires, die with his knowledge alone;
even in times of terrible distress, he must never sow it in barren soil.
Knowledge, having approached a Brahmin, says: "I am your treasure; protect me."
"Do not give me to one who is censorious; thus may I be most powerful.
But to whichever pure man you know to be self-restrained and a student of sacred knowledge—to that Brahmin, a guardian of the treasure, who is vigilant, speak me."

But he who should acquire the Veda from one who is studying it without permission is guilty of stealing the Veda and falls into hell. This applies whether the Veda be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual (adhyātmika).

One should first salute him from whom one receives knowledge. A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better even if he possesses only the essence of the Sāvitrī mantra, than one who is unrestrained, even if he knows the three Vedas, eats all kinds of food, and sells all kinds of goods.

One should not sit upon a bed or seat already occupied by a superior; nor, while remaining on a bed or seat, should one greet him without first rising. For the vital breaths of a young man rise upward when an elder approaches.

By rising to meet them and by saluting them, he recovers those qualities. For one who is habitually inclined to salutation and who constantly serves the elders, four things increase: life-span, merit, fame, and strength. [The four increase together.]
After the initial greeting, a Brahmin greeting an elder should announce his own name, saying: "I am so-and-so by name.
For those who do not know how to respond to the announcement of one's name, [he should simply say: "I salute you."

A wise man should say "I am [Name]" to them, and likewise to all women. At the end of his own name when offering a salutation, he should utter the word "bhoḥ. For the seers have declared that the nature of the word "bhoḥ" is the very essence of names.
"May you be long-lived, O gentle one"—thus should a Brahmin be addressed upon greeting.
And at the end of his name, the vowel *a* that precedes the final syllable should be pronounced with prolation (*pluta*).
A Brahmin who does not know how to respond to a greeting...

He is not to be saluted by a learned man; he is exactly like a Śūdra. Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should ask after his welfare (*kuśala*); a Kṣatriya, after his freedom from illness (*anāmaya*); a Vaiśya, after his prosperity (*kṣema*); and a Śūdra, after his health (*ārogya*).

A consecrated person (dīkṣita), even if he be younger, must not be addressed by name; one who knows the law should address him by prefixing "bhoḥ" or "bhavat. But as for a woman who is the wife of another and is not related to one by birth, [she must be addressed as "Lady"].
One should address her thus: "Lady," "Fortunate One," or "Sister.
Upon rising, one should say "I am so-and-so" to maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than oneself.

A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a father’s sister, and a paternal aunt are to be honored like the wife of one’s guru; they are equal to the wife of a guru. The wife of a brother of the same caste is to be saluted by clasping her feet, even on a daily basis.
Upon returning from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet of the women who are kinswomen and relatives.
Toward his father’s sister, his mother’s sister, and his own elder sister, he should maintain the same conduct as toward his mother;
yet the mother is more venerable than they.
Friendship among citizens is said to arise after ten years; among artists, after five years;
and among those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), after three years—even by a shorter period—among those of the same lineage.
A Brāhmaṇa of ten years [is like] a king of a hundred years.
One should recognize that both father and son exist, yet between the two, the Brāhmaṇa is the father. Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—
these are the grounds for respect, each subsequent one being weightier than the preceding.
Among the five [classes] within the three [upper] castes, he who possesses many qualities and is preeminent is worthy of honor here, even if he be a Śūdra who has reached the tenth stage of life.
[One should yield the way] to a chariot-bearer, to one who has reached the tenth stage, to the sick, to one carrying a burden, and to a woman.
The way must be yielded to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom.
Among these three when they meet, the *snātaka* and the king are to be honored;
and between the king and the *snātaka*, the *snātaka* receives the honor due to a monarch.

That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the secret doctrines (Upaniṣads), is called an Ācārya. Furthermore, one who teaches a single portion of the Veda or even the Vedāṅgas [is called an Upādhyāya].

He who teaches for the sake of his livelihood is called an *upādhyāya*. That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* according to the rules and supports him with food is called a *guru*.

He who, having been chosen, performs for another the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the cooked sacrifices (*pākayajña*), and the great sacrifices (*makha*) such as the *agniṣṭoma* and others— he is called his officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) in this world.
He who truly fills both ears with the Veda (*brahman*) is [the true priest].
He is to be known as mother and he is to be known as father; one should never bear malice toward him.
Ten preceptors (*upādhyāya*) are equal to one teacher (*ācārya*); a hundred teachers are equal to one father;
but a mother exceeds even a thousand fathers in terms of venerability.
Between the one who procreates and the one who gives the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is superior;
for the Vedic birth of a Brahmin is eternal, both after death and in this world.
As for the mother and father who procreate him through mutual desire—
One should know that his true birth is that which he receives from his mother’s womb;
but the caste that the teacher, who has mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule by means of the Sāvitrī— that is the real, undecaying, and immortal birth.
One should know that person as a guru in this world by virtue of that service of learning, who benefits another with what he has heard, whether it be little or much.
He is the one who effects the Vedic birth and is the instructor of one’s own duty.
Even a young Brahmin becomes the father of an elder by virtue of dharma. The sage Aṅgiras, the son of Aṅgiras, taught his elders after embracing them with knowledge, saying, "O my sons!"
With their anger aroused, they questioned the gods regarding that matter.
And the gods, having assembled, said to them: "The preceptor has spoken what is right to you.
Indeed, the child is ignorant, while the one who imparts the sacred mantras is the father."

For they say that one who is ignorant is a child, but he who imparts the sacred mantras is a father. Neither by years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen did the seers establish dharma; he among us who is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) is great.
The seniority of Brahmins is based on knowledge, that of Kṣatriyas on valor,
that of Vaiśyas on grain and wealth, and that of Śūdras alone on birth.
One does not become an elder simply because one's head is gray.
The gods indeed recognize as an elder that man who, though young, is learned.
As an elephant made of wood and a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three merely bear the name.
As a eunuch is fruitless with women, as a cow is fruitless with a cow,

and as a gift given to an ignorant man is fruitless, so is a Brahmin who has not studied the Rigveda fruitless. By non-violence toward all living beings alone should the instruction of what is beneficial be performed.
And speech that is sweet and gentle should be employed by one who desires dharma. He whose speech and mind are pure and always properly guarded indeed attains the entire fruit taught in the Vedānta.

Even when afflicted, one should not be a wounder of others' vital parts, nor should one have a mind intent on deeds that harm others; one should not utter that speech by which another is agitated, for such speech leads away from the world of the righteous. A Brahmin should always shrink from honor as if it were poison.
One should always long for contempt as if it were nectar. For he who is held in contempt sleeps in happiness and wakes in happiness;
he moves about happily in this world, while the one who treats others with contempt perishes.
By this sequential method, having purified his self, the twice-born man, dwelling with his teacher, should gradually accumulate the austerity conducive to the acquisition of the Veda,
through various specific forms of austerity and vows prescribed by rule.

The entire Veda, together with its secret portions (the Upaniṣads), must be mastered by the twice-born. The best of the twice-born, desiring to perform austerity, should constantly practice the Veda alone;
for the study of the Veda is declared to be the highest austerity for a Brahmin in this world.

"Even though he wears a garland, that twice-born man who studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability performs the highest austerity, even unto the tips of his nails. But the twice-born man who,
without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other matters,"

He, along with his lineage, quickly attains the status of a Śūdra while still alive. According to the injunction of the Veda, for a twice-born man there is a first birth from the mother, a second at the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass, and a third at the initiation for sacrifice.
Among those, that which is his Vedic birth, marked by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass—
therein the Sāvitrī is said to be his mother, and the teacher his father.
Because of the imparting of the Vedas, they call the teacher "father."
For no ritual action whatsoever is appropriate for him prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
He should not utter the Veda, except for the recitation of *svadhā*.
For he is equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born through the Veda.

For one who has undergone the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the undertaking of vows is prescribed, as well as the sequential acquisition of the Veda according to the rules (Manu 2.173). Whatever skin, sacred thread, and girdle have been ordained for him [should be used]. (Manu 2.174a)
Whatever staff and whatever garment he has, those he shall retain even during his religious observances.
But while living with his teacher as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*),
he should observe these rules for the sake of increasing his own austerity, having fully restrained the collection of his senses.
Having bathed daily and being pure, he should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors;
likewise, he should perform the worship of the deities and the placing of fuel on the sacred fire.
He should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, and women.
All fermented acids, as well as the harming of living beings,
anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes, and carrying an umbrella;
likewise, lust, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments— [these should be avoided].
Gambling, idle gossip, slander, and likewise falsehood;
gazing at and touching women, and injury to others—[he should avoid these].
He should always sleep alone and never let his semen spill.
For by emitting semen out of desire, one destroys his own vow.
A twice-born student who has involuntarily emitted semen during sleep shall bathe,
worship the sun, and mutter three times the verse beginning with "punar mām."
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow-dung, earth, and *kuśa* grass—
as much as required—
and he should go out for alms day after day from those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifice, and who are praised for their own duties.
A student, being self-restrained, should collect alms daily from the houses [of others],
avoiding the family of his teacher, as well as the families of his paternal kinsmen and maternal relatives.
If alms cannot be obtained elsewhere, he should avoid the aforementioned houses in the reverse order of their mention.
Or, if those previously mentioned are unavailable, he may wander through the entire village, restraining his speech with self-control; however, he must avoid those who have been accused of crimes.
Having fetched the fuel-sticks from afar, he should place them upon a raised spot.

He should untiringly offer oblations with those [verses] into the fire every evening and morning. If, while not being ill, he fails to go for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance prescribed for one who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇi-vrata).
One who observes the vow should always subsist on alms and should not eat the food of a single person.

For one observing the vow, subsisting on alms is declared to be equal to fasting. When performing rites for the gods or for the ancestors, he should act like a deity; otherwise, he should act like a seer.
If invited, he may eat at his pleasure; his vow is not thereby violated.
This duty has been taught by the wise for the Brāhmaṇa alone;
however, this duty is not ordained for the Rājanya or the Vaiśya in this manner.
Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged,
he should apply himself to his studies and to the welfare of his teacher. He should likewise control his body, speech, intellect, senses, and mind.
Restraining himself, he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of his teacher.
He should always keep his hands raised, maintain virtuous conduct, and remain well-restrained. And when told, "Be seated," he should sit down facing the teacher.

He should always have inferior food, clothing, and dress in the presence of his teacher. He should rise before him and go to sleep after him. While lying down, he should not engage in answering a call or in conversation.

One should not serve [food] while seated, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor with one's face turned away. One should serve while standing to one who is seated; by approaching, to one who is standing; by going out to meet, to one who is coming toward him; and by running after, to one who is running.
Facing one who has his back turned, approaching the presence of one who is far away,
bowing to one who is reclining, and standing at the command of one who is sitting— his bed and seat must always be lower than the teacher’s when in his presence. (Manu 2.197–198)
In the presence of his guru, he should not sit as he pleases within the range of his vision.
He should not utter his name even in his absence,
nor should he ever mimic his gait, speech, or gestures.
Wherever censure or even slander of one's teacher occurs, there one should either cover one's ears or depart from that place to another.
Through such censure one becomes a donkey; through reviling, one indeed becomes a dog.
One who consumes [the teacher's food] becomes a worm; one who is envious becomes an insect.
One should not honor him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman. And if one is seated in a vehicle or on a seat, one should descend from it before saluting him.
One should not sit with one's teacher in a position where the wind blows from him toward oneself or from oneself toward him,
nor should one say anything at all that might cause a breach of privacy regarding the teacher.
One should likewise avoid sitting on vehicles drawn by cattle, horses, or camels, on palaces, on mats of straw, or on ordinary grass mats.
He should sit together with his teacher on rocks, wooden planks, or boats.
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, he should behave toward him as he would toward his teacher. And, unless permitted by his teacher, he should not pay homage to his own teachers.

In this very same way, one should always behave toward teachers of knowledge as toward one's own parents, and likewise toward those who restrain one from unrighteousness and those who instruct one in what is beneficial. Toward those who are superior, one should always practice the same conduct as toward a teacher.
Among the teacher’s sons who are noble, and among the teacher’s own kinsmen,
a young boy, or one of equal age, or even a student at a sacrificial rite—
such a son of the teacher, while teaching, deserves honor as the teacher himself.

One should not perform the massaging of the limbs, the bathing, or the eating of the leftovers for the teacher’s son, nor should one wash his feet. The wives of the teacher who are of the same caste (varṇa) should be honored like the teacher himself.
But women of a different caste should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
One must not perform the anointing, bathing, massaging of the limbs,
or the dressing of the hair for the wife of one's guru.
But a young wife of one's teacher must not be saluted by touching her feet here in this world by a man who has completed twenty years of age and understands virtues and faults.
This is the nature of women: they are a source of corruption for men in this world.

Therefore, the wise do not become negligent regarding wealth on account of women. For in this world, a woman is capable of leading astray both the ignorant and even the learned man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger.
One should not sit in a secluded place with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a learned man.
However, a young man may, at his pleasure, [sit] on the ground with the young wives of his teachers.

One should perform a formal salutation according to the rules, saying, "I am so-and-so. Having returned from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet [of the teacher's wife], and every day thereafter,
one should offer a respectful greeting to the wives of the guru, keeping in mind the dharma of the virtuous.
Just as a man digging with a spade obtains water,
so does one who is intent on service obtain knowledge that resides in the teacher.
He may be shaven-headed, or wear matted hair, or have his hair matted except for a single lock left at the crown.

The sun should never set while he is in a village, nor should it ever rise while he is there. If the sun should rise while he is lying down out of negligence, or if it should set while he is unaware, he must fast for the day while muttering prayers.
For he who is asleep when the sun sets, or who is asleep when the sun rises,
if he does not perform the penance, he shall be joined with great sin. Having sipped water, being pure and composed, he should always perform both the twilight devotions.
In a clean place, he should perform his recitation according to the prescribed rule.
If a woman or a person of lower status should perform some virtuous act,
he should practice all of that with diligence, as well as whatever brings him mental delight.
Dharma and wealth are said to be the highest good; pleasure and wealth, or even dharma alone, are also [said to be so].
Or rather, wealth alone is the highest good in this world; such is the settled rule regarding the three aims of life (trivarga).
A teacher, a father, a mother, and an elder brother—these are [to be honored].
Even when distressed, one must not show contempt for them, especially by a Brāhmaṇa.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahman, the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati,
the mother is the embodiment of the Earth, and one's own brother is the embodiment of oneself.
The suffering that parents endure during the birth of human beings cannot be compensated for even in hundreds of years.
One should always do what is pleasing to them, and likewise always to one's teacher.
When these three are satisfied, all austerity is fully accomplished.
Service to these three is said to be the highest austerity;
one should not practice any other duty without their permission.
For they are indeed the three worlds, they are the three stages of life (āśramas),
they are the three Vedas, and they are said to be the three sacred fires:
the father is the Gārhapatya fire, and the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire.
The teacher is indeed the Āhavanīya fire; thus, this triad of fires is most venerable.
By being vigilant toward these three, the householder shall conquer the three worlds.
Shining with his own body, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
By devotion to his mother he wins this world, by devotion to his father the middle world, and by service to his teacher he attains the world of Brahman.
All duties are honored by him who honors these three.
But for him by whom these [elders] are disregarded, all his ritual acts are fruitless.
As long as those three live, he should not perform any other [independent rite];
he should always practice service toward them alone, devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial to them.

Whatever one may perform for the sake of the next world, provided it does not conflict with their interests, that he should announce to them through thought, word, and deed. For in these three, a man’s duty is fully accomplished.

This is the supreme dharma directly; any other is called a secondary dharma (upadharma). A person of faith should acquire auspicious knowledge even from a lowly source; likewise, one should accept the highest dharma even from another, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family.
Even from poison one should take the nectar; even from a child, a well-spoken word;
even from an enemy, good conduct; and even from an impure place, gold. Women, jewels, knowledge, dharma, purity, and well-spoken words [are to be accepted from anyone].
And various crafts may be acquired from anyone.
In times of distress, study under one who is not a Brahmin is permitted;
however, one must follow and serve that teacher as long as the study continues.

A pupil should not dwell for life with a teacher who is not a Brāhmaṇa, nor even with a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied the Veda, if he desires the highest goal. However, if he should choose to dwell permanently in the family of his teacher, [he may do so with one who is a Brāhmaṇa].
One should attend upon him with devotion until the liberation of the body.
That Brahmin who serves his teacher until the completion of his physical existence goes directly to the eternal abode of Brahman.

One who knows the Dharma should not offer anything to the teacher beforehand. However, when he is about to bathe and has been permitted by the teacher, he should provide for the teacher's needs according to his ability—be it a field, gold, a cow, a horse, an umbrella, sandals, or a seat. [Or at least an umbrella and sandals.]

He should bring satisfaction to his teacher by offering grain, vegetables, or clothing. When the teacher has indeed passed away, he should behave toward the teacher’s son who is endowed with good qualities,
or toward the teacher’s wife, or toward a sapinda relative, just as he did toward the teacher.

When these [teachers] are not available, one who maintains his standing, sitting, and movements, and applies himself to the service of the sacred fires, should perfect his own body. The Brahmin who thus practices the vow of studentship (*brahmacarya*) without violation—
He goes to the highest station and is not born here again.
One should observe the vow pertaining to the three Vedas under a teacher for thirty-six years.

Having studied the Vedas— either all of them, two of them, or even one— in due order, and having remained steadfast in his vow of celibacy, he should enter the stage of the householder, whether for half that time, for a quarter, or until the completion of his study.
When he has been recognized by his own dharma as the heir to his father’s Vedic inheritance,
one should first honor him with a cow while he is wearing a garland and seated upon the marriage bed.
Having bathed and returned home according to the prescribed rule with the permission of his guru, [he should perform the rites].
A twice-born man shall marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks;
she must not be a *sapiṇḍa* of his mother nor of the same *gotra* as his father. Such a woman is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of marriage for sexual union.

Even if they are great and prosperous in cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain—one should avoid these ten types of families in forming alliances with women: (3.6) those deficient in sacred rites, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic hymns, those who are excessively hairy, and those afflicted with skin diseases. (3.7)
Nor should he marry from families afflicted with consumption, disease, epilepsy, leucoderma, or leprosy. He should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with extra limbs, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown.
One should not marry a woman named after a bear, a tree, or a river; nor one named after a low-caste person or a mountain;
nor one named after a bird, a snake, or a servant; nor one with a terrifying name. She should have no missing limbs, possess an auspicious name, and have the gait of a swan or an elephant.
One should marry a woman who has fine body hair, hair, and teeth, and whose limbs are soft. However,
a wise man should not marry a girl whose brother does not exist or whose father is unknown,
for fear of the illegality of her being an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).
For the twice-born, a wife of the same caste is recommended first for the rite of marriage;
however, for those who proceed out of desire, these following women are the inferior options in their respective order.
A Śūdra woman alone is prescribed as a wife for a Śūdra, while for a Vaiśya, both she and a woman of his own caste are recorded as permissible.

These [wives] and their own [wives], O King, as well as those [wives] and their own [wives] belong to the twice-born. For even in times of distress, when a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya is living, a Śūdra woman is never prescribed as a wife under any circumstances whatsoever.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of inferior caste,
quickly lead their families, along with their offspring, to the state of Śūdras.
According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste].
Because of the birth of a son from a Śūdra woman, Śaunaka became the offspring of Bhṛgu. By mounting a Śūdra woman for sexual intercourse, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he is indeed fallen from his Brāhmaṇahood.
But for him whose rites for the gods, the ancestors, and guests are centered primarily upon her (the Śūdra woman),
neither the ancestors nor the gods will eat his offerings, and he does not go to heaven.
[This applies to] one who has drunk the foam from a Śūdra woman's mouth and has been defiled by her breath.

And for one born of such a woman, no atonement is prescribed. Now learn briefly these eight forms of marriage for the four castes, which determine what is beneficial and harmful both after death and in this world.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya,
the Āsura, the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca as the eighth and lowest;
for whichever [form] is lawful for which caste, and whatever its merits and defects may be—
I shall declare all that to you, as well as the merits and defects regarding procreation.
One should know that for a Brāhmaṇa there are six in order, for a Kṣatriya four lower ones,
and for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra those same ones, which are lawful and not Rākṣasa.
Sages know that the first four [forms of marriage] are recommended for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Rākṣasa alone is for a Kṣatriya, and the Āsura for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Of these five, three are declared here to be lawful and two unlawful.
The Paiśāca and the Āsura forms of marriage must never be performed under any circumstances.
The two forms of marriage previously mentioned—
the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa— are traditionally held to be lawful for the Kṣatriya, whether practiced separately or mixed together.

Having clothed and honored him who is learned in the Vedas and endowed with good character, and having invited him himself, the giving away of the daughter is proclaimed as the Brāhma rite. But when a sacrifice is properly performed and the officiating priest carries out his duties, [the gift of the daughter is the Ārṣa rite].

Giving away a daughter after adorning her is declared to be the *daiva* rite. Taking one or two pairs of cattle from the bridegroom according to the law and giving away the daughter in accordance with the prescribed rule is called the *ārṣa* rite.
Having addressed them with the words, "May you both perform your duty together," and having honored the bridegroom, the giving away of the girl is known as the Prājāpatya rite.
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the girl herself according to one's ability...
The giving away of a maiden at one's own will is called the Āsura rite.
When there is a union between the maiden and the bridegroom through mutual desire, that should be known as the Gāndharva rite; it arises from passion and has sexual intercourse as its purpose.

Having killed, wounded, or broken [the way], while she is crying out and weeping, the forcible abduction of a maiden from her home is called the *rākṣasa* rite. Where he approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged—
That is the most sinful of marriages, the eighth and lowest being the Paiśāca. For the foremost of the twice-born, the gift of a daughter with water alone is distinguished as superior;
for the other castes, however, it is by mutual desire.

O Brahmins, listen as I fully proclaim all those qualities which Manu has declared for each of these forms of marriage, as I describe them all to you. [O Brahmins, listen as I properly proclaim them. By this, one purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and oneself as the twenty-first.
The son of a woman wedded according to the Brāhma rite, having performed meritorious deeds, liberates his ancestors from sin.
The son born of a woman wedded by the Daiva rite likewise [liberates] seven generations before and seven after;
the son born of a woman wedded by the Ārṣa rite [liberates] three before and three after; and the son born of a woman wedded by the Kāya (Prājāpatya) rite [liberates] six before and six after.
In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma, in their respective order,
sons are born who possess Vedic luster, are esteemed by the learned,
endowed with beauty and the quality of goodness, wealthy, and renowned.
Those who possess sufficient means of enjoyment and are most righteous live for a hundred years.
But in the remaining [prohibited] marriages, sons who are like men in their conduct, speakers of falsehood,
and haters of the Veda and dharma are born.
Through blameless marriages with women, the offspring becomes blameless; through blameworthy ones, the offspring of men becomes blameworthy. Therefore, one should avoid blameworthy unions.
The sacrament of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste.
This rule regarding the act of marriage with women of a different caste should be understood as follows:
a *śara* (reed) must be grasped by a Kṣatriya woman, a goad by a Vaiśya maiden,
and the hem of the garment by a Śūdra woman when marrying a man of a higher caste.

He should approach his wife during her season, always remaining devoted to his own wife; observing that vow, he may go to her out of a desire for pleasure, except on the forbidden lunar days. The natural season of women is traditionally held to be sixteen nights.
Together with the other four days,
which are censured by the virtuous— namely, the first four of those nights, as well as the eleventh and the thirteenth— the remaining ten nights are praised.
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights. Therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during her season on an even night.
A male child is conceived when the man's seed is in excess, and a female child when the woman's is in excess.
If the semen is equal [to the blood], the offspring is neuter; if it is equal in quantity to both male and female, they are twins; and if it is diminished or very small, the reverse occurs.
By avoiding women on the eight censurable nights and others, one remains a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) one inhabits.
A wise father shall not accept even the slightest bride-price for his daughter.
For by accepting a bride-price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring.
And those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off a woman’s property, [are likewise at fault].
Those wicked men who take women, vehicles, or clothing [as a fee] go to a downward state.
Some say that a pair of cattle is the bride-price (*śulka*) in the *ārṣa* marriage; that is indeed false.
Whether it be small or even great, it remains nothing other than a sale.
When the kinsmen do not take a bride-price for them, that is not a sale;
it is merely an honor for the maidens and a total absence of cruelty.
Thus these [women] are [honored] by fathers, brothers, husbands, and likewise by brothers-in-law.
They should be honored and adorned by those who desire abundant prosperity.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, all ritual acts there become fruitless.
Where female relatives grieve, that family quickly perishes;
but where they do not grieve, that family indeed prospers forever.
Those households which female relatives enter when they have not been properly honored perish on all sides, as if struck by a magical spell (*kṛtyā*).
Therefore, these women should always be honored with ornaments, clothing, and food.

By men desiring prosperity, [this should be done] constantly during rites of hospitality and at festivals. In that family where the husband is always contented with his wife, and likewise the wife with her husband, there indeed prosperity is certain.

For if a woman does not find pleasure, she will not delight her husband; and from a lack of delight on the part of the man, procreation does not proceed. But when a woman is pleased, the entire family is pleased.
But when that [lineage] does not shine, nothing at all shines.
(Manu 3.62c) Through ill-contracted marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the failure to study the Vedas, and by neglecting Brahmins, noble lineages fall into a state of ignobility. (Manu 3.63)
[One falls from caste] through the practice of crafts, through trade, by having offspring solely with Śūdra women,
by means of cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, service to the king,
by officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice, and by atheism regarding ritual acts.
Families that are deficient in sacred knowledge (mantra) quickly perish;
however, families that are enriched by sacred knowledge, even if possessing little wealth,
attain the rank of noble lineages and acquire great renown.
[From here on, the numbering is "-10"] A householder should perform the domestic rites according to the rules in the nuptial fire,
as well as the performance of the five sacrifices and the daily cooking.
A householder has five slaughter-houses:
the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water jar; by using these, he is bound.
To provide atonement for all of them in their respective order, the great seers have prescribed—

The five great sacrifices (mahāyajña) are ordained for householders every day: teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña); the libation to the ancestors is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña); the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods (daivayajña); the bali-offering is the sacrifice to the elements (bhūtayajña); and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men (nṛyajña).
He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability,
even while living constantly in the house, is not tainted by the defects of the slaughterhouse. He who [provides for] the deities, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself—

He who does not offer the oblations to the five breaths does not truly live, even while breathing. They declare that the five sacrifices consist of the *ahuta*, the *huta*, the *prahuta*, the *brāhmya-huta*, and the *prāśita*.
Recitation is the *ahuta* offering; the *homa* sacrifice is the *huta*; the *prahuta* is the offering to the spirits (*bhūta-bali*);

the *brāhmya-huta* is the honoring of the foremost of the twice-born; and the *prāśita* is the libation to the ancestors. One should be constantly engaged here in the study of one's own Veda and in rites directed toward the gods.
For it is he who, engaged in rites for the gods, sustains this world of moving and unmoving beings.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is produced, from rain comes food, and from that, living creatures.
Just as all living beings exist by depending upon the wind,
so do all other stages of life (āśramas) exist by depending upon the householder.
Since even those belonging to the other three stages of life are supported daily by his knowledge and his food, [the householder is the most excellent].
The householder alone sustains them; therefore, the householder’s stage of life is the most excellent.
It must be maintained with effort by one who desires imperishable heaven, and by one who desires ultimate happiness in this world—even though it is difficult for those of weak senses to maintain.
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, all living beings, and likewise guests—these expect [support] from householders; therefore, one who understands his duty should act toward them.
He should honor the sages through the private recitation of the Veda and the gods with burnt offerings, according to the prescribed rules.
One should satisfy the ancestors with *śrāddha* offerings, men with food, and the elemental spirits (*bhūta*) with the *bali* offering. One should perform the *śrāddha* daily with food,
water, or even milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing pleasure to the ancestors.

One may invite even a single Brahmin for the sake of the ancestors during the *pāñcayajñika* rite; however, one must never invite anyone at all for the *vaiśvadeva* portion. Having prepared the *vaiśvadeva* food according to the rules over the domestic fire, Manu 3.83a: One may invite even a single Brahmin for the sake of the ancestors during the *pāñcayajñika* rite. Manu 3.83c: But one must never invite any twice-born man here for the *vaiśvadeva*. Manu 3.84a: Of the *vaiśvadeva* food that has been prepared according to the rule over the domestic fire...
A Brāhmaṇa should perform the fire-oblation (homa) daily for these deities:
first for Agni and Soma, then for those two together,
then for the Viśvedevas and for Dhanvantari.
To Kuhū, to Anumati, and to Prajāpati;
likewise to Dyāvāpṛthivī together, and finally to Sviṣṭakṛt. Having thus duly offered the oblation, he should circumambulate in a clockwise direction toward all the quarters.
One should offer oblations to Indra, Antaka (Yama), and Apatīndu (Varuṇa), along with their followers.
One should cast [an offering] at the door saying "To the Maruts," and likewise into the water saying "To the Waters.
