In this manner, one should offer [an oblation] upon the pestle and mortar saying "To the Vanaspatis."
One should offer an oblation for Śrī at the head of the bed and for Bhadrakālī at the foot.
One should present the sacrificial offering (bali) to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the middle of the dwelling.
And one should cast an oblation into the air for the Viśvedevas.

On the back part of the house, he should offer a Bali-oblation to the beings that roam by day and those that roam by night, for the sake of the welfare of all beings. He should then carry all the remainder of the Bali-offering to the south for the ancestors.
And for slaughterhouses, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases,
birds, and worms— one should gradually cast [the food] upon the ground. The Brāhmaṇa who thus daily honors all beings in this manner—
He goes to the supreme abode, embodied in light, by the straight path.
Having performed this rite of offerings in this manner, he should first seat the guest and give alms to the mendicant and the religious student according to the rule.
Whatever meritorious fruit a householder twice-born man obtains by giving a cow to his teacher according to the prescribed rule,
that same meritorious fruit he obtains by giving alms,
even if it be only a bowl of water, having honored it according to the ritual.
One should bestow [the gift] upon a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas.
Offerings to the gods (havya) and offerings to the ancestors (kavya) do not reach those ignorant men,
being given by donors out of delusion to Brāhmaṇas who have become like ashes.

An oblation offered into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins who are enriched by knowledge and austerity saves one from distress and even from great sin. To a guest who has arrived, one should offer a seat and water.
And food, having honored it according to one's ability and in accordance with the prescribed rule— (Manu 3.99c).
Even from one who constantly gathers gleanings and constantly offers oblations into the five fires,
a Brāhmaṇa residing unhonored takes away all his merit (Manu 3.100).
Grass for a seat, ground for resting, water, and fourthly, pleasant speech— these are never lacking in the houses of the virtuous. A Brāhmaṇa staying for even a single night is considered a guest.
For because he stays for only a short time, he is called an *atithi* (guest).
One should not consider a Brahmin from the same village, nor one who has arrived by chance,
as a guest when he has arrived at the house where the wife or even the sacred fires are present.
Those foolish householders who subsist on the food of others go,
after death, to the state of cattle as those who provide such food.
A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by a householder.

Whether he arrives at the proper time or at an improper time, one must not let him dwell in one's house without food. One should certainly not eat that food oneself which one does not first offer to a guest. Honoring a guest brings merit, fame, long life, and leads to heaven.
One should offer a seat, lodging, a bed, accompaniment on departure, and respectful attendance—
superior hospitality to superior guests, inferior to inferior, and equal to equals. But if another guest should arrive after the Vaiśvadeva offering has been completed, [one must provide for him].
One should also give him food according to one's ability, but one should not offer the *bali* oblation [to him].
A Brahmin should not announce his own family or lineage for the sake of a meal;
for by praising himself for the sake of a meal, he is called a "vomit-eater" by the wise.
But a Kṣatriya is not called a guest in the house of a Brāhmaṇa;
nor are a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a friend, kinsmen, or even a teacher.
However, if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, [he should be treated as such].
When the Brahmins have finished eating, he may also feed that [guest] at his pleasure.
Even a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, if they arrive at one's household as guests,
he should feed them along with his dependents, practicing compassion toward them.

To others as well— such as female friends and so forth— who have come to the house out of affection, he should, together with his wife, provide food according to his ability. He should also feed married women, maidens, the sick, and pregnant women.
One should feed these [guests] before the guests themselves, without hesitation.
But that unwise man who eats before giving to them, while eating,
does not realize that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures.
When the Brahmins, his own dependents, and the servants have finished eating,
the husband and wife may thereafter eat what remains.
[They should honor] the gods, the sages, human beings, the ancestors, and the household deities.
Having honored [the guests], the householder should thereafter eat what remains. He who cooks solely for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of the remnants of a sacrifice.

One should honor with the *madhuparka* offering a king, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a *snātaka*, a teacher (*guru*), one’s own father-in-law, and a maternal uncle, again after a full year has passed.
A king and a learned scholar (*śrotriya*) who have arrived for a sacrificial ceremony (*yajñakarman*) are likewise to be honored.

The two [guests] are to be honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka), but not so at one who does not perform sacrifices; this is the settled rule. At evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer the oblation (bali) without mantras; for this is indeed called Vaiśvadeva, and it is prescribed for both morning and evening.
Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should, at the waning of the moon,
perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month.
The wise know the monthly Śrāddha for the ancestors as the Anvāhārya.
And that [hospitality] should be performed with effort using commendable meat.
In this regard, I shall describe in their entirety which of the best of the twice-born are to be fed, which are to be avoided, how many there are, and with what kinds of food.
At a rite for the gods, he should feed two; at a rite for the ancestors, three; or one at each of the two.
Even if he is very wealthy, he should not be overly intent on a large company.
He should consider the honor shown, the place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins.
Excessive expansion destroys these five; therefore, one should not seek such expansion.
This performance for the deceased is well-known as the ancestral rite (*pitrya*) performed at the waning of the moon;
for one who is constantly engaged in that [ancestral rite], the worldly performance for the deceased is effectively accomplished.
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).
What is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit.
Even if he is the only one, one should feed a learned man at rites for the gods and the ancestors.
One obtains abundant fruit [from feeding] even many who are ignorant of the mantras;
however, one should examine from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas. He is considered a worthy recipient for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*, and he is remembered as a true guest.
For where thousands upon thousands of those ignorant of the Ṛgveda eat,
a single man who knows the mantras, being pleased, is by law worthy of all of them.
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) and offerings to the gods (havis) should be given to one distinguished by knowledge.
For hands smeared with blood are not purified by blood alone. As many mouthfuls as one who is ignorant of the mantras swallows at offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya),
for so many does he, as a departed spirit (preta), swallow glowing spikes, spears, and iron balls.
Some twice-born men are devoted to knowledge, while others are devoted to austerity;
some are devoted to austerity and Vedic study, and others are devoted to ritual action.
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) should be diligently presented to those who are devoted to knowledge.
But offerings for the gods (havya) should be presented according to the rule to all four [types of Brahmins].
If one’s father is not learned in the Vedas (aśrotriya) but his son has mastered the Vedas,
or if his son is not learned in the Vedas but his father has mastered the Vedas— [in such cases, the offering is still valid].
Of these two, one should know the elder to be him whose father is a *śrotriya*;
however, the other deserves honor for the sake of honoring the sacred mantras.
One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*, but his acquisition should be effected through wealth.
One should feed at a *śrāddha* that twice-born man whom one knows to be neither a woman nor a friend.
For him whose *śrāddhas* and sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) are primarily intended for friends,
there is no fruit after death from those *śrāddhas* or sacrifices.
That lowest of the twice-born who, out of delusion, forms social alliances through a *śrāddha* falls from the heavenly world; he is a friend to the *śrāddha* and a base Brahmin.
This is declared by the twice-born to be a "feasting together," a *dakṣiṇā* belonging to the *piśācas*.
In this very world, she remains like a blind cow in a solitary house. Just as a sower who has sown seed in barren soil does not obtain fruit,
so too a donor who offers an oblation to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda does not obtain the fruit.

By giving a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to the rule to a learned man, one makes both the giver and the recipient partakers of the fruit, both in this world and after death. At a *śrāddha*, one may at will honor a friend, but never an enemy, even if he be highly qualified.
For an oblation consumed by one who hates [the recipient] becomes fruitless after death.
One should take care to feed at a *śrāddha* a reciter of the Ṛgveda who has mastered the Veda,
or an Adhvaryu priest who has reached the end of his branch, or a singer of the Sāmaveda who has completed his study.
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at someone’s *śrāddha*,
the satisfaction of that person’s ancestors shall be eternal for seven generations.
This indeed is the primary rule regarding the offering of *havya* (oblations to the gods) and *kavya* (oblations to the ancestors).
This should be known as a secondary rule (anukalpa) always practiced by the virtuous:

one should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, the teacher, the daughter’s son, the husband of a sister, a relative, the officiating priest, and the person for whom one performs a sacrifice.
One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brāhmaṇa for a rite dedicated to the gods;
however, when a rite dedicated to the ancestors is at hand, he should examine him with great care.
Those who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, or those who follow the way of atheism—
Manu has declared those brahmins to be unworthy of offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya):
one who wears matted hair but does not study the Veda, one who is weak, a gambler, and those who officiate at sacrifices for groups of men; these one should not feed at a śrāddha.

Physicians, temple-priests, and likewise meat-sellers, as well as those who live by trade— these should be avoided at rites for the gods and the ancestors. A village servant, a servant of the king, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth [should also be avoided].
One who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer;
one afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, a younger brother who marries before his elder, one who neglects the Vedic study (nirākṛti);
a hater of Brahmins, an elder brother whose younger brother marries first, and one who belongs to a social group (gaṇa).
One of bad character, one who has broken his vow of chastity, the husband of a Śūdra woman,
a son born of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house a paramour resides; likewise, one who teaches for a fee and one who is taught by a paid teacher.
A Śūdra who is a pupil, a teacher of a Śūdra, one who is foul-mouthed, and the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* sons;
one who has abandoned his mother, father, or teacher without cause;
and one who has entered into alliances with outcasts through Vedic or matrimonial connections.
An arsonist, a poisoner, one who subsists on the food of a harlot, a seller of Soma, one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-miller, a forger,
one who disputes with his father, a gambler, and likewise a drinker of intoxicants— [these are excluded from the Śrāddha].
One afflicted by a chronic disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, a seller of liquids (poisons);

the maker of bows and arrows, and he who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is still unmarried; a betrayer of friends, one who subsists by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher to his own son.
One who suffers from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one afflicted with vitiligo, as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and a reviler of the Vedas— these should be excluded.
So too should one who trains elephants, cattle, horses, or camels, and one who lives by astrology.
One who raises birds, as well as a teacher of combat;
one who diverts watercourses and one who delights in obstructing them; a house-mover, a messenger, and also a planter of trees.

One who plays with dice, one who lives by falconry, a defiler of maidens, a violent man, one who subsists as a servant to a Śūdra, and a priest for a multitude; one devoid of proper conduct, a eunuch, and likewise one who is constantly begging— these are unworthy of the funeral cake.

One who lives by agriculture, one with elephantiasis, and one censured by the virtuous; a shepherd, a keeper of buffaloes, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and a carrier of corpses— these must be avoided with great effort.

A learned man, the best of the twice-born, should avoid both at [the rites of] the ancestors and the gods those lowest of the twice-born who are censured for their conduct and are unworthy of the company at a meal. For a Brāhmaṇa who does not study the Veda is extinguished like a fire of straw.

To him no sacrificial offering (havya) should be given, for an oblation is not poured into ashes. I shall explain in its entirety the future fruit that accrues to a donor from giving to one unworthy of the row (apāṅktya), whether at a rite for the gods (daiva) or for the ancestors (pitrya).
What is eaten by twice-born men who have not observed their vows, as well as by those such as one who marries before his elder brother (a *parivettṛ*),
and by others who are unworthy of the row (*apāṅkteya*)— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
He who enters into marriage and the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried]...
He should be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother), while the elder brother is the *parivitti*.
The *parivitti*, the *parivettṛ*, she through whom the marriage is contracted (*parividyate*),
the giver [of the girl], and the officiating priest— these five all go to hell.
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of a deceased brother—
even though she has been appointed to him according to dharma— is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*. Two types of sons, the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, are born from the wives of others.
If the husband is alive, he is a *kuṇḍa*; if the husband is dead, he is a *golaka*.
These two beings, born in another's field, ruin the offerings of sacrificial oblations (*havya*) and ancestral gifts (*kavya*) made by the givers, both in this world and after death.

As many members of a company as an unworthy person (apāṅktya) looks upon while they are eating, for so many does the foolish giver fail to obtain the fruit of that act. Upon seeing one who is blind, he loses the merit of ninety; one who is one-eyed, of sixty; and one who has leprosy, of a hundred.
One afflicted with a foul disease destroys the fruit of a gift for a thousand [recipients].
(Manu 3.177c) As many Brahmins as a priest who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs, for that many the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the meritorious gift. (Manu 3.168c)

Even a Brahmin who knows the Vedas, by accepting a gift from him out of greed, quickly goes to destruction like an unbaked clay vessel in water. To one who sells Soma, [the gift becomes] excrement; to a physician, pus and blood.
A gift given to a temple-priest (*devalaka*) is lost; one given to a usurer finds no foundation.
That which is given to a merchant benefits neither in this world nor in the next;
it is like an oblation poured into ashes, even so is a gift to a twice-born man born of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*).
But regarding the others who are unworthy of the company (*apāṅktya*), as previously specified— those who are unrighteous—
the wise declare that their food is like fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone.
The row (*paṅkti*) defiled by those unworthy of the company is purified by those best of the twice-born.
Learn now in their entirety those foremost of the twice-born who purify the company at a meal:
those who are preeminent in all the Vedas and in all the expositions of the scriptures,
and who are born into lineages of Vedic scholars— these should be known as the purifiers of the company.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymn, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one born of a lineage where the Veda was given as a religious gift, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman; one who knows the meaning of the Vedas, an expounder of the Veda, a lifelong celibate student, and one who has given away a thousand cows.
Brāhmaṇas who have lived a hundred years should be known as purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvanas).
When the rite of Śrāddha is at hand, either on the previous day or on the following day,
one should properly invite at least three Brāhmaṇas as described above.
A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors (pitrya) should always remain self-restrained;
he must not recite the Vedic hymns (chandāṃsi), and that [rite] shall be his śrāddha.
For the ancestors attend upon those invited twice-born men.
They follow [the guests] like the wind, and likewise wait upon them while they sit. But that best of the twice-born who, having been duly invited to a rite for the gods or the ancestors,
somehow neglects it, becomes a sinner and shall go to the state of a pig.
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha, rejoices with a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī),
incurs all whatever evil deed the giver has committed.
Those who are free from anger, devoted to purity, and constantly practicing celibacy—
The ancestors, those highly fortunate ancient deities who have laid down their weapons—
since from them the origin of all these [beings] has proceeded without exception,
learn now by what rules they are to be honored and by whom.
The sons of all those sages, beginning with Marīci, who were the offspring of Manu, the son of Hiranyagarbha, are remembered as the classes of Pitṛs.
The Somasads, the sons of Virāj, are remembered as the Pitṛs of the Sādhyas.
The Agniṣvāttas are renowned in the world as the Pitṛs of the gods; the Barhiṣads, born of Atri,
are remembered as those of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rakṣases,
Suparṇas, and Kinnaras.
Among the Brahmins, they are named Somapās; among the Kṣatriyas, Havirbhujs;
among the Vaiśyas, Ājyapās; and among the Śūdras, Sukālins.
The Somapās are the sons of Kavi, and the Havirbhujs are the sons of Aṅgiras.

The Ājyapas are the sons of Pulastya, and the Sukālins are the sons of Vasiṣṭha. One should designate the Agnidagdhas, the Anagnidagdhas, the Kāvyas, the Barhiṣads, the Agniṣvāttas, and the Saumyas as belonging specifically to the Brahmins.
These principal groups of Pitṛs have been proclaimed;
it should be understood that their sons and grandsons here are infinite.
From the sages the Pitṛs were born, and from the Pitṛs the gods and humans.
To the gods, however, belongs the entire world, both moving and stationary, in due order.
Even water given to them with faith, using silver vessels or those adorned with silver, conduces to inexhaustible merit.
For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) is superior to the rite for the gods (daivakārya);
indeed, the rite for the gods is traditionally taught as the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors.
One should first employ the rite for the gods as a protective shield for those [ancestral rites].
Rākṣasas plunder a śrāddha that is devoid of protection.

One should perform it beginning and ending with the deities; it should not begin and end with the ancestors. For one who performs it beginning and ending with the ancestors, he quickly perishes along with his lineage.

One should smear a pure and secluded place with cow dung, and one should also diligently ensure that it slopes toward the south. Indeed, this should be done in open spaces, in clean places, and likewise on the banks of rivers.
The ancestors are always satisfied by what is given in secluded places.
Having prepared separate seats for each, strewn with sacred grass (barhis),
he should cause those Brahmins, who have properly sipped water, to sit down upon them.
Having seated those blameless Brahmins upon their seats,
he should worship them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with those invited for the gods. Then, having brought water for them along with *pavitra* grass and sesame seeds—
Permitted by the Brahmins, a Brahmin should perform [the rite] in the fire together with the Brahmins.
Having first performed the satiation of Agni, Soma,
and Yama, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors according to the rule by the offering of oblations.
In the absence of fire, however, one should place [the offering] directly into the hand of a Brahmin;
for that twice-born man is called "fire" by the Brahmins who perceive the sacred mantras. They say that these ancient ones were free from anger and possessed of great serenity.
Having honored the best of the twice-born, who are the gods of the *śrāddha* and are intent on the nourishment of the world,
he should perform the entire circumambulation with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). Then,
with his hand in the *apasavya* position, he should pour water upon the ground.
Then, having formed three *piṇḍas* from the remainder of that sacrificial offering (*havis*), being composed in mind,
he should offer them facing south according to the very same procedure as the water-libation (*audaka*).
Having then offered those *piṇḍas* with self-restraint according to the prescribed rule, he should proceed.
On those *darbha* grasses, he should wipe that hand [on which the food was smeared] for the sake of those who partake of the smears (the *lepabhājinaḥ*).
Having sipped water (*ācamya*), having turned toward the north (*udakparāvṛtya*), and having slowly restrained his breath three times,
he should pay homage with mantras to the six seasons and to the ancestors.
He should slowly pour the remaining water near the piṇḍas again.
With a concentrated mind, he should smell those piṇḍas in the order in which they were placed.
Taking very small portions from the piṇḍas in successive order— [taking a tiny portion from the piṇḍas]—he should consume them.
One should first cause those very Brahmins to sit down according to the prescribed rule. While one’s father is still living, however, one should offer the oblation to the ancestors alone;
or else, in that *śrāddha*, one should seat one’s own father as if he were a Brahmin guest.
If one's father has passed away but the grandfather is still living,
he should pronounce his father’s name and then proclaim the great-grandfather’s name. Or rather, the grandfather himself should partake of that *śrāddha*— so Manu has declared.
Or, having been permitted, he may perform it himself at his pleasure. Having placed *tila* and water along with *pavitra* grass-grass blades into their hands,
he should offer the first portion of that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for them."
Having personally taken the increased portion of food with both hands,
he should slowly place it near the Brahmins while meditating upon the ancestors. Whatever food is served when released from both hands—

The Asuras, who are evil-minded, suddenly plunder that [food]. One should first, being self-restrained and composed, place upon the ground itself the various ingredients such as soups, vegetables, milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey.
Having brought all that— various kinds of food and drink, roots and fruits,
as well as savory meats and fragrant beverages—
he should present it slowly and with great composure.
Being pure, he should serve the food while praising all its qualities.
He should never shed a tear, nor become angry, nor speak untruth.
He should not touch the food with his foot, nor should he shake it.

Anger sends the departed spirits (pretas) to tears, falsehood sends enemies, and touching with the foot sends the Rākṣasas; shaking [the limbs] sends the evildoers. Whatever may be pleasing to the Brahmins, that he should give without envy.

He should engage in discourses concerning the Brahman; this is what is desired by the ancestors. Indeed, at the ancestral rite, he should cause them to hear the private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), the treatises on Dharma, as well as narratives, histories, Purāṇas, and supplementary texts.
Being satisfied himself, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them very gradually. He should repeatedly encourage them with food and drink, as well as with words of praise.
Even if he is observing a vow, one should take care to feed a daughter's son at the *śrāddha*.
One should provide a *kutapa* blanket as a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.

At a *śrāddha*, three things are purifying: a daughter’s son, a *kutapa* blanket, and sesame seeds. Furthermore, three qualities are praised in this context: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
All the food should be very hot, and they should eat while remaining silent. The twice-born should not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering even when asked by the giver.
As long as the food remains warm and as long as they eat in silence, [so long do they obtain the reward].
The ancestors do not eat as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offerings have not been described.
Whatever one eats with his head wrapped, whatever he eats facing south,
and whatever he eats wearing shoes— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
A Caṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, and likewise a dog,
as well as a woman in her menses and a eunuch— these must not look at twice-born men while they are eating.
Whatever is looked upon by these during a burnt offering (homa), a gift, or a meal, [is rendered impure].
In an offering to the gods or to the ancestors, that [food] becomes unfit for the purpose.
A pig destroys it by smelling, a cock by the wind of its wings,
a dog by the fall of its gaze, and one born of a low caste by touch.
Whether he be lame or one-eyed, or even a servant of the giver,
or one with deficient or redundant limbs— one should remove such a person as well.
Likewise, a Brahmin or even a mendicant who has approached for the sake of food [should be removed if he is unworthy].

Having been permitted by the Brāhmaṇas, he should honor them according to his ability. Having gathered together the food and other offerings from all castes and sprinkled them with water, he should scatter it on the ground in front of those who have finished eating.

For those who died before receiving the sacraments, for those who have abandoned their families, and for women of the household, the food-leavings on the *darbha* grass and that which is scattered there constitute their share. Also, the remnants fallen upon the ground belong to one who is upright and free from deceit.
They declare that this is the share of the group of slaves at a rite for the ancestors (pitrya).
However, for a twice-born man who has died before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony has been performed,
one should feed those invited at the *śrāddha* without an offering to the gods (*adaiva*) and offer only a single funeral cake (*piṇḍa*).
But when the *piṇḍakriyā* (the rite of offering the rice-balls) has been performed for him according to the law,
his sons must perform the offering of the *piṇḍas* by this very same procedure.
He who, having eaten at a *śrāddha*, gives the leavings to a *vṛṣala* (a low-caste person), [is guilty].
That fool goes to the Kālasūtra hell,
head-first. He who, having eaten at a śrāddha, approaches the bed of a low-caste woman on that same day—
his ancestors dwell in her excrement for that entire month.
Having asked, "Was it well-savored? he should then cause those who are satisfied to rinse their mouths.
Once they have rinsed, he should dismiss them with the words, "May you rest at your ease.
Immediately thereafter, the Brāhmaṇas should say to him, "Let there be *svadhā*!"
For in all rites for the ancestors, the utterance of *svadhā* is indeed the highest blessing.
Then, after they have eaten, he should inform them regarding the remainder of the food. Having been authorized by the twice-born, he should do exactly as they direct.
At a rite for the ancestors (pitrya), one should say "It is well-tasted" (svaditam); at a rite for cattle, "It is well-cooked" (suśṛtam);
at a rite for prosperity (abhyudaya), "It is excellent" (saṃpannam); and at a rite for the gods (daiva), "It is pleasing" (rucitam).
Likewise, the afternoon, darbha grass, the preparation of the site, and sesame seeds [are required].
Abundance in the *śrāddha* rites consists of the creation [of food], its refinement, and the foremost of the twice-born.
Darbha grass, purificatory means, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial foods (*haviṣya*),
as well as whatever purificatory items were mentioned previously, should be known as the requisites for the sacrificial offering (*havya*).
The food of sages, milk, soma, meat that is unseasoned,
and salt not derived from saline earth are by their very nature called sacrificial oblation (havir).
Having dismissed those Brahmins, being self-controlled, silent, and pure— [having dismissed those Brahmins according to the prescribed rule].
Facing the southern direction, he should pray for these boons from the ancestors:
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
Having thus performed the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), he should immediately thereafter cause a cow,
a Brahmin, a goat, or the fire to consume them, or he should cast them into water.
Some, however, perform the offering of the rice-balls only afterwards.
Others cause [the corpse] to be devoured by birds, or they cast it into fire or water.
Then, a devoted wife, a lawful consort intent upon the worship of the ancestors,
who desires a son, should properly eat the middle *piṇḍa* from among them.
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence,
as well as one who is wealthy, possessed of progeny, virtuous, and righteous.
Having washed his hands and sipped water (ācamana), he should provide for his kinsmen.
Having given honored food to his paternal kinsmen, he should also feed his maternal relatives.
The remains of the meal should stay until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
thereafter, he should perform the domestic *bali* offering—thus the law is established.
I shall describe in its entirety that oblation which, when offered according to the rules to the ancestors, serves for many nights and even for eternity:
with sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits.

When given according to the prescribed rules, the ancestors of men are satisfied for one month by the gift of meat. They are satisfied for two months by the meat of fish, for three months by the meat of the deer, for four months by the meat of sheep, and for five months indeed by the meat of birds.
They are satisfied for six months with the meat of a goat, and for seven with that of the spotted deer (pārṣata);
for eight months with the meat of the black antelope (eṇa), and for nine indeed with that of the ruru deer.
They remain satisfied for ten months, however, with the flesh of the boar and the buffalo.
With the meat of a deer and a tortoise, however, the gratification lasts for exactly eleven months;
with cow's milk and milk-rice (pāyasa), it lasts for a year;
and with the meat of a vārdhrīṇasa, the gratification lasts for twelve years.
Black potherbs, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the rhinoceros and the red goat, honey,
and all kinds of food fit for sages are ordained for infinite [merit].
Whatever else one might offer mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day [is likewise effective].

That gift shall indeed be inexhaustible when given during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism. May there be born in our lineage one who might give us milk-rice with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth lunar day, and during the shadow of an elephant.
Whatever one gives according to the rules and correctly, endowed with faith—
that very thing becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the hereafter.
One should do so during the dark fortnight, beginning from the tenth day, while avoiding the fourteenth day.
These lunar days are praised for the śrāddha ceremony, whereas others are not so. By performing it on even lunar days and under even asterisms, one attains all desires;
but by performing it on odd lunar days, one obtains abundant progeny.
Just as the latter fortnight excels the former fortnight,
so does the afternoon excel the forenoon for the performance of a śrāddha.
With the sacred thread worn over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), properly circumambulating from left to right (apasavya), and without sloth—
The ancestral rite (paitrya) should be performed according to the rules until its conclusion by one who holds *darbha* grass in his hand.
One should not perform a *śrāddha* at night, for that time is declared to belong to the *rākṣasas*;
nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only recently risen.
By this rule, one should perform the Śrāddha here three times a year—
during the Hemanta, Grīṣma, and Varṣā seasons— and perform the five great sacrifices daily.
The oblation pertaining to the ancestors (paitṛyajñiya) is not ordained to be performed in a common (laukika) fire.
For a twice-born man who has established the sacred fires, there is no *śrāddha* without the *darśa* sacrifice.
Whatever satisfaction the best of the twice-born provides to the ancestors with water after bathing,
by that alone he obtains the entire fruit of performing the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*).

They call the Vasus the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and likewise the Ādityas the great-grandfathers; this is the eternal Vedic revelation. One should always eat the remains of the meal (vighasa), or always partake of the nectar (amṛta).
"Vighasa, however, is the remnant of what has been eaten, and likewise, the remnant of a sacrifice is called amṛta.
All this rule regarding the five sacrifices has been declared to you;
now let the rule for the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born be heard."
Having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher, O twice-born ones,
he should dwell in his house as a married man during the second quarter of his life.
A Brahmin should live in times of non-distress by adopting a mode of livelihood that involves no injury to living beings, or at least very little injury;
he should do so for the sake of merely maintaining his existence through his own irreproachable occupations.

One should accumulate wealth without causing distress to the body. One may live by means of the "truthful" (ṛta), the "immortal" (amṛta), the "deadly" (mṛta), or the "very deadly" (pramṛta), or even by the "true-and-false" (satyānṛta); but one should never live by the "dog's mode of life" (śvavṛtti).
The gleanings of grain are to be known as *ṛta*; what is obtained unasked is *amṛta*.
Begging for alms is called *mṛta*, while agriculture is traditionally known as *pramṛta*.
Trade, however, is *satyānṛta* (truth-and-untruth), and one may live by that as well.
Service is declared to be the livelihood of a dog; therefore, one should avoid it.
He may possess a granary full of grain, or a jar full of grain;
he may have enough for three days, or he may not even have enough for the morrow.
Among these four twice-born householders,
each subsequent one should be known as superior in terms of dharma and as more effective for conquering the worlds.
Among them, one follows six duties, while another proceeds by means of three.

One [of these] lives by two [methods], while the fourth lives by the *brahmasattra* (the perpetual sacrifice). Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of grain (*śila*) and picking up single grains (*uñcha*), and being devoted to the *agnihotra*,
he should always perform only the *iṣṭi* sacrifices prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices.
One should never, for the sake of a livelihood, follow the ways of the world in any manner whatsoever. One should live the pure, straightforward, and honest life of a Brāhmaṇa.
Seeking happiness, one should remain self-restrained, relying upon the highest contentment.

For happiness has contentment as its root, while the opposite is the root of suffering. Therefore, a twice-born Snātaka living by any one of these modes of livelihood should observe these following vows, which lead to heaven, long life, and fame.
One should constantly perform, without sloth, one's own duty as proclaimed in the Veda;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.
One should not pursue wealth through worldly attachment nor by means of forbidden actions.
He should not seek objects from here and there when they are available, nor even in times of distress;
he should not become attached out of desire to any of the objects of the senses,
and he should restrain excessive attachment to them with his mind.

One should abandon all pursuits that conflict with the study of one's own Veda; for by teaching in whatever manner possible, one fulfills one's duty, since that indeed constitutes the accomplishment of his purpose. [This applies] to one's age, occupation, wealth, sacred learning, and lineage.
He should conduct himself in this world by conforming his dress, speech,
and thoughts [to those of his teacher]. He should constantly study the scriptures that increase wisdom, as well as the beneficial and auspicious Vedas and their auxiliary branches (Nigamas).

For in whatever measure a person thoroughly masters the scripture, in that same measure he understands it, and his knowledge shines forth. He should always perform the sacrifice to the seers (*ṛṣiyajña*), the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), and the sacrifice to the spirits (*bhūtayajña*).
One should not neglect the sacrifice to men and the sacrifice to the ancestors according to one's ability.
Some people who know the scriptures on sacrifice, without making any effort for these great sacrifices,
constantly offer oblations into the senses alone.
Some always offer the breath into speech and speech into breath,
perceiving within speech and breath the imperishable completion of the sacrifice. Other Brahmins, by means of knowledge alone, always perform sacrifices with these very offerings.
Seeing that their ritual action has its root in knowledge through the eye of wisdom,
one should always offer the Agnihotra at the beginning and end of day and night,
as well as with the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month and with the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice.
At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should perform the *navasasyeṣṭi* sacrifice; likewise, at the end of each season, he should perform the *adhvara* sacrifices.
At the beginning of the solstice (*ayana*), he should perform the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and at the end of the year, the *saumika* sacrifices.
A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires must not fail to perform the *navasasyeṣṭi* and the animal sacrifice.
One who desires to live a long life should not eat new grain or meat.
For his sacred fires, being unpropitiated by offerings of new grain and animal sacrifices, will—
greedy for new grain and meat— desire to consume his very life-breaths.
No guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of his ability with a seat, food, a bed, water, or roots and fruits. He must not allow heretics,
those who follow improper occupations, those who act like cats, or rogues to reside there.
One should not honor, even with mere words, those who are rationalists or those who live like herons.

One should worship with offerings to gods and ancestors (*havya-kavya*) those householders who are learned in the Vedas, purified by their vows and sacred knowledge, and well-versed in the scriptures; one should avoid those who are the opposite.

A householder should give, according to his ability, to those who do not cook for themselves; he should also provide a distribution of food to all living beings without causing hardship to himself. A Snātaka who is suffering from hunger should seek wealth from the king.
Nor from anyone else— this is the settled rule regarding one's patron or a pupil. A learned Snātaka Brahmin must never suffer from hunger,
nor should he wear worn-out or dirty clothes if he possesses the means.
Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard, being self-controlled, wearing white garments, and pure,
he should be constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Veda and in what is beneficial for the self. He should carry a bamboo staff and a water-pot containing water.
He should wear the sacred thread, the Veda, beautiful golden earrings, and a gold ornament on his right hand.
He must never look at the sun when it is rising or setting;
nor when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky.
One should not step over a rope to which a calf is tied, nor should one run while it is raining. One should not look at one's own reflection in water; this is the settled rule.
[One should circumambulate] earth, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, and a crossroads.
One should perform circumambulations around well-known trees.
One should not approach a woman even when intoxicated during her menstrual period,
nor should one sleep with her on the same bed.
For when a man approaches a woman overwhelmed by her menses,
his wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and even his lifespan are diminished.
Therefore, he should avoid her while she is overwhelmed by her menses.
Wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and lifespan indeed increase [for him].
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating,
nor when she is sneezing or yawning, nor when she is seated at her ease.

A twice-born man who desires spiritual luster should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one who is giving birth. He should not eat his food wearing only a single garment, nor should he perform his bath naked.
One should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen;
nor on ploughed land, nor in water, nor on a sacrificial altar, nor on a mountain;
nor ever in a ruined temple, nor on an anthill.
Not in pits containing living beings, nor while walking, nor while standing;
not having reached the bank of a river, nor on the peak of a mountain;
nor while looking at the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or likewise cows.

One should never discharge feces or urine without having covered [the ground] with wood, clods of earth, leaves, grass, or the like. Restraining one's speech, purified, with the body wrapped and the head covered, one should void them.
One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day;
at night, and during the two twilights, one should face south, just as during the day.
In shade or in darkness, whether by night or by day, the twice-born [should act accordingly].
One may act as one pleases when there is danger to life. However,
the wisdom of one who urinates facing fire, facing the sun, facing the moon, water, or a twice-born man,
or facing a cow or facing the wind, shall perish.
One should not blow on the fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet over it.
One should not place it beneath oneself, nor step over it.
One should not kick him with the foot, nor should one cause him any injury to his vital breaths. One should not eat during the twilight hours, nor go out, nor lie down.
One should certainly not scratch the ground, nor remove one's own garland.

One should not discharge urine, feces, or saliva into water, nor anything else smeared with impurity, nor blood, nor poisons. One should not sleep alone in a deserted house, nor should one awaken a superior person. [One may sleep in a deserted house.]
One should not speak with a woman in her courses, nor should one go to a sacrifice unless invited.
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of Brāhmaṇas,
during Vedic study, and while eating, one should keep the right hand raised.
One should not prevent a cow from suckling, nor should one inform anyone of it.
A wise man, having seen a rainbow in the sky, should not point it out to anyone.
One should not dwell in an unrighteous village, nor in one where diseases are exceedingly prevalent.
One should not set out on a journey alone, nor should one dwell for long on a mountain. One should not reside in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one overrun by unrighteous people;
nor in a place occupied by hosts of heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes.
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice overeating.

One should not eat too early, nor too late in the evening, nor having already eaten in the evening should one eat again in the morning. One should not engage in useless exertion, nor should one drink water with the hollowed palms.
He should not eat foods from his lap, nor should he ever be a seeker of idle curiosity.
He should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments;
he should neither clap his hands, nor shout, nor, being impassioned, raise a clamor.

One should never wash one's feet in a vessel made of bell-metal; nor should one eat from a broken dish, nor from one that is defiled by its appearance. One should not wear shoes or clothes that have been worn by others.
One should not travel with draft animals that are ill-trained, nor with those afflicted by hunger or disease; one should not go with those whose horns,
eyes, or hooves are broken, nor with those disfigured by their tails.
He should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks,
and perfect in color and form, without excessively prodding them with the goad. He should avoid the morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and likewise a broken seat.
He should not cut his nails or hair with his teeth, nor should he tear at his nails [with his teeth].
He should not crush a clod of earth, nor should he cut grass with his fingernails. He should not perform any fruitless action, nor anything that results in future suffering.

The man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, or bites his nails, as well as the slanderer and the impure person, quickly goes to destruction. He should not engage in censurable conversation, nor should he wear a garland outside [of his garment].
Riding on the back of cows is in every way utterly condemned.
One should not pass through a village or a walled house by a way other than the gate,
and at night one should avoid the roots of trees from afar.
He should never play with dice, nor should he carry his sandals himself. He should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor with his hands held in his lap, nor while seated on a chair.
Furthermore, he should not eat anything mixed with sesame seeds after the sun has set.
One should not sleep naked here, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from food. One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to bed with wet feet;
for by eating with wet feet, one attains a long life.
One should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of sight;
one should not look at excrement or urine, nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms.
One should not step upon hair, nor upon ashes, bones, or potsherds.
One who desires to live a long life should not eat cotton seeds or chaff.
He should not dwell with outcasts, nor with Cāṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with those of the lowest castes, nor with Antyāvasāyins.
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor his leavings, nor food prepared for sacrifice. One should not teach him the Dharma, nor should one impose a vow upon him.
For he who explains the Dharma to him, and he who imposes a vow upon him, [is at fault].
He sinks into that darkness called "unrestrained" along with that very act itself.
He should not scratch his own head with both hands joined together;
nor, being impure from eating, should he touch it, nor should he bathe without water.
One should avoid seizing the hair and striking the head. Having bathed one's head, one should not touch any limb with oil.
One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste.
[This applies] to those who live by the slaughterhouse, the oil-press, the tavern-sign, or by prostitution.
A single oil-press is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a tavern-sign is equal to ten oil-presses;
prostitution is equal to ten tavern-signs; and a king is equal to ten prostitutes.

A butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses is equal to a king; the acceptance of gifts from him is considered terrible. He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures—
In succession, he goes through these twenty-one hells:
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
the hell Kālasūtra, and likewise Mahānaraka.
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana, Saṃhāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, Pūtimṛttika,
Lohasanku, Ṛjīṣa, Panthāna, and Śālmalī-nadī.
The Forest of Sword-Leaves and likewise the Iron Dolls—
knowing these [to be the consequences], learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and desire their own welfare after death do not accept gifts from kings.
One should wake up during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā and reflect upon dharma and artha,
as well as those bodily hardships rooted in them and the true meaning of the Vedas.
Having risen and performed the necessary duties, one should be purified and composed in mind.
One should stand reciting prayers during the morning twilight for a long time, and likewise during the evening twilight at its proper hour.
By virtue of their prolonged twilight devotions, the seers attained long life,
as well as wisdom, glory, fame, and spiritual luster.
Having performed the ritual commencement (*upākaraṇa*) according to the rules on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada,
a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months.
On the day of Puṣya, however, the twice-born man should perform the formal conclusion (*utsarjana*) of the Vedas outside [the village].
Or, when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived,
having performed the ritual abandonment of the Vedic texts outside according to the scriptures during the forenoon,
he should cease his study for the intervening night and that very day and night.
From that time forward, he should recite the Vedic hymns (*chandāṃsi*) with self-restraint during the bright fortnights;
and he should study all the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas (*vedāṅgāni*) during the dark fortnights. He should not recite them indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras.

Having studied the Veda, one should not sleep again at the end of the night while still fatigued. According to the prescribed rule, a twice-born man who is disciplined should daily recite the *chandaskṛta* (the Vedic meters) and the *brahma* (the Brāhmaṇas), except in times of distress.
One who is studying should always avoid these occasions of non-study (anadhyāya),
as should one who is teaching students according to the prescribed rules:
when there is a whistling wind at night, or when there is a rising of dust during the day.

Those who know the rules of study declare these two to be times of non-study during the rainy season. Manu has declared that when there is lightning, thunder, and rain, or when great meteors fall, there shall be immediate cessation of study for the duration of those conditions.

One should know that when these [phenomena] appear while the sacred fires have been kindled, then there shall be a suspension of study; likewise, there is a suspension during the rainy season and whenever clouds appear out of season. Also, upon a thunderous crash, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the luminaries.
One should know that these occasions for the suspension of study (anadhyāya) last until the same time the next day, even during the rainy season.

But when lightning and thunder occur while the sacred fires have been kindled, the suspension of study shall last as long as the light remains; on other occasions, it lasts for the remainder of the night, just as it does by day.
In villages and in cities, there shall always be a cessation of Vedic study for those desiring perfection in Dharma, as well as whenever a foul odor is present. Furthermore,
study must cease when a corpse is within the village or in the presence of a *vṛṣala*.
There is no study when one is weeping, nor in the midst of a crowd of people;
nor in water, nor at midnight, nor while voiding excrement or urine; nor when impure from food, nor after eating at a *śrāddha*—one should not even contemplate [the Veda] with the mind.

Having accepted an invitation to an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days during the birth-impurity of a king or during the birth-impurity of Rāhu (an eclipse). He shall not recite it as long as the scent and the smear of the *ekoddiṣṭa* food remain.
One should not proclaim the Veda in the presence of a learned Brahmin’s body [if he is impure].

Nor should one study while lying down, with feet raised, or while sitting with the knees bound by a cloth (avasakthikā). One should not study after eating meat or food from a house where a birth or death has occurred (sūtaka).
In mist, at the sound of an arrow, and during both twilights;
on the new moon day, the fourteenth day, the full moon day, and the Aṣṭakās;
for the new moon day destroys the teacher, and the fourteenth day destroys the pupil.
The eighth day of the lunar fortnight and the full moon are sacred to Brahman; therefore, one should avoid them [for study].
A twice-born man should not recite [the Veda] during a dust storm, when the quarters of the sky are aflame, when jackals howl, nor while dogs, donkeys, or camels are barking, nor in a crowd.

One should not study near a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen; nor after wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, or after accepting anything related to a *śrāddha*—whether it be animate or inanimate. Whatever may be part of a *śrāddha* offering, [one must avoid studying immediately thereafter].
Having touched that [food], there is likewise no study, for the twice-born is traditionally said to have his hand as his mouth.
When a village is harassed by thieves, during a panic caused by fire, or when it is overwhelmed by robbers—
and during all extraordinary portents— one should know that there is a temporary suspension of study.
At the Upākarma and the Utsarga ceremonies, a suspension of study for three nights is prescribed;
likewise on the Aṣṭakās and on the nights at the end of the seasons, one should suspend study for a day and a night. One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant.
One should not study while on a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel, nor standing in barren soil, nor while traveling in a vehicle;
nor during a dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle;
nor immediately after eating, nor when food is undigested, nor after vomiting, nor while suffering from indigestion (śukta).

Nor should one ever recite the *Ṛg* or *Yajus* verses after failing to invite a guest, while a strong wind is blowing, when blood has flowed from the body, or when one is wounded by a weapon; nor should one recite them during the sound of the *Sāman*.
Having reached the end of the Veda, or having studied the Āraṇyaka;
the Ṛgveda has the gods as its deities, the Yajurveda belongs to humans, and the Sāmaveda is remembered as belonging to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure.
Knowing this daily extraction of the three Vedas,
the learned first practice it in due order and afterwards study the Veda itself.
[The impurity resulting from contact with] cattle, frogs, cats, dogs, snakes, mongooses, and rats...

One should know that there is no study for a day and a night when someone passes between [the teacher and the pupil]. A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two things as unfit for study: an impure place of Vedic recitation and himself when he is impure.
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth,
a twice-born *snātaka* should always remain celibate, even during the fertile period.
He should not bathe after eating, nor when he is ill, nor at midnight.
One should not constantly wear clothes together with [the sacred thread], nor bathe in an unknown body of water.

One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, a guru, a king, a *snātaka*, or a teacher, nor that of one who is tawny-colored (*babhru*) or one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice (*dīkṣita*).
At midday, at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal, or after eating meat,
as well as during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.
One should also avoid using unguents for the body, bathing with perfumed water, and [touching] feces, urine, or blood.
One should not intentionally stand upon phlegm, spittle, or vomit.
One should not serve an enemy, nor an ally of an enemy,
nor one who is unrighteous, nor a thief, nor another man’s wife.
Indeed, there is nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man’s pursuit of another’s wife in this life. [One should avoid] a Kṣatriya, a serpent, and a Brāhmaṇa who is deeply learned.
One who desires prosperity should never despise those who are weak. For these three, when treated with contempt, may utterly consume a man;
therefore, a wise person should never despise these three.

One should not despise oneself on account of former failures; until death, one should seek prosperity and not consider it difficult to attain. One should speak the truth, one should speak what is pleasant, but one should not speak an unpleasant truth.

One should not speak pleasant falsehoods; this is the eternal law (*dharma*). One should say "bhadraṃ bhadram" (well-being, well-being), or simply say "bhadram" (well-being). One should not engage in groundless enmity or dispute with anyone.
One should not travel too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor when it is high noon;
one should not travel with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with *vṛṣalas*.
One should avoid those who have missing limbs, those with redundant limbs, those deficient in learning, and those advanced in age.

One should not insult those who are deficient in beauty or wealth, nor those who are deficient in birth. (Manu 4.141c) A Brahmin, even if impure, should not touch with his hand a cow, a Brahmin, or fire. (Manu 4.142a) Furthermore, while healthy, he should not look at the hosts of luminaries in the sky during the day while he is impure. (Manu 4.142c)
Having touched these while impure, one should always touch the vital organs with water,
as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand. One who is not ill should not touch his own bodily apertures without a specific reason.
One should avoid all private parts and body hair.
One should be devoted to auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have the senses conquered;
one should daily recite prayers and offer oblations into the fire without weariness.
For those who are devoted to auspicious customs, who are ever self-restrained,
and who constantly engage in recitation and burnt offerings, no misfortune exists.
One should always study the Veda itself at the proper times, remaining free from sloth— or rather, one should constantly recite the Veda.
For they declare that this is his supreme duty; any other is called a secondary duty.
By constant study of the Vedas, by purity, by austerity, and by non-injury toward living beings, he remembers his former birth.
Remembering his former birth, the twice-born man practices the Veda once again;
and through the constant practice of the Veda, he enjoys infinite happiness.
He should always perform the *Sāvitra* and *Śānti* oblations on the sacred festival days (*parvan*).

One should always worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā days and likewise on the Anvaṣṭakā days. One should discharge urine at a distance from one's dwelling, and likewise dispose of the water used for washing the feet and the remnants of food far away.
One should perform acts of friendliness, grooming, bathing, cleaning the teeth, and applying collyrium,
as well as the worship of the deities, specifically in the forenoon. One should also visit the deities and righteous, most excellent twice-born men.
On the festival days (parvan), he should salute the sovereign for the sake of protection, as well as his teachers and the elderly;
he should offer them his own seat and wait upon them with palms joined in reverence,
following behind them as they depart.

One should, unwearied, practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is the root of dharma, properly established in one's own duties as proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti. For through such conduct one obtains long life, and through such conduct one obtains desired offspring.
Through right conduct wealth becomes inexhaustible; right conduct destroys inauspicious marks. For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he constantly shares in suffering, being diseased and short-lived.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct,
who is full of faith and free from malice, lives for a hundred years.
One should carefully avoid whatever action depends upon others.
Whatever is under one's own control, that one should diligently cultivate. All that is under the control of another is suffering; all that is under one's own control is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering.

Whatever action brings satisfaction to his inner self while he performs it, that he should perform with diligence; but he should avoid the opposite. [He should likewise honor] the teacher, the expounder, the father, the mother, and the preceptor.
One should not harm Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics. One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities;
one should also avoid hatred, hypocrisy, pride, anger, and harshness. [Or: hatred and arrogance.]

One should not raise a staff against another, nor, when angry, should one strike him down— with the exception of a son or a pupil, whom one may strike for the purpose of correction. A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brāhmaṇa with the intent to kill [is liable to severe punishment].
He shall revolve in the Tāmisra hell for a hundred years.
Having intentionally struck [another] even with a blade of grass out of anger,
he is born into sinful wombs for twenty-one lifetimes.
By causing blood to flow from the body of a Brāhmaṇa who is not fighting,
a man, through his lack of wisdom, incurs very great suffering after death. As many particles of dust as the blood gathers from the surface of the earth...
For that many years in the next world, the one who causes the shedding of blood shall be devoured by others.
Therefore, a wise man should never even threaten a twice-born person;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body.
For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is based on falsehood,
and who is constantly devoted to violence— he does not prosper in happiness in this world. Even if he suffers for the sake of dharma, he should never set his mind upon adharma.
Seeing the swift downfall of unrighteous sinners,
one should know that unrighteousness practiced in this world does not bear fruit immediately like a cow;
however, maturing gradually, it cuts away the very roots of the doer.
If [the fruit of an action] is not seen in oneself, it appears in one's sons; if not in the sons, then in one's grandsons.
But an unrighteous act never becomes fruitless for the doer. Through unrighteousness one prospers for a time, and thereafter one beholds auspicious things.
Thereby he conquers his rivals, and they shall perish along with their very roots.
He should always apply himself to truth, righteousness, noble conduct, and purity; and, restrained in speech, arms, and belly, he should instruct his pupils in accordance with the Dharma.

One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness; and one should also abandon that righteousness which results in future unhappiness and is censured by the world. One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes, nor dishonest.
One should not be a chatterer, nor should one have a mind intent on deeds that harm others.
One should travel along the path of the virtuous by which one's fathers went and by which one's grandfathers went; traveling by that path, one does not come to ruin.

With the officiating priest, the domestic chaplain, and the teacher; with the maternal uncle, the guest, and the dependent; with the child, the aged, and the sick; with physicians, kinsmen, relations by marriage, and blood relatives;
and with one's mother and father, female cousins, brother, son, and wife— [one should not eat separately].
One should not engage in disputes with one's daughter or with the group of slaves. By renouncing disputes with these, a householder is liberated from all sins;
and by conquering them, he conquers all these worlds.
The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahman; the father is the master of the world of Prajāpati;
the guest is the lord of the world of Indra, and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods.
Female relatives [have power] over the world of the Apsarases, and kinsmen over the world of the Viśvedevas.
For kinsmen are the waters in the world, while mother and maternal uncle are the earth. The child, the aged, the emaciated, and the sick should be known as the lords of space.
An elder brother is equal to a father; one's wife and son are one's own body.
One's shadow, one's group of servants, and a daughter are the ultimate objects of compassion.
Therefore, when insulted by these, one should always endure it without resentment.
Even if one is capable of accepting gifts, one should avoid attachment to them in such circumstances.

For by accepting gifts, his Vedic luster (*brāhmatejas*) is quickly extinguished. A wise man should not accept gifts without knowing the righteous rule regarding the objects received, even if he is perishing from hunger.
But an ignorant man who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter is reduced to ashes like wood.
Gold and food consume his lifespan, while land and a cow likewise consume his body.
Horses [take away] the eyes, clothing the skin, ghee the vital energy, sesame seeds progeny. A twice-born man who lacks austerity, does not study the Vedas,
and delights in receiving gifts sinks down along with that very gift, like one in water with a stone for a raft.
Therefore, an ignorant man should fear accepting gifts from whomever they may come; for even by a very small gift, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud.
One should not offer even water to a twice-born man who follows the "cat-vow" (baiḍālavratika).

A knower of the Dharma should not give to one who follows the "heron-vow" (bakavrata), to a sinner, nor to one who does not know the Vedas. For wealth, even if acquired according to the rules, when given to these three,
results in misfortune for both the giver and the receiver in the next world.
Just as one who crosses water by means of a boat made of stone sinks down,
so do the giver and the receiver sink to the bottom when they are ignorant.
One who makes a display of righteousness, who is ever covetous, deceitful, and a deceiver of the world— [is such a person].
One who is harmful and intent on deceiving everyone should be known as a "cat-vowed" hypocrite (baiḍālavratika).
Looking downward, deceitful, and solely devoted to accomplishing his own ends— such a person is a cat-vowed hypocrite.
A twice-born man who is deceitful, falsely disciplined, and practices the "heron-vow" (bakavrata)—
those Brahmins who follow the heron-vow and those who bear the marks of a cat—
fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful deed.
Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma;
by concealing the sin with a vow, he merely practices deception upon women and Śūdras.
Such Brahmins, both in this world and after death, are censured by those who discourse on the Veda.
A vow that is practiced through deception goes to the Rākṣasas. He who, lacking the marks of an ascetic, lives by assuming the dress of one who possesses them,
takes upon himself the sin of those who truly possess those marks and is born into the womb of an animal.

One should never bathe in water reservoirs belonging to others; for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the evil deeds of the person who constructed the reservoir. His vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, and houses [are likewise forbidden].

One who uses things not given becomes a sharer in one-fourth of the sin. One should always perform one's ritual bathing in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and in mountain clefts and springs.
A wise man should constantly practice the *yamas*, but not the *niyamas* exclusively. By failing to perform the *yamas* while practicing only the *niyamas*, he falls.
Likewise, one should not attend a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), nor one performed by a priest who officiates for an entire village.
A Brāhmaṇa may, on some occasions, eat at a sacrifice offered by a woman or a eunuch, provided that those who offer the oblation there do not perform such an act as is censured by the virtuous.
This is contrary to the will of the gods; therefore, one should avoid it.
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted by disease;
nor that which is infested with hair or insects, or touched intentionally with the foot;
nor that which has been looked upon by a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan), nor even that which has been touched by a woman in her courses.
Food pecked at by birds, touched by a dog,
or even smelled by a cow; food [offered] after a public proclamation,
and especially food from a multitude (gaṇa), food from a courtesan, and that which is despised by the learned.

The food of a thief, a singer, a carpenter, and a usurer; of one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice, a miser, one bound in fetters, and one wearing shackles; of one accused of a crime, a eunuch, a woman who commits adultery with men, and a hypocrite—[one should avoid these].
One should avoid the food of a Śūdra that is sour, stale, or even his leavings;
likewise the food of a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, or one who eats the leavings of others;
as well as the food of an Ugra, the food of a woman in childbirth, and food from which water has been sipped but not yet the ten-day period of impurity has passed.
One should avoid meat that has not been honored, meat killed for no sacred purpose, and the food of a woman who has no male relatives;

likewise, the food of an enemy, the food of a city-dweller, the food of an outcast, and food that has been sneezed upon. One should also avoid the food of a slanderer, a liar, and one who sells the merit of sacrifices.
The food of an actor, the food of a tailor, and likewise the food of an ungrateful person;
the food of a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, and a stage-player; as well as the food of a goldsmith, a basket-maker, and a seller of weapons.
Of those who keep dogs, of liquor-sellers, and of the washerman; of the dyer, of the informer, and of him in whose house lives his wife’s paramour;
of those who tolerate a paramour, and of all those who are entirely ruled by women.
The food of one recently deceased, as well as that which causes dissatisfaction, [should be avoided].
The food of a king takes away one's vital energy (*tejas*); the food of a *śūdra* takes away one's spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
The food of a goldsmith takes away one's lifespan, and the food of a leather-cutter takes away one's fame.
The food of an artisan destroys one's offspring, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength. The food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds.
The food of a physician is pus, while the food of a man's wife is the loss of virility.
The food of a usurer is excrement, and the food of a seller of weapons is filth.
Regarding these others who have been proclaimed in due order as those whose food is unfit to be eaten,
the wise declare their food to be skin, bone, and hair.
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any of these, one should fast for three days;

having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance. A learned twice-born man must not eat cooked food from a Śūdra who does not perform ancestral rites (śrāddha).

If he has no other means of subsistence, he may take raw grain from him for one night’s supply. Having deliberated upon both cases, the gods have declared the food of a miserly Vedic scholar and that of a liberal usurer to be equal.
Prajāpati, having approached them, said: "Do not make the unequal equal.
The gift of a liberal man is purified by faith; that of another is destroyed by a lack of faith.
One should always perform sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) and works of public utility (*pūrta*) with faith, remaining unwearied."

For those two [types of merit] become inexhaustible when performed with faith by means of wealth acquired through righteous means. One should constantly practice the duty of giving (*dāna-dharma*) pertaining to sacrifices and public works,
with a spirit of complete contentment, whenever a worthy recipient is found, according to one's ability.

Whatever may be asked for, it should be given without grudging; for there will arise a worthy recipient who delivers one from all [sins]. The giver of water attains satisfaction, and the giver of food attains imperishable happiness.

The giver of sesame seeds obtains desired offspring; the giver of a lamp obtains excellent sight. The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold obtains a long life. The giver of a house obtains the finest dwellings; the giver of silver obtains supreme beauty.

The giver of clothing attains the same world as Candra; the giver of horses attains the same world as the Aśvins; the giver of a bull attains abundant prosperity; the giver of a cow reaches the realm of the Sun (Brahman);
the giver of a vehicle or a bed obtains a wife; and the giver of protection from fear attains sovereignty.

The giver of grain obtains eternal happiness, and the giver of the Veda attains equality with Brahman. Among all gifts— of water, food, cattle, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter— the gift of the Veda is preeminent.

With whatever disposition one bestows any gift, with that very same disposition one receives it in return, duly honored. He who accepts what is unhonored, or gives only what is honored— [he receives the opposite].
Both of them go to heaven; however, in the opposite case, they go to hell.
One should not be proud of one's asceticism, nor should one speak untruth after performing a sacrifice. Even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, nor should one boast after giving a gift.
Sacrifice perishes through falsehood, and austerity perishes through pride. Life-span is diminished by reviling Brahmins, and the merit of a gift by boasting of it.
One should gradually accumulate dharma, just as termites build up an anthill.
For the sake of a companion in the next world, one should not oppress any living beings.
For neither father nor mother stands as a companion in the hereafter; neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman remains there—dharma alone stands by one.
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes. Alone one experiences the fruit of good deeds, and alone the fruit of evil deeds.
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, [the soul departs].
Relatives turn their faces away and depart, but Dharma follows one after death.
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate Dharma for the sake of a companion;
for with Dharma as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse.
He quickly leads to the radiant world beyond that man who is devoted to dharma and whose sins have been destroyed by austerity— a man whose body is ethereal.
He should always cultivate connections with those who are superior to himself.

Desiring to lead his lineage to excellence, he should abandon those who are base. By associating with the most excellent and avoiding those who are inferior, a Brāhmaṇa attains preeminence; by the opposite conduct, he sinks to the state of a Śūdra.
One who acts with firm resolve, who is gentle and self-controlled, who does not dwell among those of cruel conduct,

and who is non-violent— such a person, through self-restraint and generosity, shall conquer heaven by observing these vows. Fuel, water, roots, fruits, and food that is offered spontaneously [should be accepted].

One may accept honey from anyone, as well as the gift of safety (*abhayadakṣiṇā*). Prajāpati considered alms-food that has been brought forward and offered, even if not previously solicited, to be acceptable even from one who has performed evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years from him who treats her with contempt, nor does the fire carry his sacrificial oblations. [One should offer] a bed,
a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, and curd.
One should not reject roasted grains, fish, milk, meat, and vegetables.
Desiring to support one's elders and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, one may accept gifts from anyone; however, one should not satisfy oneself with them.
But when his teachers have passed away, or even while living at home without them,
seeking his own livelihood, he should always accept [gifts] from virtuous persons.
A sharecropper, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave, and a barber—
Among Śūdras, these are those whose food may be eaten: those who offer themselves [to the guest].
