One should offer oneself according to what one's own nature is, what one intends to do, and how one would treat such a person.
He who represents himself to virtuous men as something other than what he truly is, is the greatest sinner in the world—a thief who robs his own soul.
All objects of speech are fixed; they have their root in speech and issue forth from speech.
But that man who steals their speech is a perpetrator of every kind of theft.
Having discharged his debts to the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rule,
and having entrusted everything to his son, he should dwell relying upon equanimity.

Alone, he should constantly reflect upon what is beneficial for his own self in a secluded place; for by reflecting alone, he attains the supreme good. This eternal rule of conduct for a Brahmin householder has been declared.
And the ritual rules for the vows of a *snātaka* increase one's inner strength and are auspicious.
A Brahmin who knows the Vedic scriptures, conducting himself according to this rule of conduct,
is eternally freed from all taint and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

Having heard these duties of the *snātaka* as they have been declared, the seers spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire: *B 5* Manu05-01a: Having heard these duties of the *snātaka* as they have been declared, Manu05-01c: they spoke this to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire.

"O Lord, how does death prevail over those Brahmins who, as previously described, perform their own duties and are learned in the Vedas and the Shastras? To them, the righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, spoke to those great seers:
Listen to the fault by which Death seeks to slay Brahmins:
through the lack of practice regarding the Vedas, the abandonment of right conduct,
through laziness, and through defects in food, Death seeks to slay Brahmins.
Garlic, leeks, onions,

and mushrooms, as well as things produced from impure substances, are unfit to be eaten by the twice-born. Likewise, red exudations from trees and those produced from incisions (or cuttings) are forbidden.
One should carefully avoid the milk of a cow that has recently calved, as well as colostrum (*pīyūṣa*).

One should also avoid *kṛsara* (rice and peas), *saṃyāva* (sweet cakes of wheat flour), *pāyasa* (milk-rice), and *apūpa* (cakes) prepared for no sacred purpose; likewise, meat not consecrated by ritual slaughter, food intended for the gods, and sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*).
The milk of a cow that has not passed ten days since calving, as well as that of camels, of one-hoofed animals,
of sheep, of a *sandhinī* cow, and the milk of a cow whose calf is missing;
and the milk of all wild animals, with the exception of the buffalo— these are forbidden.

The milk of female animals and all fermented acids (śukta) must indeed be avoided. Among these acids, however, curd may be eaten, as well as everything produced from curd. This also applies to those [fermented drinks] that are distilled from pure flowers, roots, and fruits.

One should avoid all carnivorous birds as well as those that dwell in villages; likewise, one should shun those not specifically permitted, single-hoofed animals, and the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird. One should also avoid the *kalaviṅka*, the *plava*, the swan (*haṃsa*), the *cakravāka*, and the village cock.
The *sārasa* crane, the *rajjuvāla*, the *dātyūha*, the parrot, and the *śārikā*;
the birds that peck with their beaks (*pratudas*), web-footed birds, the *koyaṣṭi*, and those that scratch with their claws;
birds that catch fish by diving, meat from a slaughterhouse, and dried meat (*vallūra*).
The crane, the balākā crane, the raven, the wagtail,
fish-eaters, village pigs, and all kinds of fish—
whosoever eats the flesh of any of these is said to be an eater of that very flesh.
One who eats fish is an eater of all kinds of flesh; therefore, one should avoid fish.
The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are to be eaten when employed in offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
So too are the *rājīva*, the *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and all those with scales.
One should not eat solitary animals or birds that are unknown,

nor any five-toed animals, even if they are specified among those permitted for consumption. Likewise, one may eat the porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare.
They declare that among five-toed animals, those with only one row of teeth— excluding the camel— are edible.
Having intentionally eaten a mushroom, a village pig, garlic, a village cock, an onion, or leek, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste].
Having unintentionally eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance; or else, one may perform the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa. For the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day.
An excellent twice-born man should perform at least one Kṛcchra penance every year.
For the purification of food eaten unknowingly, and especially for that which is known [to be impure], [one should fast].
Praised wild animals and birds may be killed by Brāhmaṇas for the sake of sacrifice, and also for the sustenance of dependents; for Agastya practiced this in ancient times.

For even in ancient sacrifices, such as those performed by Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśas*) were made from the meat of wild animals and birds. Whatever food, whether solid or liquid, is mixed with fat and is not censured, [may be offered].
That which remains as the residue of an oblation (havis) may be eaten even if it has stood overnight; likewise,
all products derived from barley and wheat, as well as preparations of milk, may be eaten by the twice-born even if they have been kept for a long time, provided they are not mixed with oil or fat.
Thus has been declared in full what is edible and what is inedible for the twice-born. Hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.
One may eat consecrated meat, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas.
But when one is appointed according to the rule, even at the risk of his own life;
for Prajāpati ordained that all this is food for the vital breath—
both the stationary and the moving are the sustenance of the vital breath.
Non-moving beings are the food of moving ones; those without fangs are the food of those with fangs;
those without hands are the food of those with hands; and cowards are the food of the brave. One who eats does not incur sin by eating edible creatures day after day.
For the Creator himself created the primary living beings as both eaters and the food;
the consumption of meat for the sake of sacrifice is recorded as the divine ordinance. Any practice other than this is called the demonic ordinance.
Having purchased it, or having produced it himself, or even having received it from another,
one does not incur sin by eating meat after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors. A twice-born man who knows the rule should not eat meat contrary to the rule when there is no distress.

For having eaten meat contrary to the prescribed rule, one becomes a helpless ghost and is devoured by those very creatures. The sin incurred by a hunter seeking wealth is not as great as that which falls upon one who eats meat in vain after death.

But that man who, being duly appointed according to the rule, does not eat meat, goes after death to the state of an animal for twenty-one births. A Brahmin should never eat animals that have not been consecrated with sacred mantras.
One who adheres to the eternal rule should eat animals consecrated with mantras.
In a time of distress, one may perform a *ghṛtapasu* sacrifice or likewise a *piṣṭapasu* sacrifice;
however, one should never desire to kill an animal in vain.
As many hairs as there are on the animal's body,
so many times does the one who slaughters an animal in vain suffer death after death in successive births.
Animals were created by the Self-existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice.
Sacrifice leads to the prosperity of this entire world; therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not considered killing.
Herbs, animals, trees, beasts, and birds that meet their death for the sake of sacrifice attain higher states of existence once again.

"In the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka), in a sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors or the gods—it is only in these cases that animals may be slain, and not elsewhere; so said Manu. A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas, when slaying animals for these purposes,"
He leads both himself and the animal to the highest state.
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-controlled twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress.

One should know that even that violence toward the moving and non-moving beings which is ordained by the Veda and restricted to this [dharma] is indeed non-violence; for Dharma has shone forth from the Veda. He who destroys harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure—
Whether living or dead, he never prospers in happiness— he who does not desire to inflict the pains of bondage and death upon living beings. He who seeks the welfare of all enjoys ultimate happiness.
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and toward whatever one forms an attachment—
that one obtains without effort, provided that one does not harm anything whatsoever.
Indeed, no meat is produced anywhere without having caused injury to living beings.

The slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat. Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the killing and binding of embodied beings, one should desist from the eating of all kinds of meat.

He who does not eat meat, even though he has disregarded the [permitted] rule, like a *piśāca*, does not become beloved in the world and is not afflicted by diseases. [Furthermore, the following are considered killers: the one who consents, the one who dissects, the one who slays, and the one who buys or sells.

The one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it— all these are killers. There is no greater evildoer than he who, without having honored the ancestors and the gods, seeks to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another.
He who should perform the horse-sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal. [Likewise,
it is equal to] subsisting on pure fruits and roots, or by eating the food of sages.
One does not obtain that fruit which comes from the total avoidance of meat.
"He who eats my flesh here, he shall eat my flesh in the next world"—
this, the wise declare, is the true nature of meat (*māṃsa*).
There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse;
for this is the natural inclination of living beings, but abstention from them yields great fruit. I shall now declare the purification for the dead, as well as the purification of objects.
For all four castes, in due order and according to rule:

when one has died—whether teeth have appeared, or they have not yet appeared, or the tonsure ceremony has been performed—all relatives remain impure; it is declared that the same applies during a birth.
Impurity on account of death (śāva) is ordained for ten days among the sapindas;
it may last until the collection of the bones, or for three days, or even for one day.
However, the status of being a sapinda ceases with the seventh person.
The status of being a *samānodaka* (a kinsman beyond the seventh degree) ceases when both the birth and the name are unknown.
Just as this period of impurity (*āśauca*) is prescribed for *sapiṇḍas*,
so too should it be in the case of birth for those who desire complete purity.

For all [relatives], there is impurity due to death; however, for the mother and father, there is birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). Birth-impurity belongs to the mother alone, while the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution (*upaspṛśya*).
Having emitted semen, a man becomes pure simply by sipping water;
however, due to the biological connection [of procreation], he should observe impurity for three days.
This consists of one day and night, along with three periods of three nights each.
Those who touch a corpse are purified after three days, as are those who offer water for it. A student, however, performing the funeral rites (pitṛmedha) for his deceased teacher,
is purified there by ten nights, together with those who carry the corpse.
In the case of a miscarriage, one is purified in as many nights as there were months of pregnancy;
when her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who was menstruating becomes pure by means of a bath.
For men whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has not been performed, purification is declared to take one night.

For those whose tonsure ceremony has been performed, purification is held to occur after three nights. A deceased child less than two years old, having been adorned, the kinsmen should place outside on pure ground, except for the collection of bones.

No consecration by fire (agnisaṃskāra) should be performed for him, nor should the water-libation rite (udakakriyā) be performed. Having abandoned him in the forest like a piece of wood, they should observe impurity for exactly three days.
The water-libation rite should not be performed by relatives for one who has not reached three years of age.

Or they may perform it for one who has cut his first teeth, or even when the naming ceremony has been performed. For a fellow student, a single day of fasting is prescribed once [the period of] impurity has passed;
however, for those who share the same water (sapinda), purification is held to occur after three nights upon a birth.

In the case of women who have not been consecrated [by marriage], their kinsmen become pure after three days; however, those of the same lineage (sapinda) become pure according to the very rule already stated. They should subsist on food free from pungent substances and salt, and they should immerse themselves in water for three days.
They shall not eat meat and shall sleep separately on the ground. This rule for impurity due to birth has been proclaimed for when one is present;
when absent, this following procedure should be known by the relatives and kinsmen.
If one hears that a person residing in a foreign land has died before the ten-day period has elapsed,
he shall remain impure for only as much time as remains of those ten days.
But if the ten-day period has already passed, he shall remain impure for three nights.
When a year has passed, however, one becomes pure simply by touching water.
Upon hearing that a kinsman has died within ten days, or upon hearing of the birth of a son,
a person becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes.
If a child, one who has gone to another country, or a person belonging to a different lineage (pṛthakpiṇḍa) dies,
one becomes pure immediately after immersing oneself in water with one's clothes on.
If, within the ten-day period, there should occur again either a death or a birth, [one must observe the full period].
A Brahmin remains impure for as long as that [period] has not yet passed ten days.
They declare that when a teacher has died, the period of impurity lasts three nights;
but for his son and his wife, it is one day and night—this is the settled rule.

Upon the death of a *śrotriya* who has arrived as a guest, one shall remain impure for three nights; likewise for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, the impurity lasts for a night with its two surrounding days (*pakṣiṇī rātri*). When a king dies, one who resides within his territory remains impure for as long as the light [of the sun or stars] lasts.

But for one who is not a *śrotriya*, the impurity lasts for the entire day; likewise for a teacher who has studied the Vedas. A Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month.

One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one interrupt the rites performed in the sacred fires. Even while performing those rites, a kinsman does not become impure. [One should avoid] a dog-cooker (divākīrti), a woman in her courses, an outcast, and likewise a woman who has recently given birth.
Having touched a corpse or one who has touched it, he becomes pure by bathing.

Having sipped water and being constantly self-restrained, he should recite hymns addressed to the Sun according to his energy, and the *Pāvamānī* verses according to his ability, upon seeing anything impure.
Having touched a human bone that still has marrow, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is bone without marrow, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun.
One who has been initiated for a vow (ādiṣṭī) shall not offer water libations until the completion of his vow.
But when [the period] is completed, having performed the water libation, one becomes pure after three nights alone.
For those born of improper mixtures, for those who persist in the life of wandering mendicants,
and for those who commit suicide, the water libation rite shall be withheld.
And for women who have resorted to heretical sects, those who act out of lust, those who harm their fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor;
[one should avoid] the teacher, one's own sub-teacher, the father, the mother, and the preceptor.
Having carried out the dead, one who observes a vow is not deprived of his vow. One should carry out a deceased Śūdra through the southern gate of the city;
however, for the twice-born, they should be carried out through the western, northern, or eastern gates as appropriate.

There is no taint of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those engaged in sacrificial sessions (sattra); for they always occupy the station of Indra and have become one with Brahman. Immediate purification is ordained for a king in his high and exalted position.
And the reason for his seat here is for the sake of protecting the subjects.
[He is pure] for those killed in a riot or battle, by lightning, or by the king;
likewise for one who died for the sake of a cow or a Brāhmaṇa, or for whomsoever the king so desires.
The king bears the form of the eight guardians of the world: Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vitta-pati, and Yama. A king presided over by the Lord of the World—no impurity is ordained for him.

For the purity and impurity of mortals are the very source and dissolution of their worlds. For one slain in battle by uplifted weapons while following the duty of a Kṣatriya, the sacrifice is immediately completed, and so too is the period of impurity; such is the settled rule.
A Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by touching water, a Kṣatriya by his mount or weapon,
a Vaiśya by his goad or reins, and a Śūdra who has performed his duties by a staff.
O best of the twice-born, this purification regarding sapinda relations has been declared to you.

Learn now the purification regarding all those who are not *sapiṇḍas* after a death. Having carried out a deceased twice-born man who is not a *sapiṇḍa* like a kinsman, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as do the maternal relatives who are his mother’s *āptas*.
If he eats their food, however, he is purified in ten days alone;
if he does not eat their food, he is purified in a single day, provided he does not dwell in that house.
Having voluntarily followed a deceased person—whether a relative or even a stranger—[he is purified by bathing].
Having bathed with his clothes on and touched fire, he becomes pure after consuming clarified butter.
One should not have a deceased Brahmin carried by a Śūdra while his own kinsmen are present;
for that offering, defiled by contact with a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind,
water, collyrium, wind, action, the sun, and time are the purifiers of embodied beings.
Among all forms of purity, purity of wealth is declared to be the highest.
He who is pure in his purpose is truly pure; he is not pure merely by being cleansed with earth and water.

The wise are purified through forbearance, and those who have committed improper acts are purified through charity. Those whose sins are concealed are purified by the recitation of prayers (*japa*), and those most learned in the Vedas are purified by austerity (*tapas*).
That which is to be purified is cleansed by clay and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation (saṃnyāsa). Limbs are purified by water, and the mind is purified by truth.
The self of beings is purified by knowledge and austerity, and the intellect is purified by wisdom. This determination regarding the purification of the body has been declared to you;
now hear the determination regarding the purification of various kinds of substances.
For objects made of metal, gems, and all things made of stone,
purification has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and earth.
A golden vessel that is free from stains is purified by water alone.

That which is born of water, that which is made of stone, and silver— provided it is not artificially refined— along with gold and silver, have emerged from the union of water and fire. Therefore, for these two [gold and silver], purification by their own source is most effective.
The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin,
and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water. For all liquids, purification is traditionally held to consist of straining.
Sprinkling with water is prescribed for solid objects, and scraping is for wooden ones.
In the performance of a sacrifice, the purification of sacrificial vessels is by wiping with the hand;
however, the purification of the *camasa* cups and the *graha* vessels is by washing.
The purification of *caru* vessels and of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is by means of hot water;
likewise for the *sphya* and winnowing basket, the cart, and the pestle and mortar.
However, the purification of large quantities of grain and clothing is by sprinkling them with water.
But for small quantities, purification with water by washing is prescribed.
The purification of skins is like that of clothes, and likewise for items made of split cane. For vegetables, roots, and fruits, purification is desired to be the same as that for grain.
Silk and woolen garments are purified with alkaline salts; blankets made of kutapa wool with ariṣṭaka fruits; fine silk cloths with bilva fruits; and linen cloths with white mustard seeds.
Conch shells, horns, bone, and ivory are purified in the same manner as linen.
Purification should be performed by one who knows [the rules] using cow urine or water.
Grass and wood are purified by sprinkling, as is straw. A house is purified by sweeping and smearing with cow dung, and an earthen vessel by being fired again.
Earthenware that has been defiled by intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, spittle, pus,
or blood can never be purified by re-firing.
[However, earthenware] may be purified by sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, sprinkling with water, and scraping.

And the ground is purified by the five [actions] involving cows: by their dwelling upon it. That which has been pecked at by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, or sneezed over, and that which is defiled by hair or insects, is purified by the scattering of earth.

As long as the odor and the stain caused by an impure substance do not depart from an object smeared with it, so long must earth and water be applied for the purification of all such articles. The gods ordained three things as purifiers for Brāhmaṇas: [earth, water, and fire].
That which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is praised by word [is pure]. Water found on the ground is pure when it is sufficient to satisfy the thirst of a cow,
provided it is not contaminated by impurity and possesses its natural odor, color, and taste.
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise spread out for sale;
almsfood received by a student of sacred knowledge is always pure—this is the settled rule.
The mouth of women is always pure, as is a bird when it causes fruit to fall.

A calf is pure when discharging its urine; a dog is pure when seizing game. Manu has declared that the flesh of an animal killed by dogs is pure, as is the flesh of one killed by other carnivorous beasts or by robbers such as Caṇḍālas and the like.
All the apertures above the navel are entirely pure;
those below are impure, as are the excretions that issue from the body.
Flies, droplets of water, shadows, a cow, a horse, and the rays of the sun [are pure].
One should declare that dust, earth, wind, and fire are pure to the touch.
For the purpose of purification after the voiding of feces and urine,
earth and water should be used in sufficient quantity, as well as for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities.
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, nasal mucus, earwax,
phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat— these twelve are the impurities of men.
One [application of earth] on the penis, three on the anus, and likewise ten on one hand.
Seven applications of clay should be given for both [hands] by one desiring purity.
This purification is prescribed for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Having voided urine or excrement, one who has sipped water (ācānta) should touch the cavities of the head;
likewise always when about to study the Veda or when eating food.
One should first sip water three times, and then wipe the mouth twice.
For a woman and a Śūdra who desire bodily purity, however, it shall be performed once each. (Manu 5.139c) For Śūdras who live according to the law, shaving must be performed every month;
their rules for ritual purity are like those of Vaiśyas, and they may eat the remnants of the food of the twice-born. (Manu 5.140)

The primary drops that fall from the mouth do not make one impure by leavings, nor do those which do not reach the body. The hairs of the beard that enter the mouth, nor what remains between the teeth, do not cause impurity.
Nor do the drops that touch the feet of one who is providing water for others to rinse their mouths.
They should be known as equal to those born of the earth; one does not become impure by contact with them.
But if one who holds something in his hand is somehow touched while still having remnants of food (ucchiṣṭa), he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that object down.

Having vomited or been purged, one should bathe and then perform the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). After eating food, one should simply sip water (*ācamana*); bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.
Having slept, sneezed, eaten, spat, or spoken untruths, [one should likewise sip water].

Having drunk water and when about to study, one should sip water even if one is already pure. This entire rule for purification, as well as the purification of objects, has been declared to you for all social classes; now learn the duties of women.

Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an aged woman, no action whatsoever should be performed by a woman independently, even within her own home. In childhood, she should remain under the authority of her father; in youth, under that of her husband.
When her husband has died, a woman should not exercise independence even among her sons.
She should not seek separation from her father, her husband, or her sons;
for by being separated from them, a woman brings reproach upon both families.

She should always be cheerful and skillful in her domestic duties; she should keep the household utensils well-maintained and be not wasteful in expenditure. To whomsoever her father may give her, or her brother with the father’s consent—
One should serve him while he lives and must not transgress against him when he has passed away.
For the sake of auspiciousness, for well-being, and as a sacrifice to Prajāpati, these rites are performed at the wedding;
however, the formal giving of the bride is the cause of the husband's ownership.
A husband who performs the consecration with mantras both out of season and during the fertile period is the constant bestower of happiness upon his wife, both in this world and in the next.
Even if he is ill-behaved, driven by lust, or devoid of good qualities, [he remains her lord].
A virtuous wife must always serve her husband like a god.
For women, there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, and no fasting;
by serving her husband, she is exalted in heaven.
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, should do nothing whatsoever displeasing to her husband, whether he be living or dead. She may, however,
at her will emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits.
But she must not even utter the name of another man once her husband has died.
Until death, she should remain patient, self-restrained, and chaste,
desiring that unsurpassed dharma which belongs to women devoted to a single husband.

Many thousands of young Brahmins, remaining celibate students (*kumāra-brahmacārin*), have gone to heaven without having produced offspring for their lineage. When her husband has died, a virtuous wife who remains steadfast in celibacy [attains the same state].
Even those who are childless go to heaven, just like those celibate students.
But that woman who, out of desire for offspring, transgresses against her husband,
incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world.
In this world, there is no offspring produced by another man, nor even upon the possession of another;
nor is a second husband ever prescribed for virtuous women.
She who, having abandoned her own inferior husband, resorts to one who is superior— Manu 5.162–163a.
She becomes indeed contemptible in the world and is called "one who has had a previous husband. Through infidelity toward her husband, a woman incurs reproach in the world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by diseases resulting from her sin.
She who does not act treacherously toward her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the world of her husband and is called a "virtuous woman" by the righteous. By this conduct, a woman remains restrained in mind, speech, and body.

In this world he attains supreme fame, and in the next world, the realm of his husband. A twice-born man who knows the Law should cause a wife of equal caste, who has conducted herself in this manner and who dies before him, to be cremated with the *agnihotra* fire and the sacrificial implements.
Having given the sacred fires to his wife who has died before him during the funeral rites,
he may again perform the act of taking a wife and likewise the re-establishment of the fires.
By this rule, he should never neglect the five daily sacrifices.
Having taken a wife, he should dwell in his house during the second stage of life.
Thus, having remained in the stage of the householder according to the rules, the twice-born man who has completed his Vedic studies—
He should dwell in the forest, self-restrained and with his senses fully conquered, according to the rule.
But when a householder perceives his own skin wrinkled and his hair turned gray,
and sees the offspring of his offspring, then he should take refuge in the forest.
Having completely abandoned food fit for village life and all personal belongings,
he should entrust his wife to his sons and go to the forest, or else depart together with her,
taking with him the *agnihotra* fire and the domestic implements required for the sacred fires.
Having departed from the village for the forest, he should dwell there with his senses restrained. Subsisting on various kinds of pure food fit for sages— such as vegetables, roots, and fruits—
he should perform these very same great sacrifices according to the prescribed rules.
He should wear either a skin or a garment of bark; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always bear matted hair, as well as his beard, body hair, and nails.
Whatever may be his food, from that he should offer the bali-oblation and alms according to his ability.
He should honor those who have come from their respective stages of life with water, roots, fruits, and alms-food.
He should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda, self-controlled, friendly, and composed;
he should be a constant giver, never a receiver, and compassionate toward all living beings.
He should perform the Vaitānika Agnihotra sacrifice according to the prescribed rules,
not omitting the New Moon (Darśa) and Full Moon (Paurṇamāsa) sacrifices at their proper times.
He should also perform the Nakṣatreṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
He should also perform the *turāyaṇa* and the *dākṣāyaṇa* sacrifices in their proper sequence.
With pure food fit for sages, gathered by himself during the spring and autumn seasons,
he should separately offer sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and oblations (*caru*) according to the prescribed rules.
Having offered that most pure wild grain as an oblation to the deities,
he should consume the remainder for himself, as well as salt prepared by himself.
He may eat vegetables growing on land or in water, as well as flowers, roots, and fruits.
One should eat oils derived from pure trees and those produced from fruits;
one should avoid honey, meat, mushrooms growing from the earth,
bhūstṛṇa grass, the śigruka plant, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree.

In the month of Āśvayuja, he should discard the food of sages previously stored, as well as his worn-out clothes and his vegetables, roots, and fruits. He should not eat food grown on land tilled by a plow, even if it has been discarded by someone.
Even when distressed, he must not take roots or fruits grown in a village [or flowers and fruits].
He may either eat food cooked by fire, or eat only what is ripened by time;
he may also be one who grinds with a stone, or one who uses his teeth as a mortar.
He may either wash away his food immediately, or store enough for a month;
he may store enough for six months, or even enough for a year.
Having gathered food according to his ability, he may eat it at night, or during the day.
He may eat at every fourth mealtime, or even at every eighth mealtime;
or he may conduct himself according to the rules of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance during both the bright and dark fortnights;
or he may eat boiled barley-gruel once at the end of each fortnight.

Or, remaining steadfast in the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas, he should always subsist solely on flowers, roots, and fruits that have ripened in due time and fallen of their own accord. During the day, he should either roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes.

He should pass his time standing during the day and sitting at night, bathing at the three ritual sessions; in summer he should practice the "five-fire" penance, in the rainy season he should live under the open sky,
and in winter he should wear wet clothes, gradually increasing his austerity.
Performing ablutions three times a day, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
practicing even more rigorous austerity, he should wither his own body.
Having formally internalized the Vedic sacrificial fires within himself according to the prescribed rule, he should dwell as a forest hermit.
He should be without a sacred fire and without a fixed dwelling, a silent sage subsisting on roots and fruits;
he should be effortless regarding objects of pleasure, a celibate student, sleeping on the ground;
he should have no sense of ownership over shelters and should take his abode at the foot of a tree.
He should obtain alms sufficient for his sustenance from ascetic Brahmins alone,
or from other twice-born householders living in the forest.
Or, while dwelling in the forest, he may bring eight mouthfuls from a village and eat them.
Having accepted [the alms] with a cupped hand or with his entire hand,
the Brahmin living in the forest should practice these and other initiatory rites,
as well as various Upaniṣadic teachings for the sake of self-perfection.
These have been practiced by the seers and by brahmins who were householders for the sake of increasing knowledge and austerity, and for the purification of the body. Or,
having set out toward the Aparājita direction, he should proceed straight on.
Until the fall of the body, he should remain disciplined, subsisting on water and air. Having cast off his body by means of one or another of these practices of the great seers,
the Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having thus spent the third part of his life in the forests,
he should abandon all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life;
having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations, and having conquered his senses.
Exhausted by the distribution of alms and offerings, one who renounces the world prospers after death.
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward.
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma,

and having performed sacrifices according to his ability, a twice-born man should direct his mind toward liberation. Likewise, a twice-born man who has not studied the Vedas and has not procreated sons [or offspring] should not perform the final rites.
And he who desires liberation without having performed sacrifices goes downward.
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having consigned the sacred fires into himself, a Brāhmaṇa may depart from his home as a wandering mendicant.

For that teacher of the Veda who goes forth from his home after having granted fearlessness to all beings, there exist worlds consisting of radiant splendor. Since not even the slightest fear arises for living beings from that twice-born man, [he attains those worlds].
For him who is liberated from the body, there is no fear from any quarter whatsoever.
Having departed from his home, purified by sacred observances, the sage should wander as a mendicant,
indifferent toward all objects of desire even when they are presented to him.
He should always wander alone, without companions, for the sake of attaining perfection;
seeing that perfection belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons nor is abandoned.
He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, resorting to a village only for the sake of food.

Indifferent, free from agitation, a sage whose mind is absorbed in being; an alms-bowl, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, solitude, and equanimity toward all things— this is the characteristic of one who is liberated.
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life;
one should simply await the appointed time, just as a hired laborer awaits his wages.
One should place one's foot down purified by sight, and drink water purified by a cloth.
One should speak words purified by truth and practice conduct purified by the mind. One should endure harsh speech and never despise anyone.
And, depending upon this body, one should not harbor enmity toward anyone.

One should not return anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly; and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates. Seated in self-contemplation, indifferent to the world, and free from worldly desires— Manu 6.48a: One should not return anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly. Manu 6.48c: And one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates. Manu 6.49a: Seated in self-contemplation, indifferent, and free from worldly desires.
Seeking happiness, he should wander about in this world with himself alone as his companion.
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology or physiognomy,
nor by giving instructions or engaging in discourse.

He should not approach a house crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants. Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard, and carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot, he should go about.
He should wander constantly, self-restrained, without causing pain to any living beings. His vessels should be made of non-metallic materials and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as that for the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice.

A gourd, a wooden vessel, one made of clay, and likewise one made of split bamboo—these, Svāyambhuva Manu declared, are the vessels for an ascetic. He should go out for alms only once a day; he should not be attached to an abundance of food.
For a renunciant who is overly attached to begging becomes attached even to sense objects.

A renunciant should always go for alms when the smoke has ceased, when the pestle has been laid down, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal, and when the removal of the dishes has taken place.

He should not be dejected when he gains nothing, nor should he rejoice when he gains something; he should have only as much as is necessary for the maintenance of life, being free from attachment to material things. He should, moreover, always despise gains obtained through honor.
Even a renunciant who is already liberated may become bound by gains that are highly honored.
By consuming only a small amount of food and by staying and sitting in solitude,
he should withdraw his senses when they are being carried away by sense objects.

By the restraint of the senses, by the destruction of passion and hatred, and by non-violence toward all beings, one becomes fit for immortality. One should contemplate the destinies of men, which arise from the defects of their actions.
Falling into hell and undergoing torments in the abode of Yama;
separation from loved ones and union with those who are unpleasant;
being overcome by old age and afflicted by diseases.
The departure from this body, the subsequent conception in a womb,
the wanderings of this inner self through thousands of millions of births,
and the connection with suffering for embodied beings arising from unrighteousness— [all these he beholds].
One should also contemplate the inexhaustible union with happiness that originates from dharma and artha,
as well as the subtlety of the Supreme Self through yoga,
and its manifestation within bodies, both high and low.

Even if he is corrupted, one who is devoted to any stage of life (āśrama) should practice dharma; for among all beings, equanimity is the cause of dharma, not the outward mark (liṅga). Although the fruit of the kataka tree is a clarifier of water, [it does not clarify itself].
The water does not become clear merely by uttering his name.
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day,
and even when his own body is in distress, he should always walk upon the earth after inspecting it.
Whatever living beings an ascetic kills unintentionally by day or by night,

for the sake of purifying himself from those sins, he should bathe and perform six breath-suppressions (prāṇāyāmas). Even three breath-suppressions, when performed according to the rule, constitute a complete purification for a Brāhmaṇa.
Accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*, this should be known as the supreme austerity.
Just as the impurities of metals being smelted are burnt away,
so too are the defects of the senses burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
One should burn away defects by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and sin by means of concentrations (dhāraṇā);
one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and unmastered qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna).
Among beings high and low, [the Self] is difficult to know for those who have not disciplined themselves.
Through the yoga of meditation, one should perceive the course of this inner self.
Endowed with right vision, one is not bound by actions;
but deprived of such vision, one enters the cycle of transmigration.
Through non-violence, restraint of the senses, Vedic rites,
and the rigorous practice of austerities, they attain that state in this world.
[The body] has bones for its pillars, is bound together by sinews, and is plastered with flesh and blood.
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and feces;
which is possessed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease,
afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent.

Just as a tree leaves the riverbank, or as a bird leaves a tree, so one who abandons this body is released from the crocodile of distress. One's good deeds [are transferred] to one's own loved ones, and one's evil deeds to those who are disliked.

Having cast off [all attachments] through the yoga of meditation, he attains the eternal Brahman. When one becomes free from longing toward all objects of existence by means of one's inner disposition,
then one attains everlasting happiness both after death and in this world.
By this method, gradually abandoning all attachments,
he who is liberated from all pairs of opposites remains established in Brahman alone.
All this that has been described is entirely the result of meditation.

For no one who is ignorant of the inner self (adhyātma) ever enjoys the fruit of ritual action. One should constantly recite the Brahman pertaining to sacrifice (adhiyajña), that pertaining to the deities (ādhidaivika), and that pertaining to the inner self (ādhyātmika), as well as that which is declared in the Vedāntas.
This is the refuge for the ignorant; this indeed is for those who possess knowledge.
This is for those seeking heaven; this is for those seeking infinity.
The twice-born man who renounces the world according to this sequential method—
Having shaken off evil in this world, he attains the supreme Brahman.
This dharma has been taught to you for ascetics of restrained soul who have renounced the Vedas;
now learn the yoga of action for those who have renounced the Vedas.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
these four distinct stages of life (āśramas) originate from the householder.
Indeed, all of these, when practiced in their proper sequence according to the scriptures, [lead to the highest goal].
The Brahmin who acts according to what has been prescribed attains the supreme goal.
And among all these, according to the injunctions of the Veda and the Smṛti,
the householder is said to be the best, for he supports these other three.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
even so do all those in the other stages of life find their support in the householder. And by these four classes of twice-born men belonging to the various stages of life, [the world is sustained].
The tenfold dharma should be practiced with diligent effort:
fortitude, forbearance, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity,
control of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this is the tenfold characteristic of dharma.
Those Brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of dharma, and having studied them, follow them accordingly, attain the supreme goal. One who,
with a concentrated mind, practices the dharma characterized by these ten marks, [attains that same goal].
Having heard the Vedānta according to the prescribed rule, a twice-born man, free from debts, should renounce.
Having renounced all ritual acts and having cast off the defects of karma, he should, being self-controlled,
study the Veda and dwell happily under the sovereignty of his sons.

Having thus renounced all actions, intent upon his own duty and free from longing, he destroys sin through renunciation and attains the supreme goal. This fourfold dharma of the Brāhmaṇa has been declared to you.
Meritorious and yielding inexhaustible fruit after death—learn now the duty of kings. (Manu 6.97c) I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a ruler should conduct himself. (Manu 7.1a)
How his origin occurred and how his supreme perfection was attained;
and how, by a Kṣatriya who has received the Brāhmaṇical consecration according to rule,
the protection of all this [world] must be performed in accordance with justice.
For in this world without a king, everything would have fled in all directions out of fear;
therefore, for the protection of all this, the Lord created a king from the powers of Indra,
Anila (Wind), Yama, Arka (Sun), Agni, and Varuṇa.
Having extracted the eternal portions from the Moon, from Wealth (Kubera), and from Sleep (Nidrā);
because the king was fashioned from the portions of these lords of the gods,
he therefore surpasses all beings in his splendor.
He blazes like the sun, scorching both eyes and minds;
yet no one on earth is able even to look upon him.
He becomes fire, he becomes wind, he becomes the sun, the moon, and the King of Dharma (Yama).

By his power, he is Kubera, he is Varuṇa, and he is Mahendra; even as Indra, he exists through his own majesty. A king, though he be a child, must not be disregarded on the grounds that he is merely a human being; for he is a great divinity dwelling in the form of a man.
Fire burns only the man who approaches it carelessly;
but the king’s fire, like the fire of destruction, consumes the entire family along with its cattle and accumulated wealth.
Therefore, having carefully considered the matter at hand, his own power, and the specific place and time, [the king should act].
For the sake of accomplishing dharma, he repeatedly assumes manifold forms. Prosperity dwells in his favor, victory in his valor, and death resides in his anger; for he is composed of all splendor.

But whoever, out of delusion, hates him, will undoubtedly perish; for the king sets his mind upon that person's swift destruction. Therefore, the lord of men should apply himself to whatever duty is desired by those he holds dear.
And even when it is applied to those who deserve it not, he should not deviate from that dharma.
For the sake of that [dharma],
the Lord created in the beginning the staff, which is his own son, the protector of all beings, consisting of the splendor of Brahman.

Out of fear of him, all beings, both stationary and moving, become fit for their enjoyment and do not deviate from their own duty. Having duly considered his place, time, power, and learning, [the king should act].
He should apply punishment appropriately toward men who act unjustly. He is the king, he is the personification of punishment, he is the leader, and he is the ruler;
he is recorded as the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.
Punishment governs all subjects; punishment alone protects them.
Punishment keeps watch while others sleep; the wise know punishment to be Dharma.
When properly administered after careful consideration, it brings joy to all subjects.
But when applied without due consideration, it destroys everything on all sides.
(Manu 7.19c) If the king were not vigilant in inflicting punishment upon those deserving of punishment, the stronger would devour the weaker like fish on a spit. (Manu 7.20)
A crow might eat the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), and a dog might lick the oblation (havis);
there would be no sense of ownership over anything, and everyone would behave as they pleased, superior or inferior.
The entire world is kept in order by punishment, for a pure man is indeed hard to find.
For through fear of punishment, the entire world is fit for enjoyment.
Even gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds,
and serpents are made fit for enjoyment only when restrained by punishment.
All social classes would become corrupt and all moral boundaries would be shattered;
moreover, there would be universal upheaval in the world through the misuse of punishment.
Where the rod of punishment—dark-hued and red-eyed—moves about, destroying evil, [there the people prosper].

The subjects do not go astray in that case if the leader perceives rightly. They call him a king who is a true speaker, a wise director, one who acts with circumspection, and one who is skilled in dharma, pleasure, and wealth.

A king who administers that rod of punishment properly prospers in the three aims of life; but one whose soul is dominated by passion, who is unjust and base, is destroyed by that very rod. For the power of the rod is exceedingly great and difficult to be wielded by those who have not disciplined their souls.
One who has strayed from righteousness destroys the king himself along with his kinsmen;
thereafter, he would afflict the fort, the kingdom, and the world of mobile and immobile beings,
as well as the sages dwelling in the intermediate space and the gods.
He cannot be led according to justice by one who is without assistants, who is foolish, greedy, of unrefined intellect,
and addicted to sensual pleasures;
[but he can be led] by one who is pure, true to his word, and follows the scriptures.
Punishment can be effectively administered by one who is wise and possesses good assistants.
He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, yet be severe in meting out punishment toward enemies.
He should be straightforward toward friends and affectionate, and endowed with forbearance toward Brahmins.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain or picking up individual grains,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water. But for a king who acts contrary to this and has not conquered his own self—

His fame in this world is diminished like a drop of clarified butter in water. A king has been created as the protector of all the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas), who are established in their respective duties in due order.
Whatever must be done by him along with his servants while protecting the subjects,
all that I shall declare to you exactly and in due order.
Having risen in the morning, the king should attend upon the Brāhmaṇas.
He should abide by those who are learned and advanced in the three Vedas, and remain under their instruction.
He should constantly serve elderly Brahmins who are pure and knowers of the Veda;
for one who always serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas.
Even though his own self is disciplined, he should constantly acquire discipline from them;
for a king whose self is disciplined never perishes.
Many kings, along with their retinues, have been destroyed through lack of discipline.
Even those dwelling in the forest obtained kingdoms through discipline;
whereas Vena was ruined by lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa,
Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi.
Pṛthu indeed obtained his kingdom through discipline, as did Manu himself;

Kubera obtained sovereignty over wealth, and the son of Gādhi obtained the status of a Brāhmaṇa. From those learned in the three Vedas, he received the triple knowledge and the eternal science of government (daṇḍanīti).

He should study the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), the knowledge of the self (ātmavidyā), and the various means of livelihood (vārtā) from the world. Day and night, he should apply himself to the discipline of conquering his senses;
for one who has conquered his senses is able to keep his subjects under control.

A king should strive with great effort to avoid these ten vices arising from desire, as well as the eight born of anger, which lead to miserable ends. For a lord of the earth who is addicted to the vices born of desire, [ruin follows].
One is deprived of both wealth and merit by those [faults] born of anger, but by oneself alone in the case of those born of desire.
Hunting, dice, sleeping during the day, slander, women, intoxication, the triple symphony [of song, dance, and music], idle wandering, and [vain] gossip— this is the group of ten born of desire.

Slander, violence, malice, envy, censoriousness, and the spoiling of property; harshness of speech and of punishment—this is the eightfold group born of anger. All wise men know that which is the root of both these groups.

One should conquer that greed with effort, for from it arise these two groups [of vices]. One should know this group of four— drinking, dice, women, and hunting— to be the most grievous among those born of desire.
One should know that this triad— inflicting punishment, verbal abuse, and the seizure of property—
is always difficult to endure, even when it arises from the group born of anger;
for this group of seven is everywhere connected as a consequence.
A self-possessed man should know that each preceding vice is more grievous than the one following it.
Between vice and death, vice is said to be the more painful;
for the man addicted to vice sinks lower and lower, while the man free from vice goes to heaven when he dies.

He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested. Even a task that is easy to perform becomes difficult for one man alone.

Especially by one who is without allies, how much less can a kingdom of great consequence be maintained? (Manu 7.55c) He should constantly deliberate with them regarding common matters: peace and war, stability, revenue, protection, and the consolidation of what has been acquired. (Manu 7.56)
Having ascertained each of their individual opinions separately, he should,
in matters concerning the whole body, ordain what is for his own welfare.
But with the most distinguished Brāhmaṇa among them all, who is wise—
The king should deliberate upon the supreme counsel concerning the sixfold policy;
always resting his confidence in that minister, he should entrust all affairs to him.
Having reached a decision together with him, he should then commence his action.
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, steadfast, well-examined, and capable of properly collecting revenue,
as many men as are required to accomplish his necessary duties.
He should appoint as many men who are untiring, skillful, and discerning.
For their sake, he should employ those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth at the mines and in the workshops;
and those who are timid at the inner apartments.
And he should appoint as an envoy one who is well-versed in all the śāstras,
who understands gestures, facial expressions, and physical movements, who is pure, capable, of noble birth,
devoted, honest, skillful, possessed of a good memory, and knowledgeable of place and time.
A king’s messenger is praised when he is handsome, fearless, and eloquent.
Punishment depends upon the minister, and the administration of justice depends upon punishment.
The treasury and the kingdom depend upon the king, while peace and its opposite depend upon the messenger.
For it is the messenger alone who unites those at variance and indeed divides those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are alienated. He [the king] should discern the messenger's intentions regarding his tasks through his secret gestures and conduct.
Having understood in truth the facial expressions, gestures, movements, and the intentions of the servants of the enemy king,
he should exert such effort so that he does not bring suffering upon himself.
One should dwell in a region that is arid yet rich in crops, inhabited mostly by noble people, free from turmoil, pleasant, with submissive neighbors, and providing a means of self-sustenance.
[Such a place may be] a desert-fortress, an earth-fortress, a water-fortress, or even a forest-fortress.
Having taken refuge in a human fort or a mountain fort, he should dwell in a city.
But with every effort, he should take refuge in a mountain fort;
for among all these, the mountain fort is distinguished by its many superior qualities.
Among these, the first three are inhabited by wild animals, those living in holes, and aquatic creatures;
the latter three are inhabited, respectively, by monkeys, humans, and gods.
Just as enemies do not harm these when they have taken refuge in such strongholds, so it is with those who dwell in fortresses.
Likewise, enemies do not harm a king who has taken refuge in a fortress.
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight a hundred; a hundred can fight ten thousand. Therefore, a fortress is ordained.
That [fort] should be well-equipped with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles;
it should also be provided with Brāhmaṇas, artisans, machines, fodder, and water.
In its center, he should have a spacious residence built for himself.
Having occupied a dwelling that is well-guarded, suitable for all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees,
he should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks,
is born of a noble family, is pleasing, and is endowed with beauty and virtue.

He should appoint a domestic priest and likewise choose officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires. The king should sacrifice with various kinds of sacrifices accompanied by liberal fees.
For the sake of dharma, he should give enjoyments and wealth to the Brahmins;
he should cause the tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trusted officials once a year;
he should be devoted to the sacred tradition in this world and behave toward his subjects like a father.
He should appoint various learned supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the men engaged in his service.
He should be a worshiper of those Brahmins who have returned from the house of their teacher.
For this is declared to be the imperishable Brahman-treasure of kings.
Neither thieves nor enemies can carry it off, nor does it ever perish.
Therefore, the king should deposit this imperishable treasure with the Brāhmaṇas.
It does not spill over, it does not suffer harm, and it never perishes—
what is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices.
A gift given to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa is equal [in merit], while a gift to one who merely calls himself a Brāhmaṇa is twofold.

One hundred thousandfold [is the merit] for one who has studied [the Veda], and infinite for one who has mastered the Vedas. [For a teacher, it is a hundred thousandfold. [According to Nārada: for a teacher, it is a thousandfold.
Indeed, according to the excellence of the recipient and through faith alone, one enjoys the fruit of a gift—whether small or great—after death.
Whatever is given to a worthy recipient (*pātra*) according to the rules of place and time, accompanied by faith (*śraddhā*),
that is the means for accomplishing *dharma*.
When challenged by equals, superiors, or inferiors while protecting his subjects,
the king, mindful of the duty of a Kṣatriya, must not retreat from battle.
Not retreating in battles and the protection of subjects— these are his duties.
And service to Brāhmaṇas is the supreme means for the welfare of kings.
When kings, desiring to slay one another in battles,
fight with their utmost strength and do not turn their backs, they go to heaven.
While fighting his enemies in battle, he shall not strike them with treacherous weapons,

nor with barbed arrows, nor with poisoned ones, nor with those whose points are ablaze with fire. Furthermore, he shall not slay one who has ascended to high ground, nor a eunuch, nor one who joins his palms in supplication.
One should not strike one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours";
nor one who is asleep, nor one who has removed his armor, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed;
nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is looking on, nor one who is engaged with another.

Recalling the dharma of the virtuous, one should not strike one who is beset by the calamity of weapons, nor one who is distressed, nor one who is severely wounded, nor one who is terrified, nor one who has turned back from battle. But he who, terrified and having turned back, is slain by his enemies in combat—
Whatever evil deed her husband has committed, she incurs all of it;
and whatever good deed he has acquired for the sake of the hereafter,
her husband takes all of that from her if she is killed after turning back [from battle].

Chariots, horses, elephants, umbrellas, wealth, grain, livestock, women, all types of goods, and base metals—whatever one wins belongs to him. Furthermore, they shall give a special share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king shall give to all the warriors that which was not won individually.
This has been declared as the eternal law of warriors, unadorned by hypocrisy;
a Kṣatriya, slaying his enemies in battle, must not deviate from this duty.
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired, protect with effort what has been acquired,
increase what has been protected, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
One should know that these four constitute the purposeful application of human endeavor.
He should always perform its practice correctly and without sloth.
He should seek what is not yet obtained by means of force; he should protect what has been obtained with vigilance;
he should increase what has been protected by means of growth; and he should bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
He should always have his rod of punishment raised, always display his prowess,
always keep his secrets concealed, and always seek out the vulnerabilities of his enemy. The entire world trembles before one who has his rod of punishment perpetually raised.
Therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of punishment alone.
He should conduct himself with complete sincerity and never with deceit.
Being ever well-guarded, he should remain constantly vigilant against the deceit employed by his enemies.
An enemy should not discover his weakness, but he should discover the weaknesses of the enemy;
like a tortoise, he should hide his limbs and guard his own vulnerability.
He should deliberate on his objectives like a heron and display prowess like a lion.
He should snatch [booty] like a wolf and spring forth like a hare.
Thus, for one who is victorious, those who may stand as his adversaries,
he should bring them all under his control by means of the expedients beginning with conciliation (*sāman*).
If, however, they do not abide by those [admonitions] through the first three means,
he should bring them under control by force, using punishment alone, gradually. Scholars say that among the four means beginning with conciliation (*sāman*), [the latter ones are more effective].
They always praise conciliation and punishment for the constant prosperity of the kingdom.
Just as a weeder pulls out the weeds while protecting the grain,
so should the king protect the realm and slay those who stand as obstacles.
That king who, out of delusion and through lack of foresight, exhausts his own kingdom,
shall soon be deprived both of his kingdom and his life, along with his kinsmen. Just as the vital breaths of living beings perish from the emaciation of the body, so it is for him.
Likewise, the lives of kings are diminished by the exhaustion of their kingdom.
Therefore, for the constant maintenance of the kingdom, he should practice this ordinance;
for a king whose kingdom is well-maintained prospers in happiness.
He should establish a *gulma* (military outpost) in the midst of two, three, or five [villages],
and likewise he should organize the collection of taxes for hundreds of villages throughout the kingdom.
He should appoint a lord over a village, and likewise a lord over ten villages.

The village headman himself shall gradually settle the disputes arising within the village among the lord of twenty, the lord of a hundred, and the lord of a thousand; the lord of twenty shall report them to the lord of a hundred,
and the lord of a hundred to the lord of a thousand.
The lord of twenty villages shall present all of that to the lord of a hundred;
the lord of a hundred villages, however, shall himself present it to the lord of a thousand.
Whatever is to be given daily by the village-dwellers to the king [must be paid accordingly].
The village headman shall receive food, drink, fuel, and other such provisions.
The *daśin* (leader of ten households) shall enjoy one household, while the *viṃśin* (leader of twenty households) shall enjoy five households.
The superintendent of a hundred villages shall receive an entire village, and the lord of a thousand [villages] shall receive a city.

Indeed, their village affairs as well as their individual matters should be overseen by a trusted minister of the king, other than [the judge], who is vigilant. And in every city, he should appoint one official to consider all matters.
Like a planet among the stars, he should occupy a high position of formidable aspect. He himself should always inspect them all personally,
and he should thoroughly ascertain their conduct throughout the realms by means of his spies.

For those appointed by the king to protect who seize the property of others are generally deceitful servants; he should guard these subjects from them. Those evil-minded ones who would take wealth simply from litigants [must be restrained].
The king shall confiscate all their property and carry out their banishment. For women and servants employed in the king’s service,
he should daily provide a livelihood and a place of residence according to the nature of their work.
A paṇa should be given as the daily wage for a low-caste servant, and six paṇas for a high-caste one;
likewise, clothing is provided every six months, and a droṇa of grain every month.
[The master shall provide] the purchase and sale [of goods], travel expenses, food, and incidental costs.
Having carefully considered their security and well-being (*yogakṣema*), the king should cause merchants to pay taxes.

In such a way that both the king and the performers of the work are joined with their respective fruits, the monarch should always determine the taxes within his realm. Just as water-weeds, calves, and bees consume their food only very little by little, so should the king take from his subjects.
Likewise, the king should collect from the realm an annual tax that is very small.
A fiftieth part of cattle and gold should be taken by the king;
as for grain, an eighth, a sixth, or even a twelfth part.
He may take a sixth part of trees, meat, honey, and clarified butter;
likewise of perfumes, medicinal herbs, juices, flowers, roots, and fruits;
as well as of leaves, vegetables, grass, hides, and articles made of split bamboo.
Nor, even when dying of hunger, should a king take a tax from a *śrotriya* for earthenware vessels or anything made of iron; nor should a *śrotriya* living within his realm perish from starvation.
In whose kingdom a Śrotriya perishes from hunger,
his kingdom likewise will perish from hunger before long. Having ascertained his learning and conduct, the king should provide him with a righteous means of subsistence.
He should protect him in every way, as a father protects his own biological son. When protected by the king, whatever dharma he performs daily,
by that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase.
The king should cause even the common people in his realm who live by trade to pay some small amount known as a tax for the sake of the year.
He should likewise do so for artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras who subsist by their own manual labor.
The lord of the earth should cause each individual task to be performed month by month.
He should not, through excessive greed, cut off his own root or that of others;
for by cutting off his own root, he would bring suffering upon himself and them as well.
The lord of the earth, having examined the matter at hand, should be both severe and mild;
indeed, a king who is both severe and mild is highly esteemed.
[He should appoint] a chief minister who knows the law, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth.
He should sit upon that throne when he is weary from overseeing the affairs of men.
Having thus arranged all these duties of his own,
he should protect these subjects, both diligent and vigilant.

If the subjects of his kingdom are being carried off by bandits while they cry out for help, that king who looks on with his servants is as good as dead; he does not truly live. For a Kṣatriya, the supreme duty is indeed the protection of his subjects.
For the king who enjoys the fruits as they have been assigned is joined with righteousness.
Having risen during the last watch of the night, having performed his purifications and being composed,
having offered oblations into the fire and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.
Standing there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects with a joyful greeting;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate with his ministers,
having ascended to a mountain peak or a secluded palace terrace.
In the forest or in a secluded place, he should deliberate unobserved.
That king whose counsel common people do not learn upon gathering together enjoys the entire earth, even if he is destitute of a treasury.
At the time of reciting the mantras, one should remove those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, animals, and those past their youth; as well as women, Mlecchas, the diseased, and the deformed.
For those who are held in contempt, as well as animals, betray the secret counsel.

And women especially; therefore, one should be careful in that regard. At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue, he should reflect upon dharma, kama, and artha, either together with them or alone.
The acquisition of those who are mutually opposed to one another,
the giving away of daughters in marriage, the protection of sons,
the dispatching of envoys, and likewise the remainder of the duties to be performed.
The movements within the harem and the activities of the secret agents;
the entire eightfold business and the five-fold group in their true nature; as well as loyalty and disloyalty, and the conduct of the circle of states.
The conduct of the middle king, the activities of one desiring conquest, the conduct of the neutral king, and likewise that of the enemy— these, with diligent effort,
are in brief the constituent elements that form the foundation of the circle of states (*maṇḍala*).
Eight others are enumerated, and thus they are traditionally remembered as twelve.
Furthermore, there are five others known as the minister (*amātya*), the realm (*rāṣṭra*), the fort (*durga*), the treasury (*artha*), and the army (*daṇḍa*).
These have been described individually; in brief, they total seventy-two.
One should know that immediately adjacent to one's own territory is the enemy, and likewise the one who serves the enemy. Next to the enemy is the friend, and beyond those two is the neutral king.
One should win over all of them by employing diplomatic means such as conciliation and the rest.

He should always deliberate upon the six measures of policy— peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge— both individually and collectively, through personal prowess and prudent statesmanship.

Having examined the task at hand, he should employ a seat of peace, as well as marching, alliance, war, the double policy, and seeking refuge. A king should know that both alliance and war are of two kinds.
Both [types of] vehicles and seats, as well as the two kinds of shelter, are recorded [in tradition].
Likewise, there is that which shares the same vehicle-activity and that which is the opposite;
then, the peace treaty (saṃdhi) connected with the future should be known as having these two characteristics.

War is declared to be of two kinds: that undertaken by oneself for the sake of a specific objective, either out of season or at the proper time, and that waged against a friend when an injury has been committed.
Furthermore, there is war waged alone when an urgent matter arises by chance.
Marching is said to be of two kinds for one who is united with an ally:
either by gradual reduction due to fate or by the consequences of past actions.
Sitting encamped is likewise recorded as being of two kinds: either out of necessity due to one's own depletion or out of deference to an ally.

The stationing of both the army and its master for the sake of accomplishing the objective is declared to be of two kinds as "dual policy" (dvaidhībhāva) by those who know the qualities of the six measures of statecraft— specifically,
when one is being oppressed by enemies and seeks to achieve one's purpose.
Among the virtuous, association is recorded as being of two kinds: reputation and reliance.
When one perceives that one’s own future prosperity will be certain and substantial, while the immediate suffering is slight, then one should resort to peace.

When he considers all his constituent elements to be exceedingly joyful, and likewise considers himself to be highly exalted, then he should wage war. When he considers his own army to be cheerful in spirit and well-nourished, [then he should wage war].
When the opposite is true for the enemy, then he should march against the foe.
But when he is himself depleted in terms of mounts and troops,
then he should remain on guard with diligence, gradually conciliating his enemies.

When the king considers his enemy to be stronger in every respect, then, having divided his army into two parts, he should accomplish his own purpose. When, however, he becomes most vulnerable to the forces of the enemy...
At that time, however, he should quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king—
one who would exercise restraint over his own subjects and against the enemy's forces.
He should serve such a king constantly with all his efforts, as if he were a preceptor.
If, even in that case, he perceives a fault arising from seeking refuge,
he should engage in fair battle there as well, free from hesitation.
A king who is skilled in policy should act in such a manner by all possible means.

He should act so that his friends, neutrals, and enemies do not gain superiority over him. He should deliberate upon the future and the present state of all undertakings, as well as the merits and defects of all past actions in their true nature.
One who understands merits and defects regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present,
and who knows the remaining tasks from the past, is not overcome by enemies. [He acts] so that friends, neutrals, and enemies do not plot against him.
In this manner he should arrange everything; this is the summary of the policy. Then the lord should set out on a military expedition against the enemy's kingdom;
at that time, he should proceed slowly toward the enemy's city according to this rule.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the lord of the earth should set out on his expedition;
or else, according to his strength, during the months of Phālguna or Caitra. However, even at other times, he may go when he perceives certain victory.
Then he should march forth after declaring war, especially when a calamity has arisen for the enemy;
having made proper arrangements for his base and his expedition according to rule,
