and having secured a foothold and duly stationed his spies.
Having thoroughly cleared the three types of roads and his own sixfold forces,
he should march toward the enemy's city according to the rules for an expedition. He should be especially vigilant regarding a friend who secretly serves the enemy.
And indeed, one who has gone away and returned is a most dangerous enemy.
He should march along that path in a staff-like array (*daṇḍavyūha*), or in a cart-like array (*śakaṭavyūha*),
or in the form of a boar, a crocodile, a needle, or a garuḍa.
From whichever direction he anticipates danger, toward that side he should extend his forces;
and he himself should always take up his position in the *padma* (lotus) formation.
He should station the commander-in-chief and the chief of the army in all directions.
In whichever direction he anticipates danger, toward that direction he should turn the front. He should station trusted scouts on all sides,
who are skilled in both remaining stationary and in combat, who are fearless, incorruptible, and have been given secret signals.

One should cause a small number of troops to fight in close formation, while a large number may be deployed at will. Having arrayed them in the *sūcī* (needle) or *vajra* (thunderbolt) formations, one should make them fight.
One should fight on level ground with chariots and horses, and likewise on marshy ground with boats and elephants.

In terrain covered by trees and shrubs, one should employ bows; on open ground, swords, shields, and other weapons. One should station long and short men from Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and the lands of the Sūrasenas at the front lines of the army.

Having arrayed his forces, he should encourage them and examine them thoroughly; he should also discern the movements of his enemies even as they are fighting. Having besieged the enemy, he should remain encamped and harass his kingdom.
He should constantly spoil his fodder, food, water, and fuel;
he should likewise break his tanks, as well as his walls and moats.
He should also launch a surprise attack upon him at night and likewise terrify him.
He should instigate those who are susceptible to sowing dissension, and he should remain aware of their actions.
When fate is favorable, he should fight, free from fear and desiring victory.
He should employ conciliation, bribery, and sowing dissension—either collectively or individually.
One should strive to conquer one's enemies by no means through war;
for victory is seen to be uncertain for two combatants, and defeat in battle may also occur. Therefore, one should avoid war.
When even the three aforementioned expedients are not possible,
he should fight in such a manner that, being well-equipped, he may conquer his enemies. Having conquered, he should worship the gods and the righteous Brāhmaṇas.
He should grant exemptions and proclaim assurances of safety.
Having ascertained the collective intention of all these [officers] in brief,
he should appoint a member of their own lineage to that office and establish a formal agreement.
And he should establish legal authorities for them according to the duties as they have been declared;
and he should honor him with jewels along with his principal officers.
Taking is unpleasant, while giving is a source of pleasure.
Among desired objects, that which is appropriate for the right time is praised.
All this action is dependent upon the divine and the human;
of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, whereas in the human there exists effort.

The following three *ślokas* are found only in M (Kṛṣṇa’s edition does not include them in its numbering of the text, although Medhātithi provides a commentary on them): [Manu 7.207a] That which proceeds as human activity, joined with divine ordinance, [not in K] [M: *ayuktam*] [Manu 7.207c] Accomplishes its purpose through great hardship. [not in K]
Even for one who is joined with destiny, if it is devoid of human effort,
the field does not yield fruit without human exertion.
The moon, the sun, and other planets, as well as wind, fire, and water likewise— [all depend upon human action].
In this world, things are accomplished through destiny and through diligent human effort.
Or, being prepared, he may march together after having carefully made a treaty,
perceiving the threefold fruit consisting of allies, gold, or land.
Having carefully considered the rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*) as well as the ally-in-distress (*ākranda*) within the circle of states,
a king may obtain the fruit of his expedition from either a friend or even an enemy. A monarch does not prosper so much by the acquisition of gold or land [as he does by securing these].
Just as one who has obtained a firm friend, even if weak, yet capable of enduring for the future—
One who knows the law, is grateful, and whose nature is contented; A light friend who is devoted and steadfast in his undertakings is highly praised.
The wise declare that an enemy who is intelligent, well-born, brave, capable, generous, grateful, and steadfast is difficult to overcome.
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, and compassion— these are the qualities [of such a foe].
He should always possess great munificence and the quality of remaining impartial toward all.
A king should, without hesitation, abandon for his own sake even a land that is secure, productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of cattle.
One should protect one's wealth for the sake of times of distress; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth. Having thoroughly considered all calamities that may arise together, [one should act accordingly].
A wise man should employ all means, both those that are combined and those that are separate.
Relying upon these three— the pursuer, the goal to be attained, and all the means in their entirety— he should strive for the accomplishment of his purpose.
Having thus deliberated upon all this together with his ministers, the king,
having exercised himself and bathed at midday, should enter the inner apartments to eat. There,
he should be attended by trustworthy servants who are loyal to him, skilled in the knowledge of time, and incorruptible.

He should eat food that has been thoroughly examined, using mantras that destroy poison. He should treat all his belongings with anti-poisonous medicines, and he should always, with self-restraint, wear gems that counteract poison.
Women who have been thoroughly examined by means of fans, water, and incense,
and who are purified by their dress and ornaments, should touch him with great composure. One should exercise such care regarding his vehicle, bed, seat, and food.

After bathing, adorning himself, and putting on all his ornaments, he may enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments once he has finished his meal. Having thus diverted himself for the appropriate time, he should again attend to his duties.
Adorned, he should inspect the martial class of people again,
as well as all the mounts, weapons, and ornaments.
Having performed the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), he should listen [to reports] in the inner apartment while bearing his weapon.
He should also investigate the conduct of those who report secrets and of his secret agents.
Having gone to another chamber and dismissed those people,
he should enter the inner apartments again for the purpose of eating, surrounded by women.
Having eaten there again a little, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments,
he should go to sleep at the proper time and rise free from fatigue.
A healthy lord of the earth should observe this rule.
But if he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants. Desiring to inspect legal cases, however, the king, together with Brāhmaṇas, [should enter the court].
Instructed by ministers who are knowledgeable in the sacred mantras, he should enter the court. There,
either seated or standing, raising his right hand,
with modest dress and ornaments, he should examine the legal cases of the litigants.
Day by day, by means of reasons observed in local custom and those prescribed in the scriptures,
[the cases] are settled separately within the eighteen titles of law.
Of these, the first is the non-payment of debt, followed by deposits, sale without ownership, and so forth.

Joint undertakings, the non-delivery of what has been given, the non-payment of wages, and the breach of agreements; disputes regarding purchase and sale, and the legal relations between an owner and his herdsman.
The law concerning boundary disputes; verbal and physical assault;
theft, violence, and the abduction of women;
the duties of husband and wife, partition of inheritance, gambling, and betting.
These eighteen titles are the foundations for the administration of justice here.
In these matters, the king should settle the disputes of men engaged in litigation by relying upon the eternal Dharma.
But when the king himself does not personally attend to the inspection of legal cases, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to inspect those cases. He,
surrounded by three members of the court, shall examine his judicial affairs.
Having entered the foremost assembly hall, whether seated or standing,
they know that to be a *sabhā* (court of justice) where three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together with a learned official appointed by the king.
When Dharma, pierced by Adharma, approaches the assembly,
and the members of that assembly do not extract the barb, they themselves are pierced. Either one should not enter the assembly at all, or one should speak what is just.
A man becomes guilty of sin whether he remains silent or speaks falsely.
Where dharma is slain by adharma and truth by falsehood while the members look on, there the members of the assembly are themselves slain.
Dharma, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when preserved, protects.
Therefore, Dharma must not be violated, lest violated Dharma destroy us. For the Blessed Dharma is a bull; he who does violence to it indeed commits a great offense.
The gods know him as a *vṛṣala* (outcaste); therefore, one should not violate the law (*dharma*).
Dharma alone is the true friend that follows one even in death;
for everything else perishes along with the body and does not go with one.
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness;
one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king.
But the king becomes free from sin, and the members of the court are likewise released.
The sin goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured.
Or, he may at will be a "so-called Brahmin" (brāhmaṇabruva) who subsists merely by his caste;
but a Śūdra must never be the expounder of dharma for the king under any circumstances.
But that kingdom where a Śūdra performs the judicial investigation of dharma for a king, that kingdom perishes like a cow sinking in the mud while being watched.
That kingdom which consists mostly of Śūdras, which is overrun by atheists, and which is devoid of the twice-born...
That entire realm, afflicted by famine and disease, will quickly perish.
Having ascended the seat of justice, properly clothed and composed in mind,
he should bow to the guardians of the world and begin the investigation of legal cases.
Having understood both profit and loss, as well as pure dharma and adharma,
he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes.
He should discern the internal disposition of men by means of external signs.
By means of tone, complexion, gestures, and facial expressions, as well as by the movement of the eyes;
and by outward appearance, hints, gait, behavior, and speech,
as well as by changes in the eyes and face— the mind within is perceived.
The king shall protect the inheritance of a minor and so forth until he has returned from his teacher’s house or until he has passed his childhood—
or until he has passed his childhood. The same protection should be afforded for women who are widowed, childless, and without kinsmen.
And toward women who are devoted to their husbands, as well as those who are widows or afflicted by illness—
those kinsmen who would seize the property of such women while they are still alive,
the righteous lord of the earth shall punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves.
Property whose owner has disappeared, the king shall cause to be kept in deposit for three years;
within three years the owner may take it, but after that time the king may take it.
He who says "this is mine" should be questioned according to the prescribed rule.
Having verified the appearance, number, and other characteristics, the owner deserves that property.
One who fails to accurately report the place and time of the loss,
as well as its color, appearance, and size, deserves a fine equal to the value of the object.

Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king should take a sixth part of property lost and found, or even a tenth or a twelfth part. Property lost and found should remain under the supervision of appointed officials.
The king shall have those thieves caught therein executed by an elephant.
If a man should truthfully declare of a treasure-trove, "This is mine," the king may take a sixth or even a twelfth part of it.
But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own property,
or a smaller fraction calculated according to the value of that very treasure.
However, a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited, [shall take it].

He may take [the treasure] entirely, for he is the lord of all. But whatever ancient treasure the king may discover buried in the earth, having given half of it to the twice-born, he should deposit the other half in his treasury.
Of ancient treasures and minerals buried in the earth,
the king shall take one half as his share for protecting them, for he is indeed the lord of the soil.
And the king must restore to all social classes any wealth stolen by thieves.
And a king who makes use of that [stolen property] incurs the guilt of the thief.
(Manu 8.40c) One who knows the law, having carefully examined the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds, and the laws of families, should establish his own duty. (Manu 8.41)

Even when they are far away, men who perform their own duties and remain steadfast in their respective tasks become dear to the world. Neither the king himself nor his official should create a legal case.
And he must never, under any circumstances, swallow up wealth that has been brought forward by another.
Just as a hunter traces the track of a deer by drops of blood,
so should the king trace the path of dharma through inference.

Established in the rules of legal procedure, he should consider the truth, the matter at hand, himself, the witnesses, the place, the form, and the time. That which has been practiced by virtuous and righteous twice-born men—
He should determine that [penalty] so as not to conflict with the customs of the region, the family, or the caste.
(Manu 8.46c) Urged by the creditor for the purpose of recovering the debt from the debtor, the king shall cause the debtor to pay the amount established as due to the creditor. (Manu 8.47)
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own wealth,
by those very means he should constrain the debtor and compel him to pay.
[He may do so] through moral pressure, legal process, artifice, or customary practice.
He should recover the wealth lent by means of the fifth method as well.
If a creditor recovers his own wealth from the debtor by his own effort,
he must not be prosecuted by the king for recovering what is his own.

But one who denies a debt when it has been proven by evidence should be made to pay the creditor's wealth and a fine according to his capacity. When a debtor, upon being told "Pay! in the assembly, denies it...
The plaintiff shall point out the place where the transaction occurred, or he shall indicate another means of proof.
He who points to what is not a valid means of proof, he who denies after having pointed it out,
and he who does not understand the contradictory meanings of the preceding and following arguments— [these are liable to defeat].
He who, having made a statement, then retracts it; he who, when questioned, does not acknowledge a matter that has been properly established;
or he who converses secretly with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden.
He who does not wish to answer a question being put to him, or who walks away; he who, when told "Speak!", does not speak; or who, having spoken, fails to substantiate what was said;
or who cannot distinguish between what precedes and what follows—that man is defeated on that point.

If one who has been asked "Are there witnesses for me? says "There are in such-and-such a direction," yet does not produce them, the judge, by these grounds, should declare him to be defeated—even if he is otherwise innocent. If the plaintiff does not speak, he should be bound and punished according to the law.
If he does not speak within three fortnights regarding the legal matter, he is defeated. Whatever amount of wealth a man may deny, or whatever amount he may falsely claim,
those two— being ignorant of the law— must be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount.
But one who, having been summoned by a creditor seeking his wealth, denies the debt after having entered into a formal agreement,
must be proved [guilty] by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and Brahmins.
Such witnesses as should be employed by creditors in legal proceedings—
I shall now fully declare who such persons are, and how the truth must be spoken by them:

Householders, those with sons, and those of hereditary standing—born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes—who have been summoned for the sake of the matter, are worthy to give testimony; no others whatsoever, except in times of distress.
Trustworthy persons from all castes should be appointed as witnesses in legal matters;

they must be knowers of all duties and free from greed, while those who are the opposite should be avoided. Neither those with a financial interest, nor friends, nor associates, nor enemies [should be witnesses].
Those whose faults have been observed must not be made witnesses, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupted.
A king must not be made a witness, nor an artisan, nor an actor or singer;
nor one learned in the Vedas, nor one living in a religious order, nor one who has withdrawn from all worldly attachments.
One who is not dependent on another, nor one who is subject to censure, nor a slave, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
nor one who is aged, nor a woman, nor one alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired senses;
nor one who is distressed, nor intoxicated, nor insane, nor oppressed by hunger or thirst.
Neither one oppressed by fatigue, nor one oppressed by passion, nor one who is angry, nor even a thief [should give testimony].
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men;
and virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras, while those of the lowest birth for the lowest castes.
But whoever is an eyewitness may give testimony for litigants in the interior of a house,
in a forest, or even in a case involving the loss of life;
and when such a person is unavailable, the testimony may be given by a woman, a child, or an elderly man.

One should recognize that the speech of those who speak falsely in witness-depositions— whether they be a pupil, a relative, a slave, or a hired servant, or those who are children, the elderly, or afflicted by illness— is unstable; the same applies to those whose minds are arrogant.
In all cases of violence, theft, and adultery,
as well as in verbal and physical assault, the king shall not examine the witnesses. In the event of a conflict between witnesses, the ruler should accept the majority.

But when the witnesses are equal, those distinguished by superior qualities [should be chosen]; and when there is a conflict between those of high quality, the best among the twice-born [should be selected]. Testimony is established through seeing in person and through hearing; in that case, a witness who speaks the truth does not fall away from merit or wealth.

A witness who gives testimony in an assembly of noble men that differs from what was seen or heard goes headlong to hell after death and is excluded from heaven. Where one might see or hear something even though not formally appointed [as a witness], [he too must testify].
Even when questioned there, he should speak exactly as it was seen and exactly as it was heard.
A single witness who is free from greed may be accepted, but not women, even if they are many and pure;
for the intellect of women is unsteady, and others also who are tainted by faults are disqualified.
Whatever they may say spontaneously is to be accepted as the basis for legal proceedings;
whatever else they might state, even if for the sake of dharma, is useless.
When the witnesses have arrived within the court in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, [the judge should question them].
The judge shall interrogate them, consoling them with this procedure:
"Whatever you know regarding the mutual conduct of these two parties in this matter, declare it all in truth; for you are the witnesses here."
By speaking the truth in his testimony, a witness attains abundant and blameless worlds;
and in this world, he gains unsurpassed fame—this speech is honored by Brahmā.
Speaking falsehood in testimony, one is bound tightly with the nooses of Varuṇa.
A hundred births shall be spent in separation from his kin; therefore, one should speak the truth as witness.
By truth a witness is purified, and by truth dharma increases.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all social classes.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self. Do not despise your own self, the supreme witness among men.
Indeed, evildoers think to themselves, "No one sees us."
But the gods behold them, as does the inner person within one's own self.
Heaven, earth, water, the heart, the moon, the sun, fire, Yama, and the wind, night,
the two twilights, and Dharma— these know the conduct of all embodied beings.

In the presence of the gods and Brāhmaṇas, he should question the twice-born witnesses truthfully— being himself pure and addressing those who are pure— in the forenoon, while they face either north or east. He should ask a Brāhmaṇa, "Speak," and a Kṣatriya, "Speak the truth."
A Vaiśya by [stealing] cattle, seed, or gold; a Śūdra by all [these] and by all mortal sins.

Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, and those for the killers of women and children, and for the betrayer of a friend and the ungrateful man—those shall be his who speaks falsely.
"O auspicious one, whatever merit you have performed since birth—
all that shall go to a dog if you speak otherwise.
O virtuous one, you who think of yourself, 'I am alone'— "
This sage, the observer of merit and sin, stands eternally within your heart. The divine Yama, son of Vivasvat, who resides here in your heart—
if you have no dispute with him, then go neither to the Gaṅgā nor to the land of the Kurus.

Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, tormented by hunger and thirst, and blind, he who gives false testimony shall go to his enemy's house as a beggar. Headlong into blinding darkness, that sinner shall go to hell.
He who, being questioned in a legal determination of duty, gives a false answer,
eats fish along with their bones like a blind man. He who, having entered the court, speaks of a matter that is either deficient in its facts or beyond his personal observation [is likewise guilty].
For the gods know no other man in this world more excellent than him, whose testimony a learned *kṣetrajña* (one who knows the field) does not distrust when he speaks.
As many kinsmen as one destroys by speaking falsely in a legal proceeding, so many does he himself slay.
Listen, gentle one, to the sequence of those [sins] according to their number:
he kills five by lying about small cattle, ten by lying about cows;
he kills a hundred by lying about horses, and a thousand by lying about men.

One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those born and those unborn; one destroys everything by speaking falsehood regarding land—do not, therefore, speak falsely regarding land. Regarding water, they say it is like land, as is the case with the enjoyment of women and sexual intercourse.
And in the case of gems produced in water, as well as all those made of stone—
having considered all these faults that arise from speaking untruth,
speak everything exactly and straightforwardly, just as it was heard and just as it was seen.
One should treat like Śūdras those Brāhmaṇas who are cattle-herders, traders, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers (Manu 8.102).
When speaking of legal matters, a man who knows the truth should state it according to the law, even if he knows otherwise (Manu 8.103).

One does not fall from the heavenly world who utters such divine speech. Where the telling of the truth would result in the execution of a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa, there it is right to speak a falsehood; for that is superior to the truth.
They should sacrifice to Sarasvatī with sacrificial porridges (caru) dedicated to Speech,
performing the highest expiation for that sin of untruth.
Or else, they should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras.
Or he may recite the verse beginning with "ud" addressed to Varuṇa, or the three verses whose deity is Water.

(Manu 8.106cd) If a man, being healthy, fails to give testimony regarding debts and other matters within three fortnights, he shall be liable for that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth on the whole amount. (Manu 8.107)
If, within seven days of the testimony being given,
disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman should befall a witness who has spoken as prescribed, he shall be made to pay the debt and a fine.
But in matters concerning which there are no witnesses, between two parties disputing with one another...
If one does not discover the truth in its actual state, one may cause it to be obtained even by means of an oath.
Oaths were taken by the great seers and by the gods for the sake of determining legal matters;
and Vasiṣṭha also swore an oath before King Paijavana.

A wise man should not take a false oath, even for a trivial matter; for by taking a false oath, one perishes both in this world and after death. [This applies except] in matters concerning women, marriages, fodder for cows, and fuel.
And in the case of assisting a Brāhmaṇa, there is no sin in taking an oath. One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons,
a Vaiśya by his cattle, seed-corn, and gold, and a Śūdra by all [the aforementioned] sins.

One should cause him to enter the fire, or cause him to be submerged in water; or one should make him touch the heads of his son and wife separately. He whom the kindled fire does not burn, and whom the waters do not cause to rise [to the surface], [is purified].
And he who does not quickly meet with misfortune should be known as pure in his oath.
For in ancient times, when a calf was falsely accused by its younger brother,
the fire— the touchstone of the world— did not burn even a single hair of his, because of his truthfulness.

In whatever legal dispute false testimony has been given, that very case shall be overturned; even if it has been decided, it shall be as if undone. [This applies when testimony is given] out of greed, delusion, fear, friendship, lust, or likewise anger.
If testimony is given falsely through ignorance or childishness—
whether in any one of these circumstances, he who speaks a lie as witness—
I shall now declare the specific punishments for him in their proper order.
Out of greed, he should be fined one thousand; out of delusion, the first amercement;
out of fear, two middle amercements; out of friendship, four times the first amercement;
out of lust, ten times the first amercement; and out of anger, three times the highest amercement.
Two full hundred [paṇas] for giving false testimony through ignorance, and one hundred for being a minor—
these, they say, are the punishments declared by the wise for perjury,
for the sake of ensuring that dharma does not deviate and for the restraint of unrighteousness.
A righteous king should fine the three castes who give false testimony and then banish them;
however, he should only exile a Brāhmaṇa.
Manu, the son of the Self-existent, has declared ten places for the infliction of punishment.
Whatever offenses may exist among the three castes, a Brāhmaṇa should depart from them unhurt.
The private parts, the stomach, the tongue, the two hands, and the fifth, the feet;
the eyes, the nose, the two ears, as well as wealth and the body itself—[these are the ten organs].
Having fully ascertained the motive, as well as the place and time in their true nature,
and having considered the capacity [of the offender] and the offense, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
Unjust punishment in this world destroys reputation and ruins fame.
And it leads to the loss of heaven in the next world as well; therefore, one should avoid it.
By punishing those who do not deserve punishment, and by failing to punish those who do deserve it, a king incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
First, one should inflict the punishment of speech; immediately after that, the punishment of censure;
thirdly, the punishment of fines; and beyond that, the punishment of corporal chastisement.
But when one is unable to restrain these offenders even by corporal punishment—

Then he should employ all these four [weights] among them. I shall declare in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold that are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions.

The minute particle of dust that is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening is called the *trasareṇu*, the first of all measurements. Eight *trasareṇus* should be known as one *likṣā* in terms of measurement.
Three of those [black mustard seeds] make one white mustard seed (*gaurasarṣapa*); three of those [white mustard seeds] make one barleycorn (*yava*).
Six barleycorns make one middle-sized *kṛṣṇala*, and three *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*.
Five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those [māṣas] make one *suvarṇa*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*, and ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together are to be known as one silver *māṣaka*.
Sixteen of those silver *māṣakas* make one silver *dharaṇa*, which is also called a *purāṇa*.

A copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa* or a *paṇa*. Ten *dharaṇas* of silver are to be known as a *śatamāna*. A *niṣka* is to be known by its measure as consisting of four *suvarṇas*.
Two hundred and fifty *paṇas* are declared to be the first *sāhasa* fine;
the middle one is to be known as five hundred, and the highest is indeed one thousand.
When a debt is admitted to be due, the debtor deserves a fine of five percent.
In case of denial, that fine shall be doubled; such is the instruction of Manu.
A moneylender may employ the interest prescribed by Vasiṣṭha for the increase of wealth;
he may take an eightieth part of a hundred per month.
Or, remembering the duty of the virtuous, he may take two percent interest per month;
for by taking two percent, he does not become a sinner regarding wealth.
Two, three, four, and five percent per month are likewise permitted.
One may take interest for a month according to the sequence of the social classes.
But one shall never receive usury on a pledge that provides a benefit;
nor, due to the lapse of time, is there either the forfeiture or the sale of the pledge.
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest. He should satisfy the owner with its value, otherwise he becomes a thief of the pledge.
Both a pledge and a deposit are subject to loss if the stipulated time expires.
If these two remain [unreturned] for a long period of time, they shall be liable to forfeiture.
Things used with mutual consent are never lost.
A cow, a camel, a draft horse, and any animal employed as a beast of burden [are not lost by mere use].
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years in his presence while remaining silent, he does not deserve to recover it—
provided he is not an idiot and is of legal age, and the property is being enjoyed within his own domain.
That [title] which has been defeated by legal process— the possessor deserves that property.
A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the property of a Vedic scholar do not perish through possession.

The foolish man who enjoys a pledge without the permission of its owner must relinquish half of the interest as compensation for that enjoyment. Interest on a loan, when collected at one time, shall not exceed double the principal.
In the case of grain, raw sugar, and wool used for transport, the interest does not exceed five percent. Interest exceeding the legal rate (kṛtānusāra) is not valid if it is excessive;
they call that the path of usury, which ought to be limited to five percent per hundred.
One should not take interest exceeding that for a year, nor interest that has not been previously agreed upon.
Interest may be of four kinds: compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*), periodical interest (*kālavṛddhi*), stipulated interest (*kāritā*), and corporeal interest (*kāyikā*).
If one is unable to pay the debt and wishes to make a new agreement, he may do so.
Having paid the interest that has been won over, he should renew the bond;
or, without showing the gold there, he should renew it by paying as much interest as may have accrued. He is liable to pay exactly as much interest as has accumulated.
One who has entered into a contract for compound interest (cakravṛddhi), having fixed the place and time,
shall not obtain its fruit if he transgresses that place and time.
Those skilled in sea-voyages, who perceive the requirements of place, time, and wealth, [should be consulted].
But whatever rate of interest they may establish, that shall apply to the recovery of the debt in that case.
If a man stands as a surety for another’s appearance here, and fails to produce him, he shall pay that person’s debt from his own property. [He should strive to do so.]
A son is not liable to pay for a guarantee, a frivolous debt, a debt incurred through gambling or through liquor, nor the remainder of a fine or a tax. However,
in the case of a guarantee for appearance, the rule previously ordained shall apply.
When a surety for payment has died, the court should compel even his heirs to pay.
But if the debtor does not pay, and the surety was known to be of such a nature [as to be able to pay],
why should the creditor seek the debt from the heirs after the surety has died?
But if the surety is one to whom wealth has been assigned and who possesses sufficient funds, he shall pay that from his own property;
such is the settled rule regarding one for whom wealth was assigned.
[This does not apply to those] who are intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, dependent on others, a child, or an elderly person.
And legal procedure conducted by one who is unrelated does not succeed;
even if a statement is well-established,
it is not valid if it is spoken outside of the established customary law.

A fraudulent mortgage or sale, a fraudulent gift or acceptance, or whatever is seen to be accompanied by deceit— He shall annul all such transactions. If the borrower has perished while the expenditure was made for the sake of the family, [the debt shall be paid from the family estate].
That [debt] must be paid by the kinsmen, even if they are divided, from their own property. Whatever transaction a dependent person may carry out for the sake of the family,
whether in his own country or in a foreign land, the superior [head of the household] shall not annul it.

"Whatever is given by force, enjoyed by force, or even recorded by force—Manu has declared all transactions effected by force to be null and void. Three suffer for the sake of others: witnesses, a surety, and the family."
Four, however, are increased: a learned Brahmin, a wealthy merchant, and a king.
A king, even if he is impoverished, must not take what ought not to be taken;
nor, even when prosperous, should he relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be.

By taking what should not be taken and by rejecting what should be taken, the weakness of the king is proclaimed; he perishes both in this world and after death. By taking what is his own, by preventing the intermixture of castes, and by protecting the weak—
Power arises for the king; he prospers both in this world and after death.
Therefore, like Yama himself, the lord should personally set aside likes and dislikes and conduct himself with the discipline of Yama, having conquered his anger and subdued his senses.
But that king who, out of delusion, conducts affairs unjustly,
his enemies will soon bring that evil-minded man under their control. However, he who, having restrained desire and anger, examines matters according to dharma—
The subjects follow him, just as rivers flow toward the ocean.
If a debtor who is being pressured by his will complains to the king against his creditor,
he shall be made to pay a fine of one-fourth that amount to the king, and the debt itself must be paid to the creditor.
A debtor should repay the creditor even by means of labor;
one of equal or lower caste may do so immediately, but one of superior caste should pay that gradually.
By this rule, the king [should settle] the disputes of men litigating with one another.
One should bring lawsuits established on the testimony of witnesses to a state of impartiality.

A wise man should deposit a sealed trust with one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, truthful, possessed of a large circle of supporters, wealthy, and honorable.
In whatever manner a person deposits an object in the hand of another, in that very same manner it must be received back; as was the delivery, so shall be the recovery.
He who, when being asked for it, does not return a deposit to the depositor...
In the absence of the depositor,
that [deposit] should be requested by the judge through spies who possess the appropriate age and appearance,
after having truly deposited gold with him under various pretexts. (Manu 8.181c–182)
If he should restore it exactly as it was deposited and in its original condition,
there is nothing therein for which he may be accused by others.
But if he does not return that gold to them according to the prescribed rule, [he shall be punished].
Having restrained both parties, he should cause them to pay; such is the established rule of dharma.
A deposit (nikṣepa) and a sealed deposit (upanidhi) must never be delivered to a next-of-kin. In the event of the owner's death, these two perish; however, if there is no death, they do not perish.
If one should personally deliver [the deposit] to the next-of-kin of the deceased,
he must not be prosecuted by the king nor by the kinsmen of the depositor.
He should seek that object without artifice and with affection.
Or, having investigated his conduct, he should settle the matter through conciliation alone.
This same rule for settling [disputes] should apply to all these types of deposits;
however, in the case of a sealed deposit, the [depositor] shall not recover anything from it unless he takes it back himself.
If [the deposit] has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or burnt by fire,
he need not pay for it, provided that he does not withhold anything from it.
[The king shall punish] both the one who misappropriates a deposit and the one who demands what was never deposited.
He should investigate by all means, and even by means of Vedic oaths.
He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands what he did not deposit—
both of these should be punished like thieves, or made to pay a fine equal to the value of that [deposit].

The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value; likewise, he shall do so for the one who misappropriates a sealed deposit (upanidhi), without distinction. Furthermore, whatever man should take the property of another by means of fraudulent stratagems (upadhā), [he shall be punished].
He should be executed publicly by various means of death along with his accomplices.
Whatever deposit was made by someone, and in whatever amount and in the presence of witnesses, that much alone shall it be recognized as; one who speaks falsely deserves punishment.
Whatever loan has been mutually made or accepted between two parties must be repaid in that same mutual manner; as the lending was, so should be the taking back.
This applies equally to property deposited and to what has been entrusted out of friendship.

The king shall deliver the judgment without causing injury to the holder of the deposit. He who sells the property of another without being the owner and without the consent of the owner— the king should not admit him as a witness, for he is a thief though he considers himself no thief.
If he has kin, he shall be liable to pay a fine of six hundred;
if he has no kin and no means of escape, he shall incur the guilt of a thief.
Furthermore, any gift or sale made by one who is not the owner [is invalid].
But that [title] should be understood as unestablished according to the established rule in legal proceedings.
Where possession is seen but no title is seen anywhere, there the title is the cause, not the possession; such is the settled rule.

If one should receive any wealth from a sale in the presence of the family, he indeed acquires that wealth lawfully through the act of purchase; for it is purified by such a transaction. But if the original source cannot be produced, he is cleared by the purification of the public sale.
If he is not punished by the king, the owner who lost the property shall recover his wealth. (Manu 8.202c) An item whose form has been mixed with another is not fit for sale;

nor is that which is worthless, nor that which is deficient, nor that which is far away, nor that which is concealed. (Manu 8.203) [Nor that which is defective, nor that which is deficient, nor that which is distant, nor that which is hidden.]
If, after showing one girl, another is given to the bridegroom,
Manu has declared that he may marry both for the price of a single dowry.
[This applies] provided she is not insane, nor leperous, nor has she already experienced sexual intercourse.
If a giver has previously disclosed the defects [of a maiden], he does not deserve punishment. If a chosen officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) should abandon his own duties during a sacrifice,
a share of the fee corresponding to the work performed must be given to him by the fellow-performers.
If, after the sacrificial fees have been given, one abandons his own work,
he shall receive his entire share and have it performed by another. Whatever specific subsidiary fees may be prescribed for a particular task [should be paid accordingly].
He alone shall light those fires, or all of them together may divide them.
At the establishment of the sacred fires, the Adhvaryu shall take the chariot and the Brahman the horse;
or the Hotṛ may take the horse, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of the Soma].
Among all [the partners], the principal ones take one half; others take half of that half;
the third-class take a third part, and those who take a fourth part receive a quarter.
By men acting together here in this world, performing their respective tasks, [these shares are determined].

By this application of the rule, the distribution of shares must be performed. If wealth has been given to someone who asks for it for the sake of dharma, and if that wealth subsequently does not serve that purpose, it shall not be returned; it remains with him.
If, however, he should recover that [debt] through pride or greed,
he should be made to pay one suvarṇa by the king as atonement for that theft.
This has been declared as the lawful method for the non-repayment of what was given.
Henceforth, I shall declare the non-payment of wages.
(Manu 8.214c) If a hired laborer, being not ill, fails through pride to perform the work as it was prescribed, he should be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid. (Manu 8.215)

But one who, having been ill, becomes healthy, should perform the work from the beginning exactly as it was described; he shall indeed receive that wages even after a long period of time. However, whether ill or healthy, he who does not cause that work to be performed as stipulated [shall not be paid].
No wages shall be paid to him for work that is even slightly deficient.
This entire law regarding the non-payment of wages has been declared;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the law concerning those who violate agreements.
A man who, having made a covenant by truth with a village, a district, or a corporation,
should break it out of greed, the king shall banish from his realm.
Having seized that violator of agreements, he should compel him to pay a fine.
Four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one royal śatamāna—
this is the rule of punishment that a righteous lord of the earth should impose upon those who violate agreements within villages, castes, or assemblies.
Having bought or sold anything here, if one should have cause for regret,
he may return or take back that object within ten days;
but after ten days, he shall neither return it nor cause it to be returned.
One who takes [a maiden] and one who gives her away should each be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
But he who gives away a defective maiden without having disclosed her defects,
the king himself shall impose upon him a fine of ninety-six paṇas.

If a man, out of malice, declares a maiden to be "not a maiden" without demonstrating her fault, he shall receive a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. The marriage-mantras are established as applicable only to maidens.

In no case do men [have the right] over women who are not *kanyās* (virgins), for such women have their religious duties (*dharmakriyā*) subverted. The mantras recited at the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇika*) are the definitive mark of a wife;
their completion, however, should be understood by the learned as occurring at the seventh step.
In whatever matter one may have a grievance after it has been performed,
he should be settled on the path of righteousness by this procedure.
This applies to transgressions involving cattle, whether committed by owners or by herdsmen.
I shall now fully declare the rules for disputes according to the true nature of dharma.
Liability for loss falls upon the keeper during the day, and upon the owner at night if the animal is in his house;
otherwise, if security is not maintained, the keeper shall incur the liability.

A cowherd who is supported by milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cattle, milk the best cow out of ten; that shall be his wages if he is not paid otherwise. If a cow is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by a dog, or dies on uneven ground, [the herdsman is not liable].
But the keeper alone shall make good that which is lost through human negligence.
However, if it has been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the keeper is not liable to pay,
provided he informs his own master of both the place and the time.
One should give the two ears, the hide, the tail-hair, the bladder, the sinew, and the bile to the owners of the animals; when they have died, one should show the identifying marks.
But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid, [the blame lies with the herdsman].
If a wolf should kill one by force, the guilt for that shall lie with the keeper.
But if, among those cows kept within the enclosure grazing together in the forest,
a wolf should kill one by leaping upon it, the keeper is not guilty in that case.
The pasture land surrounding a village should be one hundred bows on all sides;
for a city, it should be three times that, or else three throws of a wooden yoke-pin.
If cattle should damage unenclosed grain there, [the owner of the cattle shall be liable].
The king should not inflict punishment upon those who guard the cattle in that regard.
He should construct a fence there such that a camel cannot look over it,
and he should block every opening through which the mouth of a dog or a pig might pass.

In a field enclosed along a path, or again, one situated on the outskirts of a village, the owner of the cattle, if accompanied by a herdsman, deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; however, he should drive away the cattle if they are without a herdsman. But in other fields, the cattle deserve a fine of one and a quarter paṇas.

But in all cases, it is the settled rule that compensation must be paid to the owner of the field. Manu has declared that a cow that has calved within ten days, bulls, and sacrificial animals— whether they are attended by a keeper or not— are not to be punished.
In the event of a failure by the owner of the field, the fine shall be ten times the share [due to the cultivator]; in the case of a failure by the cultivator, it shall be half that fine.
Furthermore, if the failure is due to the ignorance of the servants, the fine for the owner of the field shall be half of that.
A righteous lord of the earth should establish this rule.
In cases of transgression involving owners of cattle, herders,
and the boundaries between two villages,
one should determine the boundary during the month of Jyeṣṭha when the landmarks are clearly visible.
One should establish boundary trees such as the Nyagrodha, Aśvattha, and Kiṃśuka;
the Śālmali, Sāla, and Tāla, as well as milky trees (kṣīrin);
various thickets, bamboos, Śamī trees, creepers, and level ground.
Thorny shrubs, hedges, and the like likewise ensure that the boundary does not disappear. Ponds, wells, large oblong ponds, and springs,
as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries.
And he should cause other hidden boundary marks to be made,
having observed that among men in this world there is constant confusion regarding the knowledge of boundaries.
[He should place] stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, and potsherds.
Cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and sand—
whatever other such things the earth does not consume over time—
one should cause these to be placed inconspicuously at the junctions along the boundary.
By these marks, as well as by long-standing possession and the constant flow of water, the king shall determine the boundary between two disputing parties;
even when the marks are visible, if there should still be doubt.

The determination of a boundary dispute shall depend solely upon witnesses. Witnesses regarding the boundary marks must be questioned in the presence of the village communities and of the two litigants themselves.
Whatever decision they, being questioned together, may declare regarding the boundary,
that he shall record as the boundary, and he shall likewise record all of them by name.
Wearing garlands and red garments, they shall take up the earth with their heads.
Supported by their respective good deeds, they should lead the case to a just conclusion. Leading it according to what has been stated, those truthful witnesses are purified;
but leading it otherwise, they shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
In the absence of witnesses, however, four inhabitants of the neighboring villages [who dwell on the borders of the villages] shall,
being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king.
In the absence of such neighbors who are witnesses to the boundary, [the king shall consult] the original inhabitants...
He should also interrogate these men who frequent the forests:
hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and other forest-dwellers.
When they have been questioned, whatever mark they declare at the junctions of the boundaries,
that the king shall establish according to dharma for the two villages.
This applies to fields, wells, tanks, groves, and houses.
The determination of boundary markers should be understood as depending upon the testimony of the neighbors.
If the neighbors should speak falsely regarding the boundary markers in a dispute between men,
they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.

One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field through intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done out of ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred. When a boundary is difficult to determine, the king himself, being conversant with the law, [shall decide].
One may assign land to some for the sake of mutual benefit; such is the settled rule. This entire law regarding the determination of boundaries has been declared in its entirety.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of verbal assault.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
a Vaiśya deserves half of that or two hundred, while a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.
A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for insulting a Kṣatriya.
In the case of a Vaiśya, the fine shall be twenty-five [paṇas], and for a Śūdra, the fine shall be twelve.
For the transgression of twice-born men against one of equal caste, the fine shall be exactly twelve. In cases of disputes that are not to be spoken of, that same fine shall be doubled.

But a man of low birth who insults twice-born men with harsh speech shall have his tongue cut out, for he is of inferior origin. Furthermore, for one who maliciously utters their names and castes, [the same punishment applies].
A red-hot iron spike, ten fingers long and blazing, shall be thrust into his mouth.
If he arrogantly imparts instruction on dharma to Brahmins,
the king shall pour boiling oil into his mouth and his ears.
If one speaks falsely out of pride regarding another's learning, country, caste, occupation, or even their body, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
This applies whether he calls a one-eyed man "one-eyed," or a lame man, or anyone else of a similar condition.
Even if speaking the truth, he shall be made to pay a fine of at least one *kārṣāpaṇa*.
One who defames his mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher shall be made to pay a hundred [paṇas]; and likewise one who does not yield the path to his teacher.
But a wise king should impose punishment upon a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the first amercement; but for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement.
In the same manner, this applies truly to Vaiśyas and Śūdras with respect to their own respective castes.
The definitive rule is that punishment shall consist of the infliction of fines, excluding corporal mutilation.
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared in its true essence;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault.

If a person of the lowest caste should injure a member of the highest caste with any part of his body, that very limb of his must be cut off; such is the instruction of Manu. If he raises his hand or a staff [in threat], he deserves to have his hand cut off.

One who strikes out of anger with the foot deserves to have his foot cut off. A person of lower birth who seeks to sit upon the same seat as one of superior birth should be branded on the hip and banished, or else one of his buttocks should be cut off.
The king shall cause the two lips of one who spits out of arrogance to be cut off;
likewise, the penis of one who urinates [upon him] and the anus of one who passes wind [upon him].
He shall cause the hands of one who seizes [him] by the hair to be cut off without hesitation.

One who breaks the skin on the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]; likewise, one who causes blood to flow. But one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished.

In the case of injury to any of the forest trees, the fine shall be inflicted in proportion to their utility; this is the settled rule. When a blow is struck against humans or animals for the purpose of causing them pain, [the same principle applies].
In proportion as the suffering is greater, so should the punishment be inflicted. Likewise, in cases of crushing a limb, or causing a wound or bloodshed,
the offender shall be made to pay the expenses of recovery, or else the full amount of the fine.
If a person should damage the goods of another, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
he shall provide satisfaction to the owner and pay an equivalent amount to the king.
This applies to leather articles, leather vessels, and those made of wood or clay.
In the case of flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value.
Regarding a vehicle, its driver, and the owner of the vehicle, they say there are ten exemptions; in any other case, a fine is prescribed.
When the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the animal turns sideways or comes facing him;
likewise when there is a breakage of the axle of the vehicle or a breakage of a wheel;
and also when there is a snapping of the harnesses, the breast-straps, or the reins.
And in the case of a cry for help, "Get out of the way!", Manu has declared that there is no punishment. But where a vehicle goes astray due to the driver's incompetence,
the owner shall be liable for the injury and must pay a fine of two hundred.
If the driver is experienced, he alone deserves the fine;
if the driver is inexperienced, all those riding in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred [paṇas]. This applies even if the vehicle is obstructed on the road by cattle or another chariot.
If one causes a living being to perish, the punishment there is immediate and without deliberation. In the case of killing a human, the guilt is instantly equal to that of a thief;
for large animals such as cows, elephants, camels, and horses, it is half [the penalty].
For the injury of small animals, however, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the fine shall be fifty.
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five *māṣas*.
But for the killing of one's own pig, the fine shall be one *māṣika*.
A wife, a son, a slave, a servant, and a uterine brother,
when they have committed an offense, may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane.

But one must strike on the back of the body, and never on the upper part of the body; for striking otherwise than this, one shall incur the guilt of a thief. This has been declared in its entirety as the legal decision regarding assault.
Therefore, I shall declare the rule for determining the punishment of a thief.
The king should exert the greatest effort in suppressing thieves;
by the suppression of thieves, his fame and his kingdom increase.

For that king who grants freedom from fear is always worthy of honor; indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra) is perpetually one where the fee is the granting of safety. A sixth part of all merit accrues to the king who protects [his subjects].
For one who fails to protect, a sixth part of even unrighteousness falls upon him.
But a sixth part of whatever he studies, whatever he sacrifices, whatever he gives, and whatever he worships, belongs to the king by virtue of his proper protection.
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices every day with fees of a hundred thousand;
yet the monarch who takes tribute, taxes, and tolls without providing protection [incurs sin].
He who takes both the share and the fine shall go immediately to hell.
They call that king who takes a sixth part as tribute but does not protect his subjects the one who carries away the entire impurity of all the world.

One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, a plunderer, who fails to protect his subjects, and who devours them instead, goes to a low state. One should strive to restrain an unrighteous king by means of three methods.
By the restraint, imprisonment, various forms of corporal punishment,
and execution of the wicked, and by the protection of the virtuous,
kings are constantly purified, just as the twice-born are purified by sacrifices.

A lord must always forgive those litigants who revile him, as well as children, the elderly, and the sick, if he seeks his own welfare. He who, being reviled by those in distress, remains patient, is exalted in heaven because of that.
But he who, out of arrogance, does not submit, goes to hell by that act.
A thief must go before the king with disheveled hair, running, confessing that theft:
"I am a doer of such a deed; punish me."
Taking a club or a staff made of khadira wood upon his shoulder,
or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron rod;
by either punishing him or releasing him, the thief is freed from the guilt of theft.
But by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief. The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife transfers hers to her husband;
a pupil and a sacrificer transfer theirs to their teacher; and a thief transfers his guilt to the king.
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed meritorious deeds.
However, he who steals a rope or a jar from a well, or he who destroys a water-shed (*prapā*), [is liable to punishment].
He shall receive a fine of one *māṣa* and must restore that [stolen property] to the owner.
For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death;
for any lesser amount, he shall be made to pay eleven times its value, and that property must be returned to him.

Likewise, for stealing more than one hundred *dharaṇas* of gold, silver, and the like, or of the finest garments, the punishment is death. However, when the amount exceeds fifty, the amputation of the hand is ordained.
But for other cases, one should prescribe a fine eleven times the value.
For the abduction of men of noble birth, and especially women,
as well as for the theft of the most precious gems, the offender deserves the death penalty.
In the case of stealing large animals, weapons, or medicine,
the king should determine the punishment after considering the time and the circumstances.
[Likewise for] cows belonging to Brāhmaṇas and for the breaking of a small knife.
For the theft of livestock as well, an immediate fine of half a pāda must be imposed.
This applies to the theft of thread, cotton, fermenting agents (kinva), cow dung, molasses,
curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass.
In the case of stealing bamboo and wicker vessels, as well as salts, earthenware,
earth, and ashes;
and likewise in the case of fish, birds, oil, and clarified butter—
For meat, honey, and whatever else originates from animals,
as well as for other such intoxicating drinks and for cooked rice—
indeed, for all kinds of cooked food— the fine shall be double their value.
For flowers, green grain, shrubs, creepers, trees,
and other things that have not been threshed, the fine shall be five *kṛṣṇalas*.
For threshed grain, as well as for vegetables, roots, and fruits, [the same fine applies].
If there is no connection [to the owner], the fine is one hundred; if there is a connection, the punishment is fifty.

But that act which is committed by force with a connection [to the owner] is *sāhasa* (violence); that which is committed without a connection, or where one denies having taken it after taking it, is *steya* (theft).

But the king should punish first that man who would steal these prepared articles, as well as one who would steal fire from the house. With whichever limb a thief commits an offense against men, by that very limb shall he be punished.
The king should confiscate that very property for the purpose of deterring such behavior.
No one— whether father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, or domestic priest—
is exempt from punishment by the king if he does not abide by his own duty.
Where an ordinary person would be fined one *kārṣāpaṇa*, the king should be fined one thousand; this is the established rule. However, for a *śūdra* who commits theft, the offense becomes eightfold.
For a Vaiśya, it shall be sixteen, and for a Kṣatriya, thirty-two; for a Brāhmaṇa, it shall be sixty-four or even a full hundred,
or twice sixty-four, for he is indeed an expert in the merits and defects of those [offenses].
Manu has declared that taking roots and fruits from trees, as well as wood for the purpose of fire, and grass for the fodder of cattle, does not constitute theft.
If a Brāhmaṇa should desire to obtain wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given, [he must act with restraint].
Even by officiating at sacrifices or teaching, he is exactly like a thief.
A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose means of subsistence are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane or two roots from another's field, does not deserve to be punished.
One who binds those who should not be bound, one who releases those who are bound,
and one who steals a slave, a horse, or a chariot, shall incur the guilt of a thief. By this method, the king, effecting the suppression of thieves, [attains merit].
A king who desires to attain fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death,
and who seeks the station of Indra along with imperishable and eternal glory,
must not neglect even for a moment a man who commits an act of violence.

A man who commits violence through abusive speech, theft, or indeed by physical assault, should be known as the worst among evildoers. Furthermore, that king who condones one engaged in such violence [is likewise culpable].
He quickly goes to destruction and incurs enmity.
A king should not, for the sake of friendship or even from the acquisition of vast wealth,
release perpetrators of violence who bring fear to all living beings.
The twice-born may take up arms when their dharma is obstructed,
and during a disorder among the twice-born castes caused by the exigencies of the times.
They may also do so for their own protection or in battle to recover sacrificial fees.

And in the case of rescuing a woman or a Brahmin, one who kills does not incur sin if he acts according to dharma. Whether it be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a Brahmin highly learned in the Vedas— if such a person approaches as an assailant (ātatāyin), one should certainly kill him without hesitation.

There is no fault whatsoever for a slayer in killing an assailant, whether the act be done openly or secretly; fury recoils upon that fury. The lord of the earth [should punish] those men who are intent upon violating the wives of others.
Having branded them with punishments that cause terror, he should banish them;
for from such acts arises the confusion of castes among the people,
by which unrighteousness, destroying the very root, leads to total ruin.

A man who engages in private conversation with another's wife, having been previously accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement. But he who, not having been previously accused, speaks to her for a valid reason, [is not liable].
He shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is indeed no transgression on his part.
He who addresses the wife of another at a sacred bathing place, in a deserted spot, or even in a forest,
or at the confluence of rivers, shall be guilty of adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*).
Service, playful dalliance, touching her ornaments and garments,
and even sitting together on the same bed— all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).
He who touches a woman in an improper place, or who allows himself to be touched by her, [is guilty].
All forms of sexual intercourse are traditionally defined as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery) when performed with mutual consent.
A non-Brāhmaṇa who commits such an act deserves a punishment ending in death;
for among all four castes, the wives are always to be most carefully guarded.
Beggars, bards, those initiated for sacrifice, and artisans may converse with women without being forbidden. However,
one who has been forbidden must not engage in conversation with the wives of others.
But one who speaks while being forbidden deserves a fine of one suvarṇa.
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers (*cāraṇa*) nor to those who live off their own bodies;
for they entice women and cause them to be secretly employed.
But he who engages in conversation with them should be made to pay a small fine;
as well as one who converses in secret with female slaves who have only one master, or with women who have renounced the world.
He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution.
A man of equal status who violates a willing woman shall not suffer corporal punishment.
One should not cause any fine to be paid for a maiden who consents to union with a superior man;
however, if she serves a man of lower status, he should keep her confined in the house.
A man of lower caste who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the highest caste deserves the death penalty;
however, if he has intercourse with a woman of equal caste, he should pay the bride-price if her father so desires.
But if a man, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force, [he shall be punished].

In that case, his two fingers should be immediately cut off, and he deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas]. But a man of equal status who defiles a willing woman shall not suffer the cutting off of his fingers;
rather, he should be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] to prevent the recurrence of such an incident.
If a maiden should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she must also pay double the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a rod.
But a woman who defiles a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head.
Or else, there shall be the cutting off of her two fingers, as well as being led away on a donkey. But that woman who, arrogant because of her kinsmen or her own virtues, violates her husband,
the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a public place crowded with many people.
One should cause a wicked man to be burned on a heated iron bed;
they shall pile wood upon him there, and the evildoer shall be consumed by fire. For a wicked man who has been accused for a year, the fine shall be double.
In the case of cohabiting with a Vratya woman or a Chandala woman, the same penalty applies.

A Shudra who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the twice-born castes, whether she is protected or unprotected, is deprived of his limb if she was unprotected, and of all his property if she was protected. [He is deprived of his limb and all his property.]
A Vaiśya shall be punished with the forfeiture of all his property after being confined for one year;
a Kṣatriya shall be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine.
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman...
One should fine a Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas] and a Kṣatriya one thousand.
But both of them, if they have violated a guarded Brāhmaṇa woman,
are to be punished like a Śūdra or burned by a fire of straw.
A Brāhmaṇa who approaches a guarded Brāhmaṇa woman by force shall be fined one thousand;
if he has united with her through her consent, he shall be fined five hundred.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the punishment of shaving the head is ordained as the penalty that ends his life.
But for the other castes, the punishment shall be one that ends in death.
One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he has committed every possible crime;
rather, one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him unhurt but stripped of all his wealth.
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a Brāhmaṇa;
therefore, a king should not even contemplate his execution in his mind.
If a Vaiśya should approach a guarded Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya a guarded Vaiśya woman...
Both of them deserve punishment for approaching an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman:

the Brāhmaṇa shall be made to pay a fine of one thousand, but if they approach her while she is protected, they both shall be punished. For a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya approaching a Śūdra woman, the fine shall indeed be one thousand.
If he approaches an unprotected Vaiśya woman, the fine for a Kṣatriya is five hundred;
however, a Kṣatriya should seek either tonsure with urine as penance or pay that very fine.
A Brāhmaṇa approaching an unprotected Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra woman [is subject to the following].
He should be fined five hundred [paṇas], but a man of the lowest caste (antyaja) who has intercourse with a woman [of his own class] should be fined one thousand.
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words,
no perpetrator of violence, and no one who strikes with a staff, shares in the world of Śakra.

The suppression of these five within his own realm by the king establishes universal sovereignty among his peers and brings him fame in the world. If a sacrificer should abandon a priest, or if a priest should abandon a sacrificer—
If those two [husband and wife] are capable of work and not guilty of a fault, the fine for each of them shall be one hundred [paṇas].
Neither mother, nor father, nor wife, nor son deserves to be abandoned. One who abandons these when they have not fallen from their caste shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
When twice-born men dispute among themselves regarding the duties of their respective stages of life (*āśrama*),
a king who desires his own welfare and seeks to uphold righteousness should not pronounce a decision himself;
rather, having honored them as is fitting along with Brahmins, the king [should let them decide].
Having first pacified them with gentle words, he should establish them in their own duty.
A Brahmin who does not feed his neighbor or next-door neighbor, or two worthy twice-born men at a festive occasion,
deserves a fine of one *māṣaka*.
If a learned *śrotriya* does not feed another virtuous *śrotriya* during auspicious ceremonies (*bhūtikṛtya*),

he shall be made to pay double the value of that food and one *māṣaka* of gold. A blind man, an idiot, one who moves about on a chair, and one who is seventy years old [are exempt from this obligation].
And those who provide service to Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) shall not be made to pay any tax by anyone.
The king should always honor a Vedic scholar, one afflicted by disease, a child, an elder, one who possesses nothing, and one born of a noble family.
A washerman, while washing, should wash clothes slowly on a smooth board made of śālmalī wood;
he should not exchange garments for garments, nor should he let them remain with him overnight.
A weaver shall give back ten palas of thread plus one pala as a fee.
One who acts otherwise than this shall be made to pay a fine of twelve [paṇas].
Experts skilled in the places where tolls are collected, who are discerning regarding all merchandise, shall fix the price according to each commodity; from that, the king shall take one-twentieth.

If a person, out of greed, exports those goods which have been declared as royal monopolies or which are prohibited, the king shall confiscate his entire property. One who avoids the customs station and buys or sells at an improper time [is likewise liable].

And one who speaks falsely regarding the calculation shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the error. Having investigated the source, the destination, the storage period, as well as both the profit and the loss, he shall regulate the purchase and sale of all commodities.
Every five nights, or else every fortnight when it has passed,
the king should publicly determine the value of these commodities.
All weights and measures must be clearly marked.
And every six months, he should examine them once again.
A carriage shall be made to pay one *paṇa* at a ferry; a man, half a *paṇa*;
cattle and women, a quarter; and an empty-handed man, half a quarter.
Vehicles filled with goods should be made to pay ferry-toll according to their value;
empty vessels and men without belongings should pay whatever is appropriate. On a long journey, the toll shall be determined according to the place and the time.

One should know that [the rule] applies to the banks of rivers; there is no such mark [of ownership] in the ocean. A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a wandering ascetic, a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks, shall not be made to pay a ferry-toll at a crossing.
Whatever belonging to the boatmen should be lost through their own negligence on board the ship,
that must be paid by the boatmen themselves, having assembled together according to their respective shares. This is declared to be the legal decision regarding those who travel by boat.
If the fault lies with the boatman, there is no punishment for the water-damage; however, if it is due to an act of God (such as a storm), there is no liability.
He should cause the Vaiśya to practice trade, money-lending, and agriculture, as well as the tending of cattle;
and he should cause the Śūdra to perform service for the twice-born.
A Brāhmaṇa should support with compassion a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood,
making them perform their own respective duties.
However, a Brāhmaṇa who, out of greed, compels initiated twice-born men to perform the work of slaves, [incurs sin].
If he does not consent, the king shall fine him six hundred [paṇas] for his arrogance. But a Śūdra, whether purchased or even unpurchased, the king should compel to perform servitude;
for he was created by the Self-existent One specifically for the service of the Brāhmaṇa.
Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that [status] is innate to him, so who can remove it?
[The types of slaves are: one captured under a banner (dhvajāhṛta), one maintained on food (bhaktadāsa), one born in the house (gṛhaja), one bought (krīta), and one given (dattrima).

The son of a female slave, one born of a woman married while pregnant, one given by the father, one purchased, one inherited, one who has entered [as a slave], and a slave by punishment—these seven are the origins of slavery.
A wife, a son, and a slave—these three alone are declared to have no property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong.
A Brāhmaṇa may confidently take property from a Śūdra;
for he has no property of his own, as all his wealth is liable to be taken by his master.
A Vaiśya and a Śūdra, however, he should cause to perform their respective duties with diligence.
For if those two fall away from their duties, they would throw this world into turmoil. Day by day, he should inspect the completion of his undertakings, the draft animals,
as well as the fixed income and expenditure, the mines, and the treasury.
Thus, by settling all these legal cases, the king,
having cast off all sin, attains the supreme goal.
For a man and a woman who abide in the path of dharma,
