I shall declare the eternal laws concerning their union and their separation.
Women must be kept in a state of dependence by their own men, day and night.
And women who become attached to sensual objects must be established under their own control. In childhood, the father protects her; in youth, the husband protects her;
in old age, the sons protect her; a woman does not deserve independence.
A father who does not give [his daughter in marriage] at the proper time is censurable, and a husband who does not take her [home] is censurable.
But when the husband has died, the son is censurable if he does not protect his mother. Women must be protected especially from even the slightest opportunities for transgression.
For if they are not protected, they bring grief to both families. Indeed,
seeing this supreme duty of all social classes,
husbands strive to protect their wives, even when they themselves are weak.
For by protecting his wife with diligence, a man protects his own offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma. Entering his wife, the husband is born here as an embryo.
For that indeed is the "wifehood" (jāyātva) of a wife, that from her one is born again. For whatever kind of man a woman consorts with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind.
Therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should protect one's wife with great effort.
No man is able to guard women by force alone;
however, they can be guarded by the application of these following means:
he should employ her in the accumulation of wealth and also in its expenditure.
In matters of purity, religious duty, the cooking of food,
and the supervision of household utensils, women who are guarded at home by trustworthy men yet protect themselves by their own efforts are well-guarded.
Drinking [intoxicants], association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about,
sleeping [at improper times], and residing in another's house— these are the six things that corrupt women.
They do not examine beauty, nor do they have regard for age.
Whether he be handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man. Due to their passion for men, their fickle-mindedness, and their natural lack of affection,
these women act perversely toward their husbands even when guarded with great effort in this world.
Having thus understood their nature, born of the creation of Prajāpati,
a man should exert the greatest effort toward their protection. [He should guard them against] the bed,
the seat, ornaments, lust, anger, dishonesty, and ignobility.

Manu ordained that women possess a disposition toward malice and engage in misconduct. (9.17c) There is no ritual action for women involving sacred mantras; such is the established rule in the Dharma.
(9.18a) For women are devoid of sensory power and lack mantras; it is settled that they are untruthful. (9.18c)
Likewise, many Vedic verses have been sung even in the Nigamas.
Listen to their expiations for the purpose of examining their specific characteristics:
"Whatever my mother, wandering about and unfaithful to her husband, lusted after..."
"May my father take back that seed"— this is the scriptural justification for this.
Whatever undesirable thing she contemplates in her mind against the will of her husband,
this is declared to be the proper means for the concealment of such transgression.

With whatever qualities a husband is endowed with whom a woman is united according to the prescribed rule, she becomes possessed of those same qualities, just as a river is by the ocean. Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, was united with Vasiṣṭha.
Śāraṅgī attained a state of high honor through Mandapāla.
These and other women in this world, though born of low origins,
have attained eminence through the various auspicious qualities of their respective husbands.
Thus has been declared the ever-auspicious way of life for husband and wife;

now learn the duties regarding progeny, which yield happiness both in this world and after death. (Manu 9.25) O highly fortunate ones, worthy of honor, you are the lights of the home for the sake of procreation. (Manu 9.26)
In households, there is no distinction whatsoever between women and prosperity (*śrī*).
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those born,
and the daily course of worldly life— each of these is visibly dependent upon the woman.
Offspring, religious duties, obedient service, and supreme delight depend upon the wife;
likewise, heaven for one’s ancestors and for oneself is dependent on her.
She who does not act perversely toward her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body, [attains these rewards].
She attains the worlds of her husband and is called a virtuous woman by the righteous. But through infidelity toward her husband, a wife incurs reproach in this world,
enters the womb of a jackal, and is tormented by foul diseases.
Listen to this meritorious discourse concerning the son, who is beneficial to all people, as it has been declared by the virtuous and by the great sages of old.
(Manu 9.31) They recognize the son as belonging to the husband; however, there is a scriptural duality regarding the progenitor. (Manu 9.32)
Some say the progenitor [is the father], while others know the owner of the field [to be the father].
The woman is remembered as being the field, and the man is remembered as being the seed;
from the union of the field and the seed comes the birth of all embodied beings.
In some cases the seed is superior, while in others it is the womb;
but where both are equal, that offspring is highly praised.
Between the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be the more excellent.
For the offspring of all beings is characterized by the nature of the seed. Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field prepared by the proper season,
that very kind of seed grows therein, manifested through its own inherent qualities.
For this earth is said to be the eternal womb of all living beings. And the seed does not develop any qualities of the womb during its growth.
Even in a single field on the earth, seeds sown by farmers at different times—
In this world, seeds arise in various forms according to their own nature:
rice, *śāli* rice, mung beans, sesame, beans, as well as barley;
they sprout according to the seed, just like garlic and sugarcane.
"It is not possible that one thing is sown and another grows;
for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts.
Thus [it was said] by a wise man, disciplined, and one who knows both theoretical knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*).
One who desires long life must never sow [seed] in the wife of another.
Regarding this, those who know the past recite the verses sung by Vāyu:
"Just as seed should not be sown by a man in that which belongs to another."
Just as an arrow, once shot, does not vanish while one continues to pierce through the air where it was first struck,
so too the seed sown in the possession of another quickly perishes.
Those who know the ancient lore recognize this entire earth as the wife of Pṛthu.
They say that one who cuts down a tree stump is like one who destroys a field of rice, and one who kills a deer is like one who destroys a field of grain.
A man is truly only this much: his wife, himself, and their offspring;
so the learned Brahmins have declared, for he who is the husband is also considered to be the woman.
A wife is not released from her husband by means of a ransom or by abandonment;
thus we know the law as it was ordained of old by Prajāpati. Once does the shoulder-fall occur; once is a maiden given away.
"I give"— these three words are uttered but once by the virtuous.
Just as one is not considered the progenitor with respect to cows, horses, camels, female slaves, buffaloes, goats, or sheep,
so it is likewise with other women.
Those who possess seed but have no field, and sow it in the field of another,
never obtain any share of the crop that is produced.
Just as when a bull fathers a hundred calves upon the cows of another, [the owner of the cows receives them].

The offspring of those who own the cows belong to the owners of the cows alone; the bull's seed is sown in vain. Likewise, those who sow seed in another’s field without owning the field work for the benefit of the owner of the field; the owner of the seed does not obtain the fruit.

But when no reward is intended, the fruit belongs to both the owner of the field and the sower; yet, as is evident, the purpose of the owners of the field prevails, for the womb is more powerful than the seed. Furthermore, that which is given for the sake of the seed arises from the agreement to perform the act.
In this world, two are seen to be sharers of that [offspring]: the owner of the seed and the owner of the field.

When seed carried by a flood or by the wind sprouts in someone’s field, that seed belongs to the owner of the field alone; the sower does not obtain the fruit. [The owner of the seed does not obtain the fruit.]
This law regarding the offspring of cows, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, sheep, birds,
and buffaloes should be understood.
Thus has been proclaimed to you the relative value— superior or inferior— of seed and womb.
Henceforth, I shall declare the duties of women in times of distress:
the wife of an elder brother is like the wife of a guru to a younger brother;
and the wife of a younger brother is traditionally regarded as a daughter-in-law to an elder brother.

The elder brother who approaches the wife of the younger, or the younger brother who approaches the wife of the elder— even if they are formally authorized— become outcasts if they do so except in times of distress.
Or, by a husband's brother or a sapinda, a woman who is properly authorized [to bear offspring]...
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, offspring should be sought for the sake of progeny.
However, one appointed to a widow shall, anointed with clarified butter and remaining silent,
produce exactly one son at night, and never a second under any circumstances.
Some who are experts in this matter consider a second procreation with women to be permissible,
seeing that the purpose of the *niyoga* for those two has not yet been fulfilled according to the law.
But when the purpose of the *niyoga* with a widow has been accomplished according to the prescribed rule—
They should behave toward each other like a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law.
But if those two, being thus enjoined, should act out of lust by disregarding the prescribed rule,
they would both become outcasts— like one who violates his daughter-in-law and one who violates the bed of his guru.
A widow must not be appointed to another man by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma.
Nowhere in the marriage mantras is such an appointment ever mentioned.
The remarriage of a widow has not been prescribed in the rules for marriage; indeed,
this practice, which is the law of beasts and is censured by the learned twice-born,
was declared [as permissible] even for humans while Vena was ruling the kingdom.
In former times, that preeminent royal sage, while ruling over the entire earth,
brought about the intermixture of the social orders (varṇas), his mind being struck by lust.
From that time forward, whoever out of delusion [approaches] a woman whose husband has died...

The virtuous censure that man who employs [his brother] for the sake of offspring. If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true, her own brother-in-law (devara) may marry her according to this rule.

Having approached her according to the prescribed rule— she being dressed in white garments and pure in her vows— he should enjoy her in private, once at each season, until she gives birth. A wise man, having given his daughter to one, should not give her again to another.
For by giving [a maiden] away and then giving her away again, one incurs the sin of lying regarding a human being.
Even after having accepted a maiden according to the prescribed rule, one may abandon her if she is blameworthy,
diseased, severely defiled, or if she was offered through deception.
But if a man gives away a defective maiden without having disclosed her defects,
he shall annul that gift of the wicked-souled giver of the maiden.
A man who has business abroad may depart after providing for his wife's maintenance.

For a woman, even one who is steadfast, may become corrupt when distressed by a lack of livelihood. When her husband has gone abroad, she should live maintaining her self-restraint after having provided for her maintenance;
but if he has gone abroad without providing for it, she should live by means of blameless crafts.
A man who has gone abroad for the sake of religious duties should be waited for eight years;
for the sake of learning or fame, six years; but for the sake of pleasure, three years.
A husband should wait for one year for a wife who shows him hostility.
But after a year has passed, he may take back her property and no longer cohabit with her.
She who neglects her husband while he is intoxicated, or insane, or afflicted by disease,
shall be abandoned for three months, deprived of her ornaments and belongings.
There is no abandonment of a wife who is insane, an outcast, impotent, sterile, or afflicted with a foul disease;
nor is there any forfeiture of her inheritance. This also applies to one who is hostile, a drinker of intoxicants, of immoral conduct, or who is antagonistic.
A wife who is diseased, cruel, or constantly wasteful of wealth must always be superseded [by another wife].
A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth year;
one who gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh year; but one who speaks unpleasantly may be superseded immediately.

But she who may be diseased, yet is beneficial and endowed with good character— having obtained her permission, she may be superseded by another wife, but she must never be treated with contempt. However, if a superseded wife should depart from the house in anger, [she shall be punished].

She should be immediately confined or abandoned in the presence of the family. But she who, even when forbidden, drinks liquor on festive occasions, or goes to spectacles and public assemblies, shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas*.
If twice-born men should marry both women of their own caste and those of other castes,
their seniority, honor, and residence shall be according to the order of their castes.
[They must perform] service to the body of the husband and the daily religious duties.

A wife of one's own caste alone should perform all these tasks for everyone; never one of a different caste. But he who, out of delusion, causes them to be performed by another woman while a wife of his own caste is present, is indeed like a *brāhmaṇa-cāṇḍāla*, as seen in ancient tradition.
To a suitor who is superior, handsome, worthy, and of equal status,

one should give the daughter according to the prescribed rule, even if she has not yet reached marriageable age. A maiden may, if she so desires, remain in her father's house until death, even if she has reached puberty.
But she must never be given to one who is devoid of good qualities. A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
after this period, however, she may find a husband of equal status.

If she approaches her husband of her own accord when he is not giving her away, she incurs no guilt whatsoever, nor does the man whom she approaches. A maiden choosing her own husband (svayaṃvarā) must not take with her any ornaments belonging to her father.

If she should take away property inherited from her mother or given by her brother, she would be a thief. But he who takes a maiden who has reached puberty need not give the nuptial fee (śulka) to the father;
for he would have exceeded his rights of ownership by obstructing her menstrual periods.

A man thirty years of age should marry a pleasing girl of twelve; or one twenty-four years old may marry an eight-year-old, if he is in haste lest his religious duty (*dharma*) suffer. A husband receives his wife as a gift from the gods; she does not obtain him by her own will.
He who acts for the pleasure of the gods should always support that virtuous wife. Women were created for the sake of procreation, and men for the sake of continuing the lineage;
therefore, in the revealed scripture (*śruti*), religious duty is declared to be common to both, performed together with the wife.
If the giver of the bride-price should die after the price has been paid for a maiden,
she should be given to the husband's brother, provided the maiden consents.
Even a Śūdra, when giving away his daughter, must not take a bride-price.

For by accepting a bride-price, one effectively commits a secret sale of one's daughter. This act— having promised her to one man, only to give her to another— neither the ancients nor any other virtuous men have ever committed.
We have never heard of such a thing, even in former births:
the sale of a daughter concealed under the name of a "bride-price" (śulka).
There shall be mutual fidelity until the end of life.
This supreme duty of women and men should be known in brief. Thus, having performed their rites, the woman and man should always strive so that,
even when separated, they do not violate each other.

This law concerning the sexual union of woman and man has been declared to you, as well as the acquisition of offspring in times of distress; now learn the law of inheritance. After the death of both the father and the mother, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide [the estate] equally.
For they have no authority over their father's estate while he is alive.
However, the eldest alone may take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the others should live dependent upon him, just as they did upon their father.
By the mere birth of the eldest son, a man becomes a father of sons and is released from his debt to the ancestors; therefore, he deserves everything.
For through him he pays off the debt, and by means of him he attains the infinite state.

He alone is known as the son born of dharma; the others, they know, are born of desire. The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers like a father; and they, in accordance with dharma, should behave toward their eldest brother as sons do toward a father.
The eldest son either causes the family to prosper or, conversely, brings it to ruin.
The eldest is most worthy of honor in the world; the eldest is not censured by the virtuous.
He who is the eldest and behaves as an eldest brother is like a mother and like a father.
But he who does not behave like an eldest brother should be honored like a kinsman.
Thus they may live together, or separately out of a desire for dharma;
for dharma increases when they are separate; therefore, separation is consistent with dharma.
The eldest shall receive an additional portion (*uddhāra*) of twenty [shares] from all the property, as well as whatever is the best;
half of that shall belong to the middlemost, and a fourth to the youngest.
Both the eldest and the youngest shall take their shares exactly as prescribed.
Those others who are between the eldest and the youngest shall receive the middlemost share of the wealth.
Of all kinds of property, the first-born shall take the best item;
and he shall also receive whatever is most excellent from among ten.

There is no preferential share (*uddhāra*) among those who are equally proficient in their respective duties; however, something small may be given to the elder as a mark of respect. When the preferential share has thus been set aside, one should distribute equal portions.
But if no preferential share has been set aside for them, this shall be the distribution of shares:
the eldest son shall take one share in excess; the younger brother next below him, one and a half shares;
and the youngest sons, one share each—thus is the law established.
The brothers shall each separately give to their unmarried sisters portions from their own respective shares—one-fourth of their own share. If they refuse to give, they become outcasts.
However, goats, sheep, and single-hoofed animals, they shall never divide unequally.
However, an odd goat or sheep is ordained for the eldest alone.
(Manu 9.119c) If a younger brother should procreate a son upon the wife of the elder, the division of property in that case shall be equal; such is the established law. (Manu 9.120)
According to the law, the subordinate cannot take precedence over the principal;
the father is the principal in procreation, therefore one should honor him according to dharma.
[Likewise,] a younger son born of an elder wife and an elder son born of a younger wife—
If a doubt should arise as to how the division [of the estate] should be made in that case:
the eldest son shall take one bull as his preferential share (uddhāra);
thereafter, the others shall each take bulls inferior to that, according to their respective mothers.

But the son born of the eldest wife, being the eldest, shall take a bull as his sixteenth share; thereafter, the remaining sons shall divide [the estate] according to their mothers—this is the settled rule. This applies to sons born of wives of equal status who are without distinction.
There is no seniority based on the mother; seniority is said to be from birth.
Even in the *subrahmaṇyā* liturgical formulas, it is recorded that the invocation is made according to birth-order seniority.
And even in the case of twins, seniority is recorded as being from birth.

A sonless man may, according to this rule, make his daughter an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), [stipulating]: "Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be the performer of my funeral rites. According to this very procedure, he indeed made appointed daughters in former times.
For the sake of increasing his own lineage, the skillful Prajāpati himself,
being pleased in spirit, gave ten daughters to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven to King Soma with due honor.
As one’s own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son. While she remains as one's very self, how could another take the wealth?
Whatever may be the mother’s separate property (yautaka), that indeed is the portion of the unmarried daughter.
The son of a daughter shall indeed inherit the entire estate of a man who has no sons.
For the son of a daughter shall take the whole inheritance of his father who has no sons;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his own father and one to his maternal grandfather.

In this world, according to the law, there is no difference between a grandson and a daughter's son; for both of them were produced from the bodies of his own mother and father. But if, after a daughter has been designated as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), a son is subsequently born [to her],...
In that case, the division shall be equal, for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman.
But when an appointed daughter (putrikā) has died without a son,
her husband shall take that wealth without hesitation.

Whether she has been formally appointed (*akṛtā*) or not, the son whom she bears from a husband of equal caste makes his maternal grandfather a possessor of a grandson; through him, the grandfather shall receive the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and inherit the wealth.
Through a son one conquers the worlds, and through a grandson one attains immortality.
Then, through his grandson, he attains the world of the Sun.
Because a son saves his father from the hell named Put,
he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-existent One himself.
In this world, no distinction is found between a grandson and a daughter’s son;
for even a daughter’s son delivers him in the hereafter, just like a grandson.
A son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should offer the first funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother.
The second [share] belongs to her father, and the third to that father’s father. However,
a son who has been adopted and is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit his estate, even though he has come from a different lineage.

An adopted son shall never inherit the lineage (*gotra*) or the estate (*riktha*) of his biological father; the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) follows the lineage and the estate, and the ancestral offering (*svadhā*) ceases for one who gives it away [to another].
Likewise, the son of an unauthorized woman, and the son obtained from a brother-in-law by a woman already having sons.
Neither of those two— the one born of an adulterer and the one born of lust— is entitled to a share. Even if born of a woman duly authorized [for levirate],
a son born contrary to the rule is not entitled to his father's inheritance, for he is begotten by one who has fallen from his caste.

A son born from a woman duly appointed for that purpose is equal to a legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*); by law, he belongs to the owner of the field (*kṣetrika*), as he is both his seed and his offspring. He who takes charge of the wealth and the wife of a deceased brother [is the heir].

Having procreated offspring for his brother, he shall give that wealth to that very child. If a woman, having been appointed, should obtain a son from another man, such as a brother-in-law, they declare him to be born of lust, not entitled to the inheritance, and begotten in vain. [Or: born falsely.]
This rule for partition among those born of a single womb should be understood.
Now learn the law concerning those born of many wives of different castes from one man.
If a Brāhmaṇa has four wives in the direct order of the castes, [the following applies].
When sons have been born from them, this rule is recorded for the partition:
the ploughman, the breeding bull, the vehicle, the ornament,
and the house shall be given as the Brahmin’s special portion (*auddhārika*), along with one share from the principal assets.
A son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take three shares of the inheritance, a son of a Kṣatriya two shares,

a son born of a Vaiśya wife shall take one share and a half, and a son of a Śūdra wife shall take one share. Or, having divided that entire collection of property into ten parts, [the shares are distributed accordingly].
One who knows the law should make a lawful partition according to this rule:
the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take four shares, the son of a Kṣatriya woman three shares,
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares, and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share.

Whether he has a legitimate son or even no son at all, one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra wife. The son of a Śūdra wife born to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas does not inherit the estate.
Whatever his father might give him, that alone shall be his wealth.
Or, all sons of twice-born men born of wives of equal caste,
having given a preferential share (*uddhāra*) to the eldest, should divide the remainder equally.

For a Śūdra, however, only a wife of his own caste is ordained, and no other. Sons born of her shall have equal shares, even if there should be a hundred sons. Regarding the twelve kinds of sons that Svāyambhuva Manu has declared for men—
Among them, six are both kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen but not heirs: the son of the body (aurasa),
the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), the adopted son (datta), the made son (kṛtrima),
the son secretly born (gūḍhotpanna), and the cast-off son (apaviddha)— these six are both heirs and kinsmen.
The son of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a pregnant bride (sahoḍha), the purchased son (krīta), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava),
the self-given son (svayaṃdatta), and the son of a Śūdra woman (śaudra)— these six are kinsmen who do not inherit property.
Just as one obtains such fruit when attempting to cross water with defective rafts, so it is with these sons.
One obtains such a fruit when crossing over the darkness with bad sons.

(Manu 9.161c) If there should be two heirs to a single estate, namely a legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*) and a son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), then whichever of them possesses the paternal estate, he shall take that, and not the other. (Manu 9.162)
The legitimate son of the body alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of avoiding cruelty, he should provide a livelihood for the rest.
He should, moreover, give a sixth share of the paternal estate to the son born of the wife (kṣetraja).
When dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa) shall take a fifth part, or indeed [the whole].
The legitimate son (aurasa) and the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) are the two heirs to the father's estate;
the other ten, however, in their respective order, are sharers in the lineage, the inheritance, and the portions.
But that son whom one shall beget oneself upon a wife of one's own caste who has been duly consecrated,
one should know him as the *aurasa* (legitimate) son, the first in rank.
That son born on the bed of one who is deceased, impotent, or diseased—

A son begotten on a wife duly appointed according to her own dharma is known as the *kṣetraja* (field-born). He whom the mother or the father may give with water in times of distress— a son who is similar [in caste] and given with affection— is to be known as the *dattima* (given) son.
But he whom one may make similar [to oneself], who is discerning of virtues and faults,
and who is endowed with the qualities of a son— he is to be known as the "artificial" (kṛtrima) son. Furthermore, he who is born in the house, but it is not known whose he is—

One born secretly in the house belongs to him on whose bed he was begotten. One whom a man may take as a son after he has been abandoned by both mother and father, or by either one of them, is called an *apaviddha* (cast-off).
But the son whom a maiden may secretly bear in her father’s house,
one should call him by the name *kānīna* (maiden-born), born of the maiden, and begotten by the man who marries her.
If a woman who is already pregnant is married— whether her condition be known or unknown— [the child born is a *saahoḍha*].

That child becomes the offspring of the man who marries her, and he is called *sahoḍha* (one taken with the bride). But he whom one purchases from the mother and father for the sake of obtaining offspring—
whether he be similar or dissimilar to them— he is his *krītaka* (bought) son.
She who, having been abandoned by her husband or being a widow, takes another husband of her own accord and bears a son,
is called *paunarbhava*.
This applies even if she has returned after having gone [to another man], provided her virginity remains intact.
She [the widow] deserves to undergo the sacramental rite again with a husband born of remarriage (paunarbhava). He who, being deprived of mother and father, or abandoned without cause,
offers himself to someone, is known as a "self-given" (svayaṃdatta) son.
The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may procreate through lust upon a Śūdra woman is known as a Pāraśava,
because he is born from one who has crossed (pārayan) the boundary;
or he may be the son of a Śūdra born of a female slave or the female slave of a slave.

"Having been authorized, he shall take a share; thus the law is settled. (Manu 9.179c) "These eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja*, as they have been described, the wise call substitutes for a son (*putrapratinidhi*), [serving] to prevent the failure of religious rites (*kriyālopa*). (Manu 9.180)

These sons who have been mentioned incidentally as born from the seed of others belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to anyone else. Among brothers born of the same father, if even one should have a son, [they all share in that son].
Manu has declared that all those [women] become possessed of a son by means of that one son. If among several wives who have but one husband, even one should have a son,
Manu has declared that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that son.
In the absence of each successive superior heir, the inferior one is entitled to the inheritance.
But if there are many of equal status, they all share the inheritance.
Neither brothers nor fathers are the takers of the father's inheritance; rather, it is the sons who inherit.
The father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, as shall his brothers. Water-offerings should be made for three [ancestors], and the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is offered to three;
the fourth is the one who presents them, and a fifth does not exist.
The wealth of each person shall belong to his nearest *sapiṇḍa*;
after him, it shall go to a *sakulya*, or else to the teacher or the pupil.
But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas shall be the heirs to the estate.
Those who possess the threefold knowledge, who are pure and self-controlled—in such a case, the Dharma is not violated.
It is the established rule that the property of a Brāhmaṇa must never be seized by the king;
however, in the absence of all others, the king may take the property of the other castes.

For one who has died without offspring, one should procure a son from a member of the same lineage (sagotra). Whatever collection of property there may be in that case, one should hand that over to him. But if two sons born of two [different men] should dispute over the wealth of their mother, [the court shall decide].

Of those two [wives], whatever belongs to the father of one, that he shall take, and not the other. But when the mother has passed away, all those born from the same womb shall divide the maternal inheritance equally, as shall the uterine sisters.

Whatever daughters they may have, to them also a suitable portion should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth out of affection. [That is,] that which was given at the nuptial fire, that which was given when she was brought home, and that which was given as a token of affection.
The sixfold property of a woman is declared to be that which she receives from her brother, her mother, or her father;
as well as the *anvādheya* (gift received after marriage), and that which is given by her husband out of affection.
This shall be the wealth for her offspring once she has passed away while her husband is still living.

In the cases of the *brāhma*, *daiva*, *ārṣa*, *gāndharva*, and *prājāpatya* marriages, it is ordained that when she dies childless, her property belongs to her husband alone. However, whatever wealth may have been given to her in the *āsura* and other such marriages [belongs to her family].
If she dies childless, that [property] is ordained for the mother and father. But whatever wealth may have been given to a woman by her father in any way whatsoever,
the Brāhmaṇī wife shall take it, or it shall belong to her offspring.
Women should not make a removal of property from the midst of a large family,
nor even from their own wealth, without the permission of their husband.
Whatever ornament may have been worn by women while the husband was alive, [that remains his].
The heirs shall not divide that [property]; those who do divide it fall from their status. One who is impotent, an outcast, one born blind, or deaf likewise;
as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense-organs—these have no share.
However, it is right for a wise man to give to all of them according to his ability;
for he who does not provide food and clothing perpetually becomes an outcast.
But if, by any means, there should be a desire for wives on the part of those who are impotent and so forth—

The offspring of those who have produced a lineage is entitled to the inheritance. Whatever property the eldest son acquires after the father has died, the younger brothers have a share in that, provided they are devoted to learning.

But if all those who are unlearned should acquire wealth through their own efforts, the division of that wealth shall be equal; such is the settled rule, for it is not ancestral property. However, whatever is acquired through learning belongs to that [individual] alone.

That brother who, though capable through his own labor, does not seek wealth from the paternal estate— whether it be that received through friendship, that obtained at marriage, or that given as the honey-mixture offering—
he shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence.
That which has been acquired by one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate,
being obtained through one's own efforts— that he need not give against his will. But as for paternal property that the father has not yet received, if he should acquire it;

One who has acquired property by his own effort need not share it with his sons against his will. If those who were previously divided choose to live together again, they shall divide the property equally; in that case, no right of primogeniture exists.
If among them the eldest or the youngest is deprived of his share at the time of distribution,
or if either one should die, his share is not lost. His uterine brothers, having assembled together, shall divide it equally.
Those brothers who are reunited, as well as uterine sisters—
if an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers,
he shall lose his status as the eldest, forfeit his share, and be restrained by the kings.

All brothers who persist in improper occupations do not deserve a share of the wealth; nor should the eldest brother make a separate acquisition for himself without giving a portion to the younger ones.
If there should be a joint effort among brothers who have not yet divided their property, [they shall share the gains].
A father shall by no means give unequal shares to his sons.
However, one born after the partition of the estate shall take the paternal wealth alone;
or he shall share it with those who were reunited with him.
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.
Once all debts and assets have been distributed according to the rule, [the heirs shall proceed].
Whatever may be discovered later, all that he should bring into equality [with the other shares].
Clothes, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women,
security and well-being (yogakṣema), and pasture grounds— they declare these to be indivisible.
This division of property among sons and the procedure for their rites has been declared to you.
Now learn, in due order, the law concerning those born of the wife and others, as well as the rules regarding gambling.
The king shall prohibit both gambling and betting within his kingdom.

These two vices cause the destruction of kings who rule the earth: gambling and betting with living creatures; for these are forms of theft committed openly. Therefore, the king should always be diligent in suppressing them.
That which is performed with inanimate objects is called *dyūta* (gambling) in the world;
that which is performed with animate beings should be known as *samāhvaya* (betting). He who either engages in gambling or betting, or causes them to be done, [is liable for punishment].

The king shall cause all those to be executed, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born. He shall quickly banish from the city gamblers, actors, cruel men, those belonging to heretical sects, those engaged in forbidden occupations, and liquor-sellers.

These, existing in the kingdom as secret thieves of the king, constantly afflict the virtuous subjects through their improper occupations. This gambling was seen in a former age to cause great enmity.
Therefore, a wise man should not indulge in gambling, even for the sake of amusement. Whatever man should practice it, whether secretly or openly,
there shall be a choice of punishment for him according to the king's will.

But a person of Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra birth who is unable to pay a fine shall discharge the debt through labor; a Brāhmaṇa, however, shall pay it back gradually, little by little. [This applies to] women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, and the sick.
The king shall inflict punishment with whips, split bamboo, ropes, and the like. But those officials appointed to judicial matters who,
being inflamed by the heat of wealth, ruin the cases of litigants, the king shall strip them of their property.
He shall put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the constituent elements of the state,
those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, and likewise those who serve his enemies. Furthermore, whatever has been adjudicated or formally decreed, wherever it may have occurred—

One should know that which has been done according to dharma as final; one must not reverse it. Whatever matter the ministers or the judge might decide incorrectly, the king himself shall settle that case and fine them one thousand [paṇas].
The slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed— these men,
as well as the one who associates with them, are to be known individually as perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin).
Furthermore, for these four who do not perform expiation, [the following applies].
One should prescribe lawful punishment involving both corporal and monetary fines.

For violating the teacher’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be branded; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag; for theft, the mark of a dog’s foot; and for killing a Brahmin, the figure of a headless man. [In the case of a thief, the mark of a dog’s foot should be branded.]
Indeed, they shall not eat together, nor sacrifice together, nor study together, nor intermarry;
excluded from all religious duties, they shall wander the earth in misery. Furthermore, these men, having been branded with the mark, must be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives.

They shall be devoid of compassion and exempt from paying homage; such is the instruction of Manu. However, members of all castes who perform penance as prescribed shall not have their foreheads branded by the king, but they should be made to pay the highest fine.
In the case of offenses committed by a Brāhmaṇa, the middle amercement shall be imposed;
or he may be banished from the kingdom along with his property and his belongings.
But others who have committed these sins unintentionally—
They deserve the forfeiture of all their property, but if [the offense was] intentional, banishment.
A righteous king must not take the wealth of those guilty of the most heinous crimes;
for by taking it out of greed, he becomes tainted with that same guilt.

Having cast that punishment into the waters, he should offer it to Varuṇa; or he should bestow it upon a Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and good conduct. For Varuṇa is the lord of punishment, since he is the wielder of the rod for kings.
The Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world.
Where the king avoids the acquisition of wealth from evildoers,
there men are born in due time with long lives.
The crops of the people grow according to how they were sown;
children do not die prematurely, nor does anything deformed come into being.
However, [the king] should punish one born of a low caste who, out of desire, harasses Brāhmaṇas.

The king shall slay [the offender] with various means of execution that cause terror. The demerit seen for a king in executing one who should not be executed is equal to the merit gained from releasing one who deserves to be executed; indeed, merit accrues to him when he administers justice.

This detailed exposition has been set forth for the determination of legal disputes between two contending parties across the eighteen titles of law. Thus, a lord of the earth, performing his duties in accordance with dharma correctly, [attains success].
He should seek to acquire territories not yet obtained and protect those already acquired. Having properly settled his territory and constructed fortifications according to the scriptures,
he should constantly exert the greatest effort in the removal of thorns.
By protecting those of noble conduct and by clearing away thorns,
kings who are devoted to the protection of their subjects go to heaven.
But that king who collects taxes while failing to punish thieves—
His kingdom becomes agitated and he falls away from heaven.
But for him whose kingdom is free from fear, relying upon the strength of his arm,
that kingdom increases constantly like a tree being watered.

The king, whose eyes are his spies, should know that there are two kinds of thieves who steal the property of others: those who are open and those who are secret. Among them, the open deceivers subsist on various kinds of merchandise.
But those who are secret deceivers—such as thieves, forest-dwellers, and the like;

bribe-takers, those who use fraudulent means, cheats, and gamblers; and those who live by giving auspicious advice, as well as fortune-tellers and those who practice divination through the eyes—are all considered such.
High officials who act improperly, physicians,
those skilled in the practice of crafts, and clever courtesans—
one should recognize these and others like them as open thorns of society.
And others who move in secret, being ignoble men wearing the marks of the noble—
having identified them through well-conducted secret agents who perform those same tasks,
and through spies stationed in various disguises, he should eliminate them and bring them under control.

Having fully ascertained their faults in relation to their respective actions according to the truth, the king should impose punishment appropriately, based on the gravity of the offense. For indeed, without punishment, it is not possible to restrain the wicked.
For thieves of evil intent who move secretly upon the earth, the following are suitable places:
assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, brothels, taverns, food-sellers' shops,
crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and spectacles.
Dilapidated gardens, forests, the workshops of artisans,
empty houses, woods, and groves—
such places as these the king should protect with both stationary and mobile military outposts.
For the purpose of suppressing thieves, he should also cause secret agents to roam about,
accompanied by their assistants who are capable of discerning various types of activities;
through these clever former thieves, he should discover and utterly destroy them.
By means of instructions regarding food and drink, by the sight of Brāhmaṇas, and by instructions regarding acts of heroism,
they should bring about a meeting with those who do not approach there and those who have been sent as spies from the root source.

The king shall forcibly slay them, along with their friends, kinsmen, and relatives. A righteous king shall not execute a thief unless he is caught with the stolen goods; however, if caught with the goods and the implements [of theft], he should execute him without hesitation.
Moreover, those in the villages who provide food to thieves, as well as those who give them shelter for their goods— all of them he shall have executed. Likewise,
those appointed to protect the realms and the neighboring chieftains who have been exhorted [to do so].

In times of attack, he should swiftly punish those who remain neutral, just as one would punish thieves. Furthermore, even that man who lives by righteousness, if he has fallen away from the covenant of dharma,
he should burn him with punishment, for he has strayed from his own duty.
In the event of a village raid, the destruction of irrigation works, or the sighting of robbery on the road,
those who do not run to assist to the best of their ability shall be banished along with their belongings.
Likewise, those who steal from the king’s treasury and those who persist in acts of hostility toward him shall be dealt with similarly.
And he shall cause those who instigate enemies to be executed by various forms of punishment. As for those thieves who commit burglary at night by breaking through a wall,
the king, having cut off their hands, shall impale them on a sharp stake.
In the first instance of seizing a knot [of stolen goods], one should have the fingers of the knitter severed;
in the second, both hands and feet; in the third, he deserves the death penalty.
Likewise for those who provide fire, food, weapons, or shelter [to thieves].
The sovereign should punish the embezzler of state funds like a thief;
he should put to death one who destroys a water-tank, or else restore it by means of simple execution.
Alternatively, if he should repair it himself, he must be made to pay the highest fine.

One should indeed put to death, without hesitation, those who break into granaries, armories, or temples, as well as those who steal elephants, horses, or chariots. Furthermore, one who diverts the water from a pre-existing tank...

Or he who should break a watercourse shall be made to pay the first amercement. But he who should discharge impurity onto the royal highway when not in a state of distress shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas and must immediately clear away that impurity.

But one who has fallen into calamity, or an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child, deserve only a reprimand; and that [debt] must be cleared—this is the settled rule. For all physicians who practice falsely, there shall be a fine.
In the case of non-human [images], the first [amercement applies]; but in the case of human [images], the middle [amercement applies].
One who breaks a bridge, a flagstaff, a sacrificial post, or an image shall repair all of that and pay five hundred [paṇas].

For the spoiling of unblemished goods, as well as for breaking them, and for the false boring of gems, the punishment is the first amercement. Furthermore, he who treats equal things as unequal, or values them incorrectly according to their price, [is liable to this same penalty].
A man shall incur the first or indeed the middle fine.
And the king should establish all prisons along the royal highway,
where the suffering and deformed doers of evil may be seen.
One should immediately banish the breaker of a wall, the filler of moats, and the destroyer of gates.
In all cases of malevolent magic (abhicāra), a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed.
One who employs root-magic (*mūlakarman*) against those who have not offended, one who performs various types of sorcery (*kṛtyā*),
a seller of non-seed as seed, one who sells superior seed, and likewise one who destroys boundaries— these shall suffer the punishment of mutilation or death.
But the king shall cause a goldsmith, who is the most wicked of all thorns and who acts unjustly,
to be cut into pieces with razors.
For the theft of agricultural implements, weapons, and medicine, [the same punishment applies].
Having considered the time and the matter at hand, the king shall determine the punishment.
The sovereign, the minister, the capital city, the realm, the treasury, the army, and likewise the ally—
these are the seven constituent elements, and the kingdom is said to consist of these seven limbs.
Among these seven constituent elements of the kingdom, one should know that, in their respective order,
each preceding one is more serious than the next as a great calamity.
For this seven-limbed kingdom is supported like a triple-staff.

Due to the mutual superiority of their respective qualities, no one among them excels all others. However, for various specific tasks, this or that particular limb is distinguished; whatever task is accomplished by which [limb], that is said to be the most excellent for that purpose.
Through spies, through the application of energy, and by the actual performance of his duties,
the lord of the earth should constantly ascertain both his own strength and the strength of his enemy,
as well as all forms of oppression and likewise all vices.
Therefore, having reflected upon the relative weight and lightness of the task, one should undertake the work.
One should indeed begin actions again and again, even when exhausted;
for prosperity attends the man who undertakes his duties.

The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages are all the modes of conduct of the king; for the king is said to be the age itself. When he is asleep, it is the Kali age; when he is awake, it is the Dvāpara age.

When intent upon his duties, he is the Tretā age; when moving about freely, he is the Kṛta age. A king should practice the conduct of splendor belonging to Indra, Arka, Vāyu, Yama, Varuṇa, Candra, Agni, and Pṛthivī.

Just as Indra pours down rain during the four months of the rainy season, so should the king, observing the vow of Indra, shower his own kingdom with the fulfillment of desires. Just as the sun draws up water with its rays during the eight months [of summer], [so should he draw taxes from his people].
In that same manner, he should always take tribute from the kingdom, for that is indeed the solar vow (*arkavrata*).
Just as the wind moves about after entering all living beings, so too should he penetrate [the realm] by means of spies; for this is the "wind-vow" (*mārutavratam*).
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when their time has come, so must subjects be restrained by the king; for that is the vow of Yama.
Just as one is seen bound by Varuṇa with his nooses, [so should the king restrain the wicked].
In this manner he should suppress the wicked; for this is the vow of Varuṇa. Just as men rejoice upon seeing the full moon, so do his subjects rejoice in that king who observes the Cāndravrata.

One who is endowed with majesty, radiant, and always intent upon evil deeds, and who is a destroyer of wicked vassals— that is remembered as the vow pertaining to Agni. Just as the earth supports all beings equally, so should he support all subjects.
Likewise, he who supports all beings fulfills the duty of a king.
Employing these and other means, always unwearied,
the king should suppress thieves both within his own realm and in that of others.
Even when fallen into the greatest distress, one should not provoke Brāhmaṇas;
for they, when enraged, could instantly destroy him along with his army and his vehicles.
By them was fire made all-consuming and the great ocean made undrinkable.
The moon, though waxed full, wanes; who would not perish by provoking them?
Those world-protectors, when incensed, could create other worlds.
They could turn gods into non-gods; who, while harming them, could prosper?
"Those upon whom the worlds and the gods always depend,
for whom the Veda itself is wealth— who, desiring to live, would harm them? Whether ignorant or learned, a Brāhmaṇa is a great deity."
Just as fire, whether consecrated or unconsecrated, is a great deity,
so too the radiant purifier (pāvaka) is not defiled even when present in cremation grounds; rather,
when oblations are offered to it in sacrifices, it increases all the more.
Thus, even if they engage in all kinds of undesirable actions,
Brahmins are in every way worthy of honor, for they are the supreme deity.
This applies to the Kṣatriya who has become excessively overbearing toward Brahmins in every respect.
The Brāhmaṇa alone should be the restrainer, for the Kṣatriya has his origin in the Brāhmaṇa. Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone;
the all-pervading energy of these subsides within their own sources.
The Kṣatriya power does not prosper without the Brāhmaṇical power; the Brāhmaṇical power does not flourish without the Kṣatriya power.
But when the Brāhmaṇical and Kṣatriya powers are joined together, they flourish both in this world and in the next.
Having bestowed wealth arising from all fines upon the Brāhmaṇas...

Having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should seek his end in battle. Acting thus and always intent upon the duties of a king, the monarch should employ all his servants in what is beneficial for the world.
This entire eternal rule of action for the king has been declared. One should know this same rule of action for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra in due order.
But the Vaiśya, having performed the purificatory rites and taken a wife, [should apply himself to his duties].
He should be constantly devoted to his livelihood and to the protection of cattle;
for Prajāpati, having created the cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya, and he entrusted all other subjects to the Brāhmaṇa and the King.
A Vaiśya should not entertain the desire, "I will not tend cattle";
and when a Vaiśya is willing [to do so], they must by no means be tended by anyone else.
[This applies also to] gems, pearls, corals, metals, and woven textiles.
He should know the relative value and strength of fragrances and flavors; he should understand the methods of sowing seeds, as well as the defects and virtues of the soil;
and he should fully comprehend the application of measures and the application of weights.
He should know the value and worthlessness of goods, the merits and defects of regions,
the profit and loss on merchandise, and the breeding of livestock;
he should also know the wages of servants and the various languages of men.
He should exert the greatest effort in the proper storage of goods, their acquisition through trade,
and the lawful increase of wealth;
and he should diligently provide food for all living beings.
For a Śūdra, the highest duty leading to supreme bliss is indeed the service of Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, householders, and illustrious (Manu 9.334).
Being pure, intent on excellent service, gentle in speech, and free from pride (Manu 9.335), he...
One who constantly relies upon a Brāhmaṇa or others attains a superior birth. This auspicious rule for the duties of the social classes in times of no distress has been declared;
now learn their respective duties in times of distress as well.
The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study [the Veda]; however,
it is a settled rule that among them, only the Brāhmaṇa may expound it, and not the other two.
The Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all [the social orders] according to the rule;
he should declare them to the others, and he himself should likewise abide by them.
This is because of his preeminence, the excellence of his origin, and his observance of restrictive rules.
And because of the distinction of their sacraments, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the castes.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya are the three twice-born castes;
the fourth is the once-born Śūdra, but there is no fifth.
Among all the castes, those sons born in the direct order (ānulomya) from wives of equal caste who have not lost their virginity are to be known as belonging to the same caste as their fathers.
Sons begotten by twice-born men on women of the next lower caste— *Manu 10.5a–6a*— [are to be treated as follows].
They say that those born of women of equal caste are indeed censured due to the defects of their mothers.
This is the eternal rule for those born of women in the next lower caste;
one should know this to be the righteous rule for those born of women two or three castes below.

From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of a Vaiśya is born one named Ambaṣṭha; from the daughter of a Śūdra is born a Niṣāda, who is called a Pāraśava. From a Kṣatriya and the daughter of a Śūdra is born one whose conduct and pastimes are cruel.

A creature with the form of a Kṣatriya or a Śūdra is born as one named Ugra. These six are declared to be base-born (apasada): three from a Brāhmaṇa in the [other] three castes, two from a King (Kṣatriya) in the two castes, and one from a Vaiśya in the single remaining caste.

From a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa maiden is born by birth the Sūta; from a Vaiśya father, the Māgadha and the Vaideha are the sons of the wives of the King (Kṣatriya) and the Brāhmaṇa respectively. From a Śūdra father are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla, the lowest of men.
From a Vaiśya, a Rājanya, and a Brāhmaṇa woman, children of mixed castes (varṇasaṃkara) are born.
Just as the Ambaṣṭha and the Ugra are recorded as being born from a one-step interval in the natural order (ānulomya),
so too are the Kṣattṛ and the Vaidehaka born from a one-step interval in the inverse order (prātilomya).

The sons of twice-born men who are born of women of the next lower caste, as described in order, are designated by the name "Anantara" (next-in-order) on account of the inferiority of their mothers. From a Brāhmaṇa, upon a woman of the Ugra caste, a son named Āvṛta is born.
An Ābhīra is born from an Ambaṣṭha woman, and a Dhigvaṇa from an Āyogavī woman.
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
are the three base-born (apasada) sons produced in the reverse order from a Śūdra.

From a Vaiśya, the Māgadha and the Vaideha are born; from a Kṣatriya, however, the Sūta alone is born. These three are born in the reverse order [of castes] and are likewise outcastes (apasada). Born of a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother, one becomes a Pukkasa by birth.
But one born from a Śūdra by a Niṣāda woman is known as a Kukkuṭaka;
likewise, one born from a Kṣattṛ by an Ugrā woman is called a Śvapāka;
and one produced by a Vaidehaka on an Ambaṣṭhā woman is termed a Veṇa.

Those whom the twice-born beget upon wives of their own caste, yet who are devoid of sacred observances, one should designate as *vrātyas*, fallen from the *Sāvitrī*. From a *vrātya* Brahmin is born the evil-souled *bhūrjakaṇṭaka*.
The Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha;
the Jhalla, the Malla, and the Licchivi born from a Vrātya Kṣatriya;
as well as the Naṭa, the Karaṇa, the Khasa, and the Draviḍa.
From a Vrātya Vaiśya are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kāruṣa,
the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sātvata.
These arise through the transgression of the castes and the marrying of women who should not be married.
And by the abandonment of their own duties, the intermixture of castes arises.
Those born of mixed origins— whether produced through the inverse or the natural order—
and those who are mutually interconnected, I shall describe them in their entirety.
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
as well as the Māgadha, the Āyogava, and the Kṣattṛ (or Kṣatrajāti),
these six beget offspring similar to themselves when they procreate within their own wombs.
They are born with the caste of their mother, even when procreated in wombs of higher rank. Just as for the three castes, his own self is born from two [of them],
so it is in the case of the outsiders (bāhya) in sequence, according to immediate proximity to their own womb.

And they, moreover, procreate upon the wives of one another many outcaste offspring who are even more defiled than those [already mentioned]. Just as a Śūdra begets an outcaste being upon a Brāhmaṇī woman, so do they produce these contemptible ones.
In this way, an outcaste begets one even more excluded from the fourfold caste system. Engaging in contrary unions, those already excluded beget further excluded offspring;
thus, they produce fifteen distinct, increasingly degraded castes.

From an Ayogava father and a Vaideha mother is born a Sairandhra (or Sairindhra), who knows how to adorn and attend to others, lives by the labor of a slave though not a slave himself, and subsists by the use of snares. From a Vaideha father and a Mādhūka mother is born a Maitreyaka.
He who constantly strikes the bell at the rising of the dawn praises men.
The Niṣāda begets a Mārgava, a Dāsa who lives by working with boats,
whom those dwelling in Āryāvarta call a Kaivarta (fisherman).
Upon women who wear the clothes of the deceased, who eat the food of those who are censured, and who are ignoble— namely, upon Āyogava women—
these three base-born castes are separately produced:
the Kārāvara is born from a Niṣāda and becomes a leather-worker.

From a Vaidehika are born the Andhra and the Meda, who have their dwellings outside the village. From a Caṇḍāla is born the Pāṇḍusopāka, who deals in bamboo; and from a Niṣāda on a Vaidehī woman is born the Āhiṇḍika.

But from a Caṇḍāla on a Pukkasa woman is born a sinful Sopāka, who subsists by the occupation of root-digging and is always despised by virtuous men. From a Niṣāda woman, however, a Caṇḍāla begets a son known as an Antyāvasāyin.
She gives birth to one who frequents cremation grounds, despised even by those outside the caste system.
These castes born from the mixture of classes have been shown according to their fathers and mothers;
whether they are concealed or manifest, they are to be known by their own actions.
The six sons born of women of their own caste or of those immediately following in rank possess the duties of the twice-born;
however, all those born of degradation (apadhvaṃsaja) are recorded as having the same duties as Śūdras.
Yet, through the power of austerity and the seed, they attain higher status in each successive age.
In this world, among human beings, there is both advancement and decline from birth. However,
through the gradual omission of sacred rites and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins, these Kṣatriya lineages have in the world fallen to the state of Śūdras.
The Pauṇḍrakas, the Coḍas and Draviḍas, the Kāmbojas, the Yavanas, the Śakas; the Pāradas, the Pahlavas,
the Cīnas, the Kirātas, the Daradas, and the Khaśas—
those castes in this world which are born from the mouth, the arms, the thighs, and the feet [of the Creator], are outside [the pale of the four varṇas].

Whether they speak the language of the Mlecchas or that of the Āryas, all such people are recorded as Dasyus. Those who are known as the outcasts (apasadāḥ) of the twice-born, and those born of degraded unions (apadhvaṃsajāḥ),
should subsist by means of those despised occupations belonging specifically to the twice-born.
For Sūtas, the management of horses and charioteering; for Ambaṣṭhas, the practice of medicine;
for Vaidehakas, service to women; for Māgadhas, the trade of commerce;
for Niṣādas, the catching of fish; and for Āyogavas, the craft of the carpenter.
The killing of wild animals is the duty of the Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus.

But the killing of creatures living in holes and their confinement is the duty of the Kṣattṛs, Ugras, and Pukkasas. The work of leather-processing belongs to the Dhigvaṇas, and the playing of drums to the Veṇas.
These [outcastes], being recognized, shall dwell at sacred trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in groves,
subsisting by their own prescribed occupations.
As for the Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas, however, their dwelling shall be outside the village.
They must be made outcastes (apapātra); their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys.
Their clothing shall be the garments of the dead, and they shall eat from broken vessels.
Their ornament shall be iron, and they must wander perpetually as mendicants.
A man practicing dharma should not seek association with them; their mutual dealings and marriages shall be among equals. Their food, dependent on others, should be given to them in separate vessels.
They shall not wander about at night in villages or cities;
by day they may go about for the sake of their business, marked with royal edicts.
And it is the established rule that they shall carry out a corpse that has no kinsman.
They shall constantly execute those deserving of death by the king’s command, in accordance with the scriptures;
they shall take the clothes, beds, and ornaments of those condemned to death. A man of unknown origin, excluded from the social classes and born of a defiled womb—
One should discern a non-Aryan who possesses the appearance of an Aryan by his own actions:
lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty, and a disposition toward the neglect of duties—
these characteristics reveal in this world a man born of a defiled womb.
He inherits the character of his father, or that of his mother, or even both;
for one of base birth cannot, under any circumstances, suppress his own nature.
Even for one born into a preeminent family, if there is a confusion of birth (yonisaṃkara), [he does not escape his true nature].
A man indeed adopts that character, whether to a small or a great extent.
But that kingdom where these corrupters of the social orders are born through intermixture will very quickly perish along with its inhabitants.

Sacrificing one’s body without regard for self-interest for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or a cow, and providing protection for women and children— these are the causes of perfection for those of the outer castes. Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses;

Manu has thus declared this summary of the law for the four castes. (10.63c) If one born of a Śūdra woman from a Brāhmaṇa father procreates with a man of a superior caste, he attains the status of that superior caste up to the seventh generation. (10.64)
A Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise attains the status of a Śūdra.

One should know that it is exactly the same for those born from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya father. Furthermore, one born from a Brāhmaṇa by chance upon a non-Aryan woman [attains the status of his mother].
If it should be asked where superiority lies even in the case of a son born to a Brāhmaṇī woman from a non-Aryan father—[if such a doubt should arise for anyone]—the certainty is this:
one born to a non-Aryan woman from an Aryan father may become an Aryan by his qualities;
but one born to an Aryan woman from a non-Aryan father is a non-Aryan.
The law is settled that both of these are ineligible for the sacraments:

the former because of the defectiveness of his birth, and the latter because he was born in the inverse order (pratiloma). Just as a good seed sown in a good field yields an excellent harvest, so it is with one born from a worthy father and mother.

Likewise, one born of an Ārya father from an Ārya mother deserves every sacramental rite. Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; yet others praise both the seed and the field, and in this matter, the settled rule is as follows: *Manu 10.69c–70b:* *Likewise, one born of an Ārya father from an Ārya mother deserves every sacramental rite.* *Some wise men praise the seed, others the field;* *while others praise both the seed and the field; in this matter, however, the settled rule is as follows:* *Manu 10.70c:* *In this matter, however, the settled rule is as follows:* (Note: The provided text fragment for verse 70c is incomplete, but the standard version of the verse concludes with the following: *The seed sown in a good field produces an abundant harvest; the seed sown in a bad field perishes along with the field itself.* *Manu 10.71:* *For indeed, seeds sown in a good field ripen in due season; but seeds sown in a bad field never reach fruition.* *Manu 10.72:* *Beans and rice, sugarcanes, sesamum, and all other cultivated plants—these, when grown in a good field, yield an abundance of fruit.* *Manu 10.73:* *But when the same seeds are sown in a bad field, they do not produce their proper fruit; rather, they perish together with the field.* *Manu 10.74:* *Therefore, the seed is considered superior, for it is the seed that transforms the field; the field is merely the receptacle for the seed’s growth.* *Manu 10.75:* *One should never sow one's own seed in the field of another; he who does so, being a thief of the field, will surely suffer the loss of his offspring.* *Manu 10.76:* *If seed is sown by one man in a field belonging to another, the produce belongs to the owner of the field; there is no fruit for the owner of the seed.* *Manu 10.77:* *In this world, the owner of the seed receives the offspring if the field-owner is unmarked; but if the seed was sown by one who is himself marked, the offspring belongs to the owner of the field.* *Manu 10.78:* *This law applies to those born of women of the same caste; but for those born of women of different castes, the status is determined by the seed alone.* *Manu 10.79:* *The son of a Śūdra woman, begotten by a Brāhmaṇa, is called a Parāśava; he is excluded from the Sāvitrī and is known as a Dāsa by birth.* *Manu 10.80:* *A Kṣatriya begets on a Śūdra woman a son called a Karaṇa, who is fit for service and skilled in mechanical arts.* *Manu 10.81:* *From a Vaiśya man and a Śūdra woman is born a son called a Vratya, who lives by the profession of a carpenter and is outside the pale of the three higher castes.* *Manu 10.82:* *These six sons, born of women of the next lower caste, are known as Anulomas, because they follow the order of the castes in ascending sequence.* *Manu 10.83:* *Now, those born in the inverse order of castes, produced by men of a higher caste from women of a lower caste, are called Pratilomas and are held to be impure.* *Manu 10.84:* *From a Śūdra is born a Pāraśava by a Brāhmaṇa woman, an Āyogava by a Kṣatriya woman, and a Dhigvaṇa by a Vaiśya woman.* *Manu 10.85:* *From a Vaiśya are born a Māgadha by a Kṣatriya woman and a Vaidehaka by a Brāhmaṇa woman; and from a Kṣatriya is born a Sūta by a Brāhmaṇa woman.* *Manu 10.86:* *These three, the Pāraśava, the Āyogava, and the Dhigvaṇa, are born of women two degrees lower, and are therefore called Vṛṣalas.* *Manu 10.87:* *The Vaidehaka, the Sūta, and the Māgadha—these three are born in the inverse order, and they are likewise excluded from the Sāvitrī.* *Manu 10.88:* *From a Śūdra is born a Cāṇḍāla by a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Veṇa by a Kṣatriya woman, and a Sairandhra by a Vaiśya woman.* *Manu 10.89:* *From a Vaiśya is born a Kṣattṛ by a Kṣatriya woman, and a Rathakāra by a Brāhmaṇa woman; these two are also born in the inverse order and are excluded from the Sāvitrī.* *Manu 10.90:* *The sons of these Pratilomas beget similar offspring upon women of their own kind or upon women of the same caste as their mothers.* *Manu 10.91:* *But when they approach women of a higher caste, they produce outcasts (vṛṣalātiga); they are more degraded than their fathers and lower than their mothers.* *Manu 10.92:* *As one who sows good seeds in a saline or barren soil reaps no harvest, so too the birth of a son from a woman of a different caste yields no fruit.* *Manu 10.93:* *When a low-caste man begets many sons upon women of successively higher castes, the very first-born among them is the most wretched.* *Manu 10.94:* *But when a high-caste man begets only one son upon a woman of a lower caste, that son is equal to the eldest son of a wife of the same caste, provided he possesses the qualities of an elder.* *Manu 10.95:* *Among these various classes of sons, some are declared to be savarna (of the same caste as the father), some are declared to be anuloma (in the natural order), and others are declared to be pratiloma (in the inverse order).* *Manu 10.96:* *The son of a Brāhmaṇa by a wife of the Kṣatriya caste is a Savarṇaka;
