the son of a Kṣatriya by a Brāhmaṇa wife is called a Māgadha; and the son of a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya wife is called an Āyogava.* *Manu 10.98:* *The son of a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Cāṇḍāla, the lowest of men; the son of a Vaiśya by a Śūdra woman is a Vaidehaka; and the son of a Kṣatriya by a Śūdra woman is a Kṣattṛ.* *Manu 10.99:* *These six sons, born of women in the inverse order of castes, are known as Pratilomas; they are excluded from the Sāvitrī and are called Vṛṣalas.* *Manu 10.100:* *The son of a Kṣatriya by a Sūta woman is an Āhiṇḍika; the son of a Vaiśya by a Māgadha woman is a Śvapāka; and the son of a Śūdra by a Vaidehaka woman is a Sairandhra.* *Manu 10.101:* *The son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣattṛ woman is a Pukkasa; the
Seed sown in a non-field perishes in the very middle;
likewise, a field without seed becomes merely a barren plot of ground.
Since, by the power of the seed, even those born as animals have become seers (*ṛṣi*).
Since they are honored and praised, therefore the seed is held in high esteem. (The seed is distinguished.
Having deliberated upon the non-Aryan who performs Aryan deeds and the Aryan who performs non-Aryan deeds, the Creator declared: "They are neither equal nor unequal."
Brāhmaṇas who abide in the source of the Veda and remain steadfast in their own duty should properly subsist by the six occupations in their due order:
teaching, studying, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, [giving, and receiving gifts].
Giving gifts and receiving them are the six duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
Of these six duties, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from pure persons.
Three duties cease with respect to a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts. Likewise, these same duties would cease with respect to a Vaiśya; such is the settled rule.

For Manu, the Lord of Creatures, did not prescribe those duties for them. Bearing weapons and missiles is the duty of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are the duties of the Vaiśya;
but their religious duties are giving, study, and sacrifice.
The study of the Vedas is the preeminent duty among one's own duties for a Brāhmaṇa, protection for a Kṣatriya,
and the occupation of trade and agriculture for a Vaiśya.
But if a Brāhmaṇa is unable to subsist by his own aforementioned occupation, [he may take to the next best].

He may live by the dharma of a Kṣatriya, for that is the next best alternative for him. But if he should find it impossible to subsist by either of these two ways, he may live the livelihood of a Vaiśya, resorting to agriculture and cattle-rearing.

But even if a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should live by the occupation of a Vaiśya, he should carefully avoid agriculture, which involves much violence and depends upon others. People consider agriculture to be a good thing, yet that occupation is censured by the virtuous.

A wooden plough with an iron tip destroys the earth as well as those who dwell upon it. However, for one who, due to a lack of livelihood, abandons his skill in dharma, the following may be sold to increase wealth: merchandise from which the set-aside portions have been removed.
One should avoid all liquids, cooked food along with sesame seeds,
stones, salt, domestic animals, and human beings; likewise,
all dyed woven cloth, as well as fabrics made of hemp, flax, and wool.
Even if they should be unstained, [he must avoid] fruits, roots, and likewise medicinal herbs;
water, weapons, poison, meat, soma, and all fragrant substances;
milk, honey, curd, clarified butter, oil, liquor, molasses, and *kuśa* grass.
All wild animals, fanged beasts, and birds;
liquor, indigo, lac, and likewise all one-hoofed animals;
and having produced [these goods] at will through cultivation, the farmer himself may sell them.
A Śūdra may sell sesame seeds that have not been kept for long, provided it is for the sake of dharma.
But if he does anything other than eating, anointing himself, or giving them away with sesame seeds,
he becomes a worm and sinks into the excrement of dogs along with his ancestors.

A Brāhmaṇa falls immediately from his caste by selling meat, lac, or salt; he becomes a Śūdra within three days by selling milk. But by intentionally selling other commodities here, he likewise falls.
A Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights.
(Manu 10.93c) Flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for flavors.
Cooked food may be exchanged for cooked food, sesame seeds for grain, and likewise sesame seeds for sesame seeds. (Manu 10.94)

A Kṣatriya who has fallen into distress may live by all these means; however, he must never at any time covet a higher mode of livelihood. He who, out of greed, being of lower birth, lives by the occupations of those superior to him—

The king, having deprived him of his wealth, should banish him immediately. (Manu 10.96c) One's own duty, even if deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed; for by living according to the duty of another, one falls from one's caste at once. (Manu 10.97)

A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may also live by the occupation of a Śūdra. One who does not perform forbidden acts should cease [from such] as soon as he is capable. However, a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born [may do so].
When a man faces the loss of his sons and wife, he may live by the work of artisans. Those activities practiced by which the twice-born are served,
as well as various crafts, are the works of artisans.
A Brāhmaṇa who remains established on his own path, yet finds himself distressed by a lack of livelihood while unable to follow the occupation of a Vaiśya,
should practice this rule:
a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into such straits may accept gifts from anyone.

That a purifier should become defiled—this is not logically tenable according to the Dharma. No fault accrues to Brahmins from teaching, from officiating at sacrifices, or from accepting gifts, even if they are censurable; for they are like fire and water.
One who, having fallen into a situation where life is at stake, eats food from any source whatsoever,
is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud.
Ajīgarta, driven by hunger, approached to kill his own son.

And Vāmadeva, though he was an expert in discerning between dharma and adharma, was not tainted by sin when, being distressed, he desired to eat his own flesh as a remedy for hunger in order to preserve his life. (Manu 10.105c–106)
The great ascetic Bharadvāja, afflicted by hunger along with his sons in a lonely forest,
accepted many cows from the carpenter Vṛdhu.
And Viśvāmitra, tormented by hunger, approached to eat the haunch of a dog.
Having accepted [wealth] from the hand of a Caṇḍāla, even one who is discerning of dharma and adharma—
whether through receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, or likewise through teaching—
such acceptance is inferior and is censured for a Brahmin after death.
Sacrificing for others and teaching are always performed by those whose souls are purified;

however, the acceptance of gifts may be done even from a Śūdra or one of the lowest birth. The sin committed through sacrificing for others and teaching is removed by silent recitations (japa) and burnt offerings (homa).
But for the sake of avoiding the necessity of accepting gifts, through renunciation and austerity alone,
a Brahmin who cannot subsist should gather grain by gleaning or picking from here and there;
for gleaning is better than accepting gifts, and even picking is praised more highly than that.

When Snātaka Brahmins are perishing, desiring base metals, or seeking wealth, they may petition the lord of the earth; however, if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned. Furthermore, from a field that has been cultivated, one may take unprepared grain, as well as cattle, goats, and sheep.
Gold, grain, and food—each preceding one is blameless [as security].
There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, performance of work, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous.
Learning, craftsmanship, wages, service, cattle-rearing,
trade, agriculture, contentment, begging, and usury— these are the ten means of livelihood.
A Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya should never engage in lending at interest.

But indeed, for the sake of dharma, one may at will give even a small amount to a more sinful person. Even when taking a fourth part as his share in times of distress, a Kṣatriya who protects his subjects to the best of his ability is released from sin.
Victory is his own duty; he must not turn his back in battle. Having protected the Vaiśyas with his weapons, he may collect the lawful tribute from them.
The tax on grain from the Vaiśyas shall be one-eighth; the minimum [tax] on gold is twenty kārṣāpaṇas.
Śūdras, as well as artisans and craftsmen, are those who subsist by manual labor.
If a Śūdra, seeking a livelihood, should wish to serve the Kṣatriya class, he may do so;
or, having served a wealthy Vaiśya, a Śūdra may seek to maintain himself.

He should propitiate Brahmins for the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both [heaven and worldly prosperity]; for one who has acquired the title of "Brahmin," that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of his purpose. Service to Brahmins alone is proclaimed as the most distinguished duty of a Śūdra.
Whatever else he performs apart from this, that becomes fruitless for him.
Their means of subsistence should be provided by him from his own family according to what is appropriate,
having regard to [his] wealth, their skill, and the number of dependents they maintain.
Leftover food should be given [to a Śūdra], as well as worn-out garments,
the shriveled husks of grains, and old household utensils.
There is no sin whatsoever in a Śūdra, nor does he deserve any sacramental rite (saṃskāra).
He has no authority regarding dharma, nor is he prohibited from dharma.
However, those who seek dharma, who know dharma, and who follow the conduct of the virtuous—
provided they avoid the Vedic mantras— they do not incur sin and they even attain praise.
For to the extent that one who is free from malice abides in virtuous conduct,
to that same extent he, being blameless, attains both this world and the next. Even by a Śūdra who is attached to worldly life, no accumulation of wealth should be made.
For a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses only the Brāhmaṇas. These duties in times of distress have been proclaimed for the four castes;
by performing them correctly, they attain the highest goal.
This entire rule of dharma for the four castes has been proclaimed;
hereafter, I shall declare the auspicious rules for penance.
One seeking offspring, one about to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions,
one who seeks wealth for the sake of his teacher, for the sake of his father or mother, one in need for the sake of Vedic study,
and one who is ill— these one should know as *snātakas*, Brāhmaṇas who are mendicants for the sake of dharma.
A gift should be given to these [other guests] who are destitute, according to the distinction of their learning.
For food accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to these foremost of the twice-born;
for others, it is said that cooked food should be given outside the sacrificial altar.

The king, however, should bestow all kinds of jewels upon those Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas, as well as sacrificial fees for the sake of the sacrifice, according to their merit. He who, having already taken a wife, obtains another wife by begging, [commits an offense].

The fruit for the giver of the material substance is merely sexual pleasure, whereas for the one who gives the offspring, it is the lineage itself. One should bestow wealth upon Brahmins according to one's ability—
upon those learned in the Vedas and living in seclusion— and thereby enjoys heaven after death.
He who possesses enough food for three years to maintain his dependents,
or even more than that, is worthy to drink the Soma.
Therefore, the twice-born man who drinks the Soma when he possesses less wealth than this [is at fault].
Even one who has previously drunk the Soma juice does not obtain its fruit [if he acts thus].
One who is attached to strangers while giving to his own kin who live in misery—
that is a semblance of dharma, which is like honey at first but bitter in taste.

Whatever funeral rite one performs by causing distress to one's dependents results in unhappiness both for the living and for the deceased. If a sacrifice of a patron should be obstructed by the absence of even a single constituent part, [it must be completed].
Especially when there is a righteous king,

[the king] may take that wealth from the household of a Vaiśya who possesses much cattle but lacks the capacity for sacrifice and does not drink the Soma juice, for the sake of accomplishing his sacrificial rites. (Manu 11.11c–12)
He may take three or two items at will from the house of a Śūdra;
for a Śūdra has no entitlement to participate in sacrifices.
Even one who possesses a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires, or one who possesses a thousand cows but does not perform sacrifices, [is not exempt].
From the households of those two as well, he should take [the grain] without hesitation.
And from a person who is habitually acquisitive and who does not give when asked, he should take it;
thus his fame spreads and his merit increases.
Likewise, having fasted for six meals, one may take food at the seventh meal-time from a person of inferior conduct who follows the "no-provision-for-tomorrow" (aśvastana) rule—
whether from his threshing floor, field, house, or wherever it may be obtained.
But if he asks, that [fact] must be told to him when he inquires.
A Kṣatriya must never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa;
however, he may take the property of a Dasyu or of one who neglects his religious duties, if he cannot otherwise subsist.

He who takes wealth from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous makes himself a boat and enables both to cross over. The wise know that the wealth of those devoted to sacrifice is the property of the gods.
But the wealth of those who do not perform sacrifices is called the property of Asuras.
A righteous lord of the earth should not inflict punishment upon it;
for through the extortion of a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa may perish from hunger.

Having ascertained his dependents and his own family, and having understood their learning and character, the lord of the earth shall provide them with a righteous means of livelihood. Having provided him with a livelihood, he should protect him on all sides.
For the king obtains a sixth part of the merit from that which has been protected.
A Brahmin should never beg wealth for the sake of a sacrifice from a Śūdra;
for by begging, a sacrificer is born as a Caṇḍāla after death.

That Brahmin who, having begged wealth for the purpose of a sacrifice, does not bestow it all, goes to the state of a crow or a crane for a hundred years. He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of Brahmins, [goes to hell].

That evil-minded man lives in the next world on the leavings of vultures. At the end of each year, he should constantly perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice for the sake of expiating those animal and Soma sacrifices that were prescribed but could not be performed.
If a twice-born man performs a duty according to the rule for times of distress when he is not in a state of distress,
it has been determined that he does not obtain its fruit in the hereafter—
so have the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great ṛṣis declared.

In times of distress, those fearing death have established a substitute for the prescribed rule. He who, though capable of following the primary rule, conducts himself according to the secondary rule— no fruit pertaining to the world beyond exists for that person of wicked intellect.
A Brāhmaṇa who knows the Dharma should not report anything to the king regarding those offending men;
he should subdue them by his own power alone.
Between one's own power and the power of the king, one's own power is more effective.
Therefore, a twice-born man should subdue his enemies by his own prowess alone. He should, without hesitation, employ the *Atharva-Aṅgiras* hymns;
for the word is indeed the weapon of a Brahmin, and with that, the twice-born man should slay his enemies.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own adversity by the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra by wealth; but the best of the twice-born by silent recitation and burnt offerings.
A Brāhmaṇa is said to be the ordainer, the ruler, the teacher, and the friend of all.
One should not speak anything unwholesome to him, nor should one utter harsh words. Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning,
nor a fool, nor one who is afflicted, nor likewise one who is unconsecrated, should serve as the *hotṛ* priest for the *agnihotra*.

For these fall into hell, as does he for whom they perform the oblation while sacrificing. Therefore, the *hotṛ* priest should be skilled in the sacrificial rites (*vaitāna*) and one who has mastered the Vedas.
Without having given a horse dedicated to Prajāpati as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), [one falls].
A Brāhmaṇa who possesses the means should not remain without having established the sacred fires (anāhitāgni). Being faithful and having his senses subdued, he should perform other meritorious acts;
however, under no circumstances should he perform sacrifices here with meager sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys the senses, glory, heaven, longevity, fame, progeny, and cattle;
therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice.
A Brāhmaṇa who, out of his own will, neglects the sacred fires becomes an Agnihotrī [who has abandoned the fires].
One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month, for that [act] is equal to the killing of a hero. Those who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice—
they are the officiating priests of Śūdras and are censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
By treading with his foot upon the heads of those who constantly disregard the injunctions and serve the *vṛṣala* (the Śūdra) fire, the giver shall cross over all difficulties.
By failing to perform prescribed duties and by practicing what is censured, [he likewise crosses over].
And a man who is addicted to the objects of the senses becomes liable to penance. Wise men know that penance is prescribed for a sin committed unintentionally;
however, some say it is also required for a sin committed intentionally, based on the evidence of the revealed scripture (*śruti*).

A sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas; but that which is committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of penances. Having become liable to penance—whether by fate or due to past deeds— [one must perform it].
A twice-born man should not associate with the virtuous until his penance has been performed.
Some wicked-souled men undergo a transformation of their physical form due to evil deeds committed in this life, while others do so because of those committed in previous lives.
A thief of gold shall have deformed nails; a drinker of spirituous liquor, black teeth;
a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, consumption; and one who violates the teacher’s bed, a skin disease. A slanderer shall have a foul-smelling nose; a calumniator, a foul-smelling mouth.
A thief of grain suffers from a deficiency of limbs, while a thief of mixed grains suffers from redundancy.
A stealer of food becomes afflicted with chronic disease, and a stealer of speech suffers from dumbness.
A stealer of clothing suffers from leucoderma, and a stealer of horses suffers from lameness.
Thus, by reason of specific actions, they are born despised by the virtuous—
stupid, mute, blind, deaf, and likewise deformed in appearance.
Therefore, for the sake of purification, one must always perform expiation.
For those who have not expiated their sins are born endowed with censurable physical marks.
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s bed,
and associating with such persons— these they call the great sins (mahāpātaka).
Falsehood for the sake of self-exaltation, malicious talebearing directed toward the king,
and persistent deception of one’s teacher— these are equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
Abandoning the Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, and the murder of a friend [are likewise equal].
Eating forbidden food or food that should not be eaten— these six are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as the theft of a man, a horse, or silver, and the theft of land, diamonds, or gems, is recorded in tradition as being equal to the theft of gold.

They consider the emission of semen in women who are one's own uterine sisters, in virgins, or in women of the lowest castes, as well as in the wives of a friend or a son, to be equal to violating the Guru’s bed (gurutaḷpa). Killing a cow, officiating at a sacrifice for those unworthy to sacrifice, adultery, and the selling of oneself— these are [equivalent to the aforementioned sins].

Abandoning one's teacher, mother, father, or son; neglecting one's Vedic study or the sacred fires; being a *parivitti* (one whose younger brother marries before him) when the younger brother remains unmarried; marrying before such a brother (*parivedana*);
giving a daughter in marriage to either of those two; and officiating as a priest for either of them.
Defiling a maiden, usury, the violation of a vow, the sale of a tank, a grove, a wife, or a child;
becoming a *vrātya*, abandoning one’s kin, and teaching for a fee; 11.61–62a.
Receiving instruction from one who is not a teacher, the sale of goods that should not be sold,
authority over all types of labor, and the operation of large-scale mechanical works; the injuring of medicinal plants, living off women, malevolent incantations, and the practice of root-magic.
Felling green trees for the sake of firewood,
undertaking actions solely for one's own benefit, eating forbidden food,
failing to maintain the sacred fires, theft, and the non-payment of debts;
Studying false scriptures, the practice of *kauśīlavya*,
theft of grain, base metals, or cattle, consorting with women who drink liquor,
killing a woman, a *śūdra*, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya, and atheism— these constitute minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that should not be smelled or intoxicants, crookedness,
and sexual intercourse with a male are declared to be acts that cause loss of caste.
Likewise, the killing of a donkey, a horse, a camel, a deer, an elephant, a goat, or a sheep [is such an act].
The killing of a fish, a snake, or a buffalo should be known as an act that causes loss of caste (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*).
Receiving wealth from censurable persons, trade, serving a *śūdra*,
and speaking untruth should be known as acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*).
The killing of worms, insects, and birds; eating food contaminated by liquor;
the theft of fruit, firewood, and flowers; and lack of fortitude—these are defiling acts.
All these sins, as they have been described individually, [are to be expiated].
Learn correctly those various vows by which [the sins] are removed.

(Manu 11.71c) A slayer of a Brāhmaṇa shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, having built a hut, subsisting on alms for the sake of self-purification, and carrying the skull of a corpse as his banner. (Manu 11.72)
Or, by his own will, he may become a target for those who bear weapons, provided they are learned men;
or he may throw himself headlong three times into a blazing fire;
or he may sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava.
Or he may perform the Abhijit or Viśvajit sacrifices, or the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut sacrifice; or,
eating sparingly and with his senses restrained, he may walk a hundred yojanas while reciting one of the Vedas in order to remove the guilt of killing a Brahmin.
He should bestow his entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas;
for wealth sufficient for livelihood, or a house together with its furnishings. Or, subsisting on sacrificial food, he may follow the Sarasvatī river against the current.
Or, with his food restricted, he should recite the *saṃhitā* of the Veda three times.
Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village,
or in a cow-pen, or in a hermitage, or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
For the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow, he should immediately sacrifice his life;
by protecting a cow or a Brāhmaṇa, he is released from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.

Or, if he loses his life for that purpose on behalf of a Brahmin, he is liberated. Thus, one who is firm in his vows, constantly a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), and composed,
casts off the guilt of killing a Brahmin upon the completion of twelve years.
Or, having gratified the gods on earth (the Brahmins) at an assembly of kings, he is released from his own sin after bathing in the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.
The Brāhmaṇa is said to be the root of Dharma; the Kṣatriya is said to be its summit.
Therefore, by confessing their sin in the presence of these [elders], one is purified.
By his very birth as a Brahmin, he is the deity even of the gods;
he is indeed the authority for the world, for the Brahmin alone is the cause in this matter.

Even three who know the Veda should declare the complete expiation for their sin; that shall serve as their purification, for the speech of the learned is indeed purifying. Therefore, having undertaken one of these rules, a Brahmin should remain composed.
By means of self-control, he removes the sin committed by killing a Brāhmaṇa. Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should perform this very same vow;
as also for having killed a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who has performed a sacrifice, or a woman who is the wife of an Ātreya.
Having given false testimony, having obstructed a teacher,
having misappropriated a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend—
this purification has been declared for having unintentionally killed a twice-born man.
No atonement is prescribed for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
Having drunk liquor out of delusion, a twice-born man shall drink liquor that is fire-colored;
when his body has been consumed by it, he is then released from that sin.
Or he may drink cow’s urine the color of fire, or water alone;
or milk, ghee, or even the liquid from cow dung until death.
Or he may eat grain-particles for a year, or oil-cake once at night.
To remove the guilt of drinking *surā*, he shall wear garments of hair, grow matted locks, and carry a flag.
For *surā* is indeed the impurity of foods, and it is called the impurity of sin;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya must not drink *surā*.
Gauḍī, paiṣṭī, and mādhvī are to be known as the three kinds of *surā*.
Just as one is, so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born.
Wine, meat, and spirituous liquor are the food of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas.

Therefore, that [liquor] must not be consumed by a Brāhmaṇa who does not eat the sacrificial oblation (havis) of the gods. Intoxicated, a Brāhmaṇa might fall into impurity, or he might recite the Veda, or he might perform some other improper act, being deluded by intoxication.
He whose Brahman residing in the body is once drenched by liquor—
his status as a Brāhmaṇa departs, and he falls into the state of a Śūdra.
This has been declared as the various expiations for the drinking of liquor.

Henceforth, I shall proclaim the expiation for the theft of gold. A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, should declare his own deed and say: "May your majesty instruct me."
Taking up a club, the king himself shall strike him once;
by execution, the thief is purified, but a Brāhmaṇa is purified only by austerity. One who desires to remove the stain born of stealing gold must perform austerity.
Clad in bark garments, the twice-born man shall perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa in the forest.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he may expiate the sin of approaching the wife of his teacher by means of these following vows.
Having committed the sin of violating the Guru’s bed, he should lie upon a heated iron bed;
or he should embrace a glowing metal image (sūrmi), and by death he is purified.
Or, having himself cut off his own penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms, [he should proceed to the fire].

He should proceed toward the southwestern direction (nairṛtī diś) straight on until he collapses. Carrying a bedpost, clothed in rags, with a beard and matted hair, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind in a solitary forest.
Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) or barley-gruel, in order to remove the sin of violating the Guru’s bed.
By these vows, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) may cast off their impurity.
Those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) shall likewise be purified by these various kinds of vows.
A cow-killer, having committed a minor offense, should drink barley-gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he should dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow.
He should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent salt, at every fourth mealtime;
for two months, with his senses restrained, he should perform his bath with cow urine.
During the day he should follow the cows, and while standing, he should inhale the dust rising from them.
Having served them and paid homage, he should remain in the *vīrāsana* posture at night.
He should stand when they stand, follow them when they walk,
and likewise sit when they sit, remaining self-controlled and free from envy.

One should rescue by all possible means a woman who is afflicted by illness, or accused of a crime, or threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers, or one who has fallen, or is stuck in a mire. Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently, [one should protect her].
One should not seek to protect oneself without first doing what one can to save the cow.
Whether it be in one's own house, in another's house, in a field, or in a threshing floor,
one should not report a cow that is eating, nor a calf that is drinking.

The killer of a cow who follows a cow according to this rule removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months. Having successfully performed the vow, he should give ten cows and one bull as a gift.
If nothing else is available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.

Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) should perform this same vow for the sake of purification, with the exception of the *avakīrṇin* rite; or alternatively, they may perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
But one who has broken his vow of celibacy (avakīrṇin) shall sacrifice to Nirṛti at night on a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey, according to the procedure for a *pākayajña*.
Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules, he should finally offer with the verse beginning "sama."

One should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fires dedicated to Vāta, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Agni. The knowers of Dharma and the exponents of the Veda declare that for a twice-born man observing a vow, the intentional emission of semen constitutes a transgression of his vow.
The fourfold Brahmanic splendor of one who has broken his vow of chastity passes away to the Maruts, Indra, the Guru, and Agni.
When this sin has been incurred, having worn the skin of a donkey...

He should go for alms to seven houses, proclaiming his own deed. Subsisting on the alms obtained from them, eating only once a day, and performing ablutions three times a day, he becomes purified in one year.

Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the *Sāṃtapana* penance; if done unintentionally, one should perform the *Prājāpatya*. For acts that cause mixture of castes or render one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātra*), the purification for one month is the *Aindava* (Cāndrāyaṇa).
For acts that cause defilement, one should subsist on hot barley-gruel for three days.
The killing of a Kṣatriya is recorded as being one-fourth of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa;
for a Vaiśya who is established in his duty, it is one-eighth; but for a Śūdra, it should be known as one-sixteenth.
But having unintentionally killed a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born,
having properly observed his vow, shall give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh;
or, with his hair matted and self-restrained, he may perform for three years the penance prescribed for a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
Living at a great distance from the village, making his dwelling at the foot of a tree,
the best of the twice-born should perform this very same penance for one year after having killed a Vaiśya who was established in righteous conduct,
and he should give one hundred and one cows.
A killer of a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months;
or he may give to a Brāhmaṇa eleven white cows along with one bull.
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, or a frog, [he must perform the same penance].
Having killed a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.
Alternatively, one may drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one yojana on foot, or bathe in a flowing river,
or mutter the hymn addressed to the Waters (the *Āpohiṣṭhīya*).

Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade; having killed a eunuch, a load of straw and one māṣa of lead. Having killed a boar, he should give a jar of ghee; but for a partridge, a droṇa of sesame seeds.
Having killed a two-year-old calf, a curlew, or a three-year-old [calf];
having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, or even a peacock; and having killed a monkey, a hawk, or a vulture—one should offer a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment and five dark-colored bulls; having killed an elephant, a goat, a ram, an ox, or a donkey, one should give a one-year-old calf.
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, however, one should give a milch cow.

Having killed carnivorous animals, a heifer, or a camel, one should give a *kṛṣṇala* of gold. For the sake of purification, one should give separately an old bow, a goat, and a sheep. Having killed women of unstable character belonging to any of the four castes, [one must perform the following].

If a twice-born man is unable to atone for the killing of snakes and other such creatures by means of giving gifts, he shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each individual creature in order to remove the sin. However, for the killing of a thousand vertebrate beings, [he must perform a different penance].
When a cartload of boneless creatures has been killed, one should perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra.
For the killing of creatures possessing bones, however, one should give some small gift to a Brāhmaṇa;
indeed, for the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred *ṛc* verses are to be recited as a penance;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
This applies in all cases to living beings produced from food and those produced from liquids.

For the unintentional cutting of plants that produce fruit or flowers, the purification is the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). For the unintentional cutting of cultivated herbs or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while observing a vow of consuming only milk.

By these vows, the sin arising from violence may indeed be removed—whether committed intentionally or unintentionally; now hear [the rules] regarding the eating of all forbidden food. Having drunk *vāruṇī* out of ignorance, one becomes pure through the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) alone.

If it was done intentionally, the punishment is death; this is the settled rule. Having drunk water that stood in a vessel for *surā* or likewise in a vessel for other intoxicants, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights.
Having touched or given liquor, or having accepted it according to rule,

and having drunk water that is the leavings of a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days. But a Brāhmaṇa who drinks Soma, having smelled the odor of one who drinks liquor, [must perform a penance].
Having restrained his breath three times in water and having consumed clarified butter, he becomes purified.
Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or anything touched by *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once again.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging alms, and the vows—
all these are dispensed with for the twice-born upon the performance of the rite of re-initiation.
However, having eaten the food of those whose food is unfit to be eaten, or the leavings of a woman or a Śūdra, [one must undergo penance].

Having eaten forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights. Having drunk fermented acids or astringent decoctions, even if they are pure, a twice-born man remains impure as long as that [substance] has not passed downward.
Having consumed the urine or excrement of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having eaten dried meats or mushrooms growing from the earth, [he shall likewise do so].
And if one eats meat from a slaughterhouse that was unknown [to be such], he should perform this very same vow.
For eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, and cocks,
as well as humans, crows, and donkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.
If a twice-born man who has not yet returned home from his teacher's house should eat food offered at a monthly Śrāddha,
he shall fast for three days and remain in water for one day. But if a student of sacred knowledge should somehow eat honey or meat, [he must perform the same penance].
Having performed the ordinary *kṛcchra* penance, he should complete the remainder of his vow.
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mouse, a dog, or a mongoose,
or food contaminated by hair or insects, he should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.

One who desires his own purity must not eat food that is unfit to be consumed. However, if it has been eaten unintentionally, it must be expiated by fasting or quickly purified by means of purificatory rites. This is the variously prescribed rule for the penances regarding the eating of forbidden food.
Listen now to the rule for the vows that remove the guilt of theft.
Having intentionally stolen grain, cooked food, or wealth from the house of a member of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the *kṛcchra* penance for one year.
For the theft of human beings, women, fields, or houses,

as well as for the theft of water from wells or tanks, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed as the means of purification. Having committed the theft of articles of small value in another's house, one should perform the penance ordained by others.
Having returned that [stolen object], he should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance for the purification of his own self.
For the theft of edible and consumable foods, as well as vehicles,
beds, and seats, and of flowers, roots, and fruits, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the means of purification.
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, and molasses;
for clothing, skins, and meat—there shall be a fast of three nights.
For jewels, pearls, corals, copper, and silver.
For iron, bronze, and stone, one must subsist on grain-particles for twelve days;
for cotton, silk, wool, animals with cloven hooves,
and single-hoofed animals, as well as for birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must drink only milk for three days.

By these penances, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft; however, he should expiate the sin of approaching those who must not be approached by means of these same vows. Having discharged semen into women of his own [lineage], he shall perform the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed.
[169c] For women who are the wives of a friend or a son, or for girls born of the lowest castes;

[170a] having approached a daughter of one’s paternal aunt, a sister, a daughter of one’s paternal aunt, or even a daughter of one’s mother’s brother, one shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. [Having approached the daughter of a close relative...]

A wise man should not take these three as wives; they are to be avoided because of their kinship, for by marrying them he falls low. [This applies to] non-human females, a woman in her courses, and those who are not born from a womb.
Having discharged semen into water, one should perform the *Sāṃtapana* Kṛcchra penance. Furthermore,
having engaged in sexual intercourse with a male or a female,
a twice-born man should bathe with his clothes on in a cow-cart, in water, or during the daytime.

Having approached a Caṇḍāla woman or a woman of the lowest castes, and having eaten or accepted gifts from them, a Brāhmaṇa falls [from his caste] through ignorance; through knowledge, however, he becomes their equal. A husband should confine a wife who has become corrupted in a single room.

Whatever penance is prescribed for a man who commits adultery with another’s wife, that same penance he shall cause her to perform. But if she should become corrupt again after being enticed by a man of equal status, then the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are declared to be her means of purification.

Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night, he removes that by constantly subsisting on alms and reciting [sacred texts] for three years. This expiation has been declared for all four types of evildoers.
Listen now to these expiations for those who associate with outcasts (patitas):
one becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for a year,
through officiating at his sacrifices, teaching him, or forming a matrimonial alliance with him— but not, however, by sharing a vehicle, a seat, or a meal.

Whatever man enters into association with any one of these outcasts, he must perform that very same penance for the sake of purification from that association. The water libation for the deceased outcast must be performed by his *sapiṇḍas* and kinsmen outside [the village].
On an inauspicious day, in the evening, in the presence of kinsmen, officiating priests, and teachers,
a female slave shall kick over a jar full of water with her foot, as if for a dead person. For one day and night, they shall observe impurity together with their relatives.

They shall cease from conversing with him and from sitting together on the same seat; likewise, the giving of inheritance and even ordinary worldly intercourse must cease. Seniority shall be forfeited, as well as the wealth that is obtained by virtue of being the eldest.

And a younger brother who is superior in merit shall obtain the seniority of that [eldest brother]. When the penance has been performed, they should bathe together with him in a sacred body of water and cast a new jar full of water into it.
Having cast that jar into the water and entered his own home,
he should perform all the rites for his kinsmen as before.
He should follow this very same rule even in the case of women who have become outcasts.

One should provide them with clothing, food, and drink, and they should live near one's house. One should not engage in any business with those who have not been purified from their sin; yet, once they have been purified, one should never despise them.

One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who betray one who has sought refuge, or those who kill women— even if they have been purified according to the law. As for those twice-born men among whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the prescribed rule...

Having made them perform three *kṛcchra* penances according to the rule, he should initiate them again. This same procedure should be prescribed for those twice-born men who, while engaged in improper acts, desire to perform expiation and have been abandoned by the Veda.

If Brāhmaṇas acquire wealth through a censurable occupation, they are purified by relinquishing that wealth, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and austerity. Having concentrated his mind, he should recite the Sāvitrī mantra three thousand times.

Having drunk milk in a cow-pen for one month, one is released from the sin of accepting gifts from the unworthy. When he has returned again from the cow-pen, emaciated by fasting and bowing down, they should ask him: "O gentle one, do you desire equanimity?"

Having spoken the truth before Brahmins, he should scatter fodder for cows; when a ford has been established by the cows, they should perform his funeral rites. Having performed the sacrifice for Vratyas or the funeral rites for others, [he becomes an outcast].

He removes the sin of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and the *ahīna* sacrifice by means of three *kṛcchra* penances. Having abandoned one who has come for refuge or having corrupted the Veda, a twice-born man expiates that sin by subsisting on barley for one year.
One who has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by domestic carnivorous animals,

as well as by humans, horses, camels, or pigs, becomes pure through breath-control (prāṇāyāma). Alternatively, one may subsist on food only at every sixth mealtime for a month, or perform the recitation of the Saṃhitā.
All regular *śrāddha* offerings (*homāḥ*) are always a means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅktyas*).
Having intentionally mounted a camel-carriage or a donkey-carriage,
a Brahmin who has bathed but remains naked becomes pure through the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
If one has discharged bodily waste without water or even while in the water when distressed,
one becomes pure by bathing outside with one's clothes on and touching a cow.
Upon the omission of the obligatory rites prescribed in the Veda, [one must perform penance].

And for the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, the penance is fasting. Having uttered the sound "huṃ" to a Brāhmaṇa, or having addressed one who is superior with the word "thou," he shall bathe and, remaining without food for the remainder of the day, propitiate him by offering salutations.

Even after striking [the teacher] with a blade of grass, or binding him by the neck with a garment, or defeating him in a dispute, one should appease him by prostrating. But for threatening [the teacher], one must fast for a hundred years; and for actually striking him, for a thousand years.
One who intends to kill a Brāhmaṇa falls into hell. As many particles of dust as the blood he sheds collects upon the surface of the earth,
for so many thousands of years shall the perpetrator dwell in hell.
Having merely threatened [to strike] a Brahmin, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance; if one actually strikes him, the *atikṛcchra*.
Having caused blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform both the *kṛcchra* and the *atikṛcchra*.
For the removal of those sins for which no specific expiation has been stated, [one should perform these].
Having considered both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin, one should prescribe the penance.
I shall declare to you those means by which a human being removes his transgressions— means practiced by gods, sages, and ancestors.
For three days he should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, and for three days he should eat food that has not been asked for;
for another three days he should not eat at all—this is the *prājāpatya* penance performed by a twice-born man.
[He should subsist on] cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass.
A fast for one night is recorded as the *sāṃtapana* penance. (Manu 11.212c) For three periods of three days, he should eat only a single morsel at each meal, as previously described.
A twice-born man performing the *atikṛcchra* penance should fast for the final three days. (Manu 11.213)
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air,
each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed.
For one who is self-controlled and vigilant, fasting for twelve days constitutes the [same].

This penance called *parāka* is the remover of all sins. One should decrease the food-ball (*piṇḍa*) by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight; performing ablutions at the three sessions of the day, this is known as the *cāndrāyaṇa*.

One should observe this entire rule in the Yavamadhya (barley-shaped) Cāndrāyaṇa: performing the Cāndrāyaṇa vow with self-restraint, beginning from the bright fortnight. When midday has arrived, one should eat eight mouthfuls of food.
With self-restraint and subsisting on sacrificial food,
one performing the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* should eat four mouthfuls in the morning with a concentrated mind,
and four when the sun has set; this is known as the *śiśucāndrāyaṇa*.

By eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) with a concentrated mind for three times eighty piṇḍas in a month, in whatever manner possible, one attains the same world as the Moon. The Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Vasus likewise observed this vow.

For the sake of liberation from all that is unwholesome, one should personally perform a fire-oblation every day with the *mahāvyāhṛtis* and the *marut* mantras, accompanied by the great seers. One should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness.
Three times during the day and three times during the night, he should enter the water with his clothes on.
He should never speak with women, Śūdras, or outcasts. He should pass his time standing or sitting, or, if unable to do so, lie down upon the ground.
He should be a student of sacred knowledge and observe his vows, worshipping his guru, the gods, and the twice-born.
He should daily recite the Sāvitrī and purificatory mantras according to his ability.
In all such vows, he should be diligent for the sake of expiation. By these vows, the twice-born whose sins have been made public are purified.
But one whose sin has not been made public should purify himself through mantras and burnt offerings (homa).
By confession, by remorse, by austerity, and by Vedic study,
as well as by giving gifts in times of distress, the doer of evil is released from that evil.
To the extent that a man, having himself committed an unrighteous act, confesses it,
to that same extent he is freed from that unrighteousness, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
To the extent that his mind censures the evil deed, [to that extent is he purified].
In that same measure, the body is liberated from that unrighteousness.
For having committed a sin, one is indeed released from that sin by means of remorse;
however, he is purified by desisting with the thought, "I shall not do this again."

Having thus reflected in his mind upon the emergence of the fruits of action after death, he should constantly perform auspicious deeds with his mind, speech, and body. If, whether through ignorance or knowledge, one has committed a censurable act, [one must atone for it].
Therefore, one seeking liberation should not perform a second [penance] for the same offense. In whatever action he has committed, if there should be a lack of lightness in his mind,
he should perform penance for it until it becomes a source of satisfaction.
All this happiness, whether pertaining to gods or humans, has austerity as its root;
it is declared by the wise who perceive the Veda that austerity is its middle and austerity its end.
For a Brāhmaṇa, austerity is knowledge; for a Kṣatriya, austerity is protection.
For the Vaiśya, however, austerity consists of his livelihood [through trade and agriculture]; for the Śūdra, austerity is service.
The sages, with self-restrained minds and subsisting on fruits, roots, and air, perceive the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, through austerity alone.

Medicines, antidotes, knowledge, and the various states of the divine—all these are accomplished through austerity alone; for austerity is their means of attainment. Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to obtain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to perform—[all are achieved by austerity].

Everything, however, is to be accomplished through austerity (*tapas*), for austerity is indeed difficult to surpass. Even those who have committed great sins (*mahāpātakin*) and others who have performed forbidden acts are liberated from that guilt by means of well-performed austerity alone.
Insects, snakes, moths, beasts, birds,
and even immobile beings go to heaven by the power of austerity. Whatever sin people commit through mind, speech, or body— [or through mind, speech, and action]— [they are purified by it].
Those whose wealth is austerity quickly burn away all that [evil] through austerity alone. For a Brāhmaṇa purified by austerity alone,
the dwellers of heaven accept his offerings and increase his desires.
The Lord Prajāpati created this treatise through austerity alone;
likewise, the seers attained the Vedas through austerity. Thus, the gods proclaim the great power of austerity—that which is this very austerity.
Beholding the supreme merit arising from all this austerity,
[Manu says]: The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability, the performance of great sacrifices,
and forbearance quickly destroy even those sins born of mortal transgressions.
Just as fire, having reached fuel, consumes it instantly with its brilliance,
so does the knower of the Veda burn away all evil with the fire of knowledge. Thus has the expiation for these sins been declared according to the rule.
Henceforth, learn the penance for secret sins.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava,
performed day after day, purify even the slayer of a learned Brāhmaṇa within a month.
By muttering the *Kautsa* hymn beginning with "apaḥ," the *Vasiṣṭha* hymn beginning with "prati," the *Māhitraka*,
and the *Śuddhavatī* verses, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified.
By muttering once the *Āsyavāmīya* and the *Śivasamkalpa*, he likewise attains purification.

But having stolen gold, one becomes stainless in an instant by reciting the *Haviṣpāntīya* and the verse beginning with "na tamaṃ ha. By muttering the *Puruṣasūkta*, one who has violated the teacher's bed is released from sin.
Desiring to remove the weight of sins, whether gross or subtle,
one should recite for a year the verse beginning with "ava" or the verse beginning with "yat kiṃ ca idam.
This applies after having accepted what should not be accepted or having eaten food that is censured.

A man who recites the *Taratsamandīya* hymn is purified in three days. However, one who has committed many sins becomes pure by performing the *Somāraudra* rite for a month, while practicing the ritual bath in a flowing river and reciting the triplet beginning with the verse to Aryaman.
One who has committed these seven offenses should mutter the "Indra" hymn for half a year;

but having performed a censurable act, he should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water. A twice-born man, having offered clarified butter with the *śākala* oblation mantras for a year, [is purified].
By reciting the verse beginning with "namaḥ," one destroys even very grave sin. One who is tainted by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by practicing the Pāvamānī hymns for a year and subsisting on alms, he becomes purified.

Or, having purified himself by three *parāka* penances, he is released from all sins by reciting the Veda-saṃhitā three times in the forest while remaining self-restrained. Alternatively, being disciplined, he should fast for three days, bathing three times a day in water.
By reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* three times, one is released from all sins.
Just as the Aśvamedha, the king of sacrifices, is the remover of all sins,
so too is the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn the remover of all sins.
Even if he has destroyed these three worlds and eats food from anywhere at all,
a Brahmin who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever. Likewise,
one who is composed may recite the Ṛk-saṃhitā or the Yajus formulas three times.
Or, by [studying] the Sāmans together with their secret doctrines (rahasya), one is liberated from all sins.
Just as a clod of earth thrown into a great lake is dissolved,
so does every evil deed sink away when immersed in the threefold Veda.

The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and various other Sāman-chants—this is to be known as the threefold Veda; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda. That which is the primordial three-syllabled Brahman, in which the triple Veda is established.
That other threefold Veda is secret; he who knows it is a knower of the Veda.
O sinless one, this entire dharma of the four castes has been declared by you.
Having truly explained the supreme accomplishment of the fruits of actions,
that righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, spoke to those great seers:
"Hear the definitive conclusion regarding this entire application of action."
Action, arising from mind, speech, and body, bears fruit that is auspicious or inauspicious.
The destinies of men—whether superior, inferior, or middling—are born of action. Of this embodied being, who possesses these three types of action and three bases, [the results follow hereafter].
One should know that for one endowed with the ten characteristics, the mind is the instigator.
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable in the mind,
and adherence to falsehood— this threefold action is mental.
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form,

and incoherent prattle— this constitutes the fourfold nature of verbal misconduct. Taking what is not given and violence contrary to the prescribed rules [constitute the two forms of physical misconduct].

And the pursuit of another's wife is recorded as the threefold bodily [evil]. This person experiences the good and evil results of mental action by means of the mind alone, that of vocal action by means of speech, and that of bodily action by means of the body alone.
Through defects of action arising from the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, to the state of a bird or a beast; and through those of the mind, to the status of a low-born caste.
Furthermore, there is the restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of the body.

He in whose intellect these are firmly established is called a "tridaṇḍin" (one who possesses the triple staff). Having laid down this triple staff among all living beings and having thoroughly restrained desire and anger, a man then attains perfection.
He who causes this self to act is called the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field);
but he who performs the actions is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self) by the wise.
There is another internal self, co-natal with all embodied beings, known as the *jīva*.
That by which one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout births—
both of these, the Great One (Mahat) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), joined with the elements,
remain pervading that [body] as it exists within high and low beings.
Innumerable forms issue forth from his body,
which constantly set in motion various beings, high and low. After death, for men who have committed evil deeds, [these forms arise] from the very five elements alone.
Another body, certainly destined for torment,
arises. Having experienced those torments of Yama with that body here [in this world],
they dissolve, part by part, back into those very same elemental constituents.
Having experienced the evils arising from attachment to sense objects, which result in future misery,
he— freed from defilement— approaches those two [parents] who possess great luster.
Alertly together, they both behold his merit and his sin.
Through these two, being joined with them, one obtains happiness or unhappiness both after death and in this world.
If he practices dharma for the most part and adharma only to a small degree— just as he acts— he,
enveloped by those very elements, enjoys happiness in heaven.

But if one mostly practices unrighteousness and only a little righteousness, abandoned by those elements, he undergoes the torments of Yama. Having undergone those torments of Yama, that living being becomes free from stain.

He returns again to those very five elements, part by part. Having observed with his own mind these destinies of this living being— resulting from both righteousness and unrighteousness— one should always fix the mind upon righteousness.
One should know that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the self (*ātman*),
by which the Great One (*mahat*) remains pervading all these states without exception. Whenever one of these qualities predominates entirely within the body, [it manifests its specific effects].
At that time, he makes that embodied being consist predominantly of those qualities.
Sattva is knowledge, tamas is ignorance, and passion (rajas) is known as attachment and aversion.
This pervasive form of these [qualities] is the substratum of all beings.
In that regard, whatever one perceives within oneself as conjoined with pleasure,
tranquil and possessing a pure luster— that one should understand to be *sattva*.
But that which is conjoined with pain and is disagreeable to the self—
One should know that *rajas* is constantly attractive to embodied beings and acts as their adversary.
But that which is joined with delusion (*moha*), unmanifest, consisting of sense objects,
inconceivable, and unknowable— one should understand that to be *tamas*.
I shall now explain in its entirety the arising of the fruits of these three qualities—whether superior, middling, or inferior. [These are:
the study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, and restraint of the senses.
The performance of righteous acts and contemplation of the Self are the characteristics of the quality of *sattva*.
Delight in undertaking [worldly] activities, lack of fortitude, devotion to ignoble deeds,
and constant indulgence in sensual objects are the characteristics of the quality of *rajas*.
Greed, excessive sleep, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism, deviation from right conduct,
a habit of begging, and negligence— these are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas).
Furthermore, these three qualities abide within the three [states].
This should be known as a summary of the characteristics of the qualities (guṇas) in their respective order:
whatever action a person feels ashamed to have done, to be doing, or to be about to do—
that should be known by the wise as having all the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas).
That action by which one desires abundant fame in this world,
and does not grieve when it fails to be achieved— that should be known as *rājasa*.
That which one desires to know through every means, and of which one feels no shame while practicing— [that is *tāmasa*].
That by which his soul is satisfied is the characteristic of the quality of *sattva*.
Desire is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while wealth is said to be that of *rajas*;
righteousness (*dharma*) is the characteristic of *sattva*. Among these, superiority increases in the order mentioned.
By whichever quality among these they attain various transmigrations,
those I shall describe in brief, in their proper order for all of this:
those characterized by *sattva* go to the state of gods, and those characterized by *rajas* go to the state of humans.
"Animality is the constant state of those characterized by darkness (tamas); such is this threefold destiny.
This threefold destiny, moreover, is to be understood as being further divided into three types—the low, the middling, and the highest—according to the distinctions of action and knowledge."
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes along with tortoises,
domestic animals, and wild beasts constitute the lowest state of darkness (tāmasī gati).
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas [constitute the next lower state].
Lions, tigers, and boars constitute the middling state belonging to *tamas*.
Cāraṇas, Suparṇas, and hypocritical men,
as well as Rākṣasas and Piśācas, are the highest state among those belonging to *tamas*.
Jhallas, Mallas, and Naṭas, as well as men who subsist by the sword,
those addicted to gambling and drinking, and those of the lowest sort— this is the Rājasa destiny. Kings, Kṣatriyas, and the domestic priests of kings [belong to this same category].
Those who are primarily engaged in verbal disputes and combat belong to the intermediate *rājasa* state.
Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are attendants of the gods,
as well as all the Apsarases, constitute the highest state among those characterized by *rajas*.
Ascetics, renunciants, Brahmins, and the classes of celestial beings who dwell in aerial chariots;
the lunar mansions, the Daityas, and so forth—this is the first, the Sāttvika state.
Sacrificers, seers, gods, the Vedas, the luminaries, and the years [constitute the second].
The Pitṛs and the Sādhyas constitute the second *sāttvika* destination.
Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—
these the wise call the highest *sāttvika* destination.
All this has been fully set forth regarding the threefold action;
thus the entire transmigratory existence of all beings is threefold and of three kinds.
Through attachment to the senses and through the non-cultivation of dharma, [the soul wanders].

The ignorant, lowest of men, pass through sinful transmigrations. Learn now, in their entirety and in due order, all the wombs into which this living soul enters in this world by virtue of its various actions.
Having endured terrible hells for many series of years, upon their exhaustion,
those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) enter these transmigrations:
[the wombs] of dogs, pigs, donkeys, camels, cows, goats, sheep, deer, and birds.
A slayer of a Brāhmaṇa enters the womb of a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa (Manu 12.55c). A Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor shall go among worms, insects, moths, venomous creatures, birds,
and predatory beasts (Manu 12.56).

A Brahmin who steals [the property of others] becomes, by the thousands, a spider, a snake, a lizard, or other water-dwelling animals, as well as predatory beasts and Piśācas. He also becomes grass, shrubs, creepers, and even carnivorous fanged creatures.

And those who commit cruel deeds, as well as those who violate the teacher’s bed, become carnivorous beasts by the hundreds. The violent become eaters of raw flesh, and those who consume impure things become worms.
Thieves who have intercourse with women of the lowest castes become devourers of one another after death.
Having entered into association with outcasts, having approached the wife of another,
and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahmarākṣasa. Having stolen gems, pearls, and corals through greed, a man [becomes a Brahmarākṣasa].

And various kinds of gems are born among those who work with gold. By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; by stealing water, a water-fowl; by stealing honey, a gadfly; by stealing milk, a crow; by stealing juice, a dog; and by stealing ghee, a mongoose.
Having stolen meat, one becomes a vulture; fat, a water-fowl; oil, the *tailapaka* bird;
salt, a cricket; and curd, a crane.
Having stolen silk, one becomes a partridge; but having stolen linen, a frog.
A crane [destroys] cotton and woven cloth; a monitor lizard, a cow; a vāgguda, molasses;
a muskrat, fragrant substances; and a peacock, leafy vegetables. A porcupine [destroys] various kinds of prepared food, while a scaly ant-eater destroys unprepared food.
By stealing fire, one becomes a crane; by stealing household utensils, a *gṛhakārī* (house-builder bird);
by stealing dyed garments, one is born as a *jīvajīvaka* (a pheasant).
By stealing deer or elephants, one becomes a wolf; by stealing horses, a tiger; and by stealing fruits or roots, a monkey.
A man who forcibly seizes any property whatsoever belonging to another becomes inevitably an animal: a bear for taking a woman, a cuckoo for water, a camel for vehicles, and a goat for cattle;
likewise, he becomes an animal for eating sacrificial oblations that have not been offered.
Women also, by stealing according to this same rule, incur guilt;

they become wives of those very creatures [from whom they stole]. For when the social classes (varṇas) fall away from their respective duties in times of non-distress, they indeed incur such consequences.
Having wandered through sinful transmigrations, they fall into servitude among their enemies or among bandits.
A Brahmin who has fallen away from his own duty becomes a *vāntāśy* (vomit-eater) or a *ulkāmukha* (fire-mouthed) *preta*;
a Kṣatriya becomes a *kaṭapūtana* who feeds on impurities and corpses.
A Vaiśya who has fallen from his own duty becomes a *preta* named Maitrākṣajyotika, feeding on pus; and a Śūdra, having fallen from his own dharma, becomes a *cailāśaka*.
To the extent that those whose nature is centered on sense objects indulge in those objects, [so does their degradation increase].

In that very way, proficiency in those respective acts arises for them. Through the repeated practice of those sinful deeds, those of small intellect encounter sufferings in various wombs here in this world.
The tossing about in the fierce hells such as Tāmisra and others;
the forests of sword-leaves and the like, along with bondage and mutilation;
various forms of torment, and being devoured by crows and owls.
The heat of parched sand and gravel, and the dreadful torments of being boiled in jars; constant births in low wombs characterized by a preponderance of suffering;
the assaults of cold and sun, and various kinds of terrors.
Repeated dwelling within the wombs and dreadful births,
as well as various forms of bondage, servitude to others,
separation from kinsmen and loved ones, and living together with the wicked.
The acquisition of wealth and its loss, the gaining of friends and enemies,
old age for which there is no remedy, the affliction caused by diseases,
various kinds of sufferings, and death itself, which is difficult to overcome— [all these he considers].
With whatever disposition one performs each particular action,
with such a body one experiences that respective fruit.
Thus has been fully declared to you the arising of the fruits of actions.
Learn now this action which brings about the supreme good for a Brahmin:
(Manu 12.82c). The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, restraint of the senses, non-violence, and service to the guru—this is the highest means for attaining the supreme good. (Manu 12.83).
Among all these auspicious actions prescribed here for a person, some are said to be more conducive to the highest good than others. Yet,
among all of these, the knowledge of the Self is traditionally held to be supreme.
For that is the foremost of all branches of knowledge, since immortality is attained through it.
Among all these six types of actions, both here and after death,
one should know that the Vedic rite is always the most conducive to the highest good.
But in the Vedic application of ritual action, all these [duties] without exception are included,
respectively, within each specific rule of performance.
[This applies to] both that which leads to worldly happiness and prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and that which leads to the supreme good (*naiḥśreyasa*).
Vedic action is twofold: active (*pravṛtta*) and withdrawn (*nivṛtta*). Action performed for the sake of desire, whether for this world or the next, is proclaimed as active.
But that which is free from desire and preceded by knowledge is taught as withdrawn.
By practicing *pravṛtta* (active) action, one attains equality with the gods;
but by practicing *nivṛtta* (withdrawn) action, one indeed transcends the five elements.
And [he sees] the Self in all beings, and all beings in the Self.
Beholding all things as equal, the one who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty.
Even having abandoned the ritual acts prescribed [for him], the best of the twice-born should be diligent in the knowledge of the Self, in equanimity, and in the study of the Veda.
For this indeed is the fulfillment of the purpose of birth, especially for a Brāhmaṇa;
having attained this, the twice-born becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done, and not otherwise.
The Veda is the eternal eye of the ancestors, the gods, and human beings.
"The scripture of the Veda is impossible to master and immeasurable; such is the established rule.

(Manu 12.94c) "Those Smṛtis which are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—(Manu 12.95a) all of them are fruitless after death, for they are declared to be rooted in darkness. (Manu 12.95c)

Whatever other things there may be that arise from this [system] and then pass away, they perish because they are of recent origin; they are fruitless and false. The four castes, the three worlds, and the four distinct stages of life—
The past, the present, and the future— all are established through the Veda.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—
these are produced from the Veda alone, arising from the qualities and their functions.
The eternal scripture of the Veda sustains all living beings;
therefore, I consider this to be the supreme means for the accomplishment of this creature’s purpose.
Generalship, kingship, and the office of the wielder of the rod of punishment likewise depend upon it.
One who knows the Vedic scriptures deserves sovereignty over all the worlds. Just as a fire that has gained strength consumes even moist trees,
so does the knower of the Vedas burn away the defects born of his own past actions.

One who knows the true meaning of the principles of the Veda and the Shastras, dwelling in whatever stage of life he may be, is fit for becoming Brahman even while remaining in this very world. (Manu 12.102) Those who have mastered the texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them in memory are better than those who merely possess the texts. (Manu 12.103)
Among those who merely uphold the sacred law, the men of knowledge are superior; among the men of knowledge, those who possess resolute application are superior.
For a Brahmin, austerity and learning are the supreme means to the highest good:
through austerity one destroys sin, and through learning one attains immortality.
Perception, inference, and the scripture consisting of various traditions—
these three must be well understood by one who desires purity in dharma.
And [one should follow] the instruction on dharma given by the sages, provided it does not contradict the Vedic scriptures.
He who investigates with reasoning knows the Dharma, and no other. This action leading to the supreme good has been declared in its entirety as it was ordained;
now the secret of this Institutes of Manu is being taught.
If it should be asked, "How should it be in the case of duties not mentioned in the traditional scriptures?"—
whatever learned Brāhmaṇas may declare, that shall be the unerring Dharma.
But those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been mastered according to the Law...

Those Brahmins who have direct perception of the Śruti as their authority should be known as the learned (śiṣṭas). An assembly of at least ten, or even three, who are established in virtuous conduct, shall determine the Dharma; that Dharma they determine shall not be disturbed.
One who is learned in the three Vedas, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, and a reciter of the Dharma;

and the three [members] belonging to the first stages of life—such an assembly shall consist of at least ten members. One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Sāmaveda.

A council of at least three persons is to be known as the authority for resolving doubts regarding the Dharma. Even a single eminent twice-born man who knows the Veda, whatever Dharma he determines, should be known as the supreme Dharma; it is not superseded by tens of thousands of ignorant men.

Among those who observe no vows, who know no sacred mantras, and who subsist merely by their caste— even if they assemble in thousands— no assembly (*pariṣat*) exists. That which ignorant fools, being shrouded in darkness and ignorant of Dharma, proclaim as Dharma...
That sin, having become a hundredfold, follows after those who speak it.
All this, which brings about the supreme good, has been declared to you;
a Brahmin who does not fall away from this attains the highest goal.
Thus that Blessed Lord, desiring the welfare of the worlds,
has declared to me this entire supreme secret of Dharma:
"One who is composed should perceive everything— both the existent and the non-existent— within the Self."
For seeing everything within himself, he does not direct his mind toward unrighteousness.
The self alone is all the deities; everything is established in the self.
For the self produces the connection with action for these embodied beings.
One should place space within the cavities, wind within movement and touch,
the supreme fire within digestion and sight, water within moisture, and earth within solid forms.
One should place the Moon in the mind, the Quarters in hearing, Viṣṇu in movement, and Hara in strength.

One should know that supreme Person as Agni when he is being uttered, as Mitra at the time of emission, and as Prajāpati during procreation; he is the ruler of all, subtler than the subtlest, radiant like gold, and accessible through the intellect in deep sleep.
Some call him Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati;
some Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman.
He pervades all beings with his five forms.
It perpetually causes [beings] to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay. Thus, he who perceives the Self within all beings by means of his own self,
having attained equanimity toward all, reaches Brahman, the supreme state.
A twice-born man who recites this treatise of Manu, proclaimed by Bhṛgu,
becomes eternally possessed of right conduct and shall attain his desired goal. [The Treatise on Dharma of Manu is completed.]
